lessons.briefing:
# V3·B1 — Reading EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE

Sector 30 taught you to name the nodes. That is table stakes. What
separates someone who *reads* plans from someone who *recognises* them is
arithmetic: knowing that a node's `actual time` includes its children, that
it is reported per loop, that in a parallel plan the row counts are
per-worker averages, and that the number you should trust is almost never
the one printed at the top.

This sector builds the schema the rest of Volume 3 runs on, then spends ten
missions turning plan output into numbers you can defend in a review.

## The `perf` schema

Everything in V3·B is built on four tables. Create them once in the lab
(`uv run dojo lab v3b01_plan_reading`) and leave them; later sectors add
indexes to them but never change the shape.

```sql
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS perf;

CREATE TABLE perf.customers (
  id          bigint PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id   int         NOT NULL,
  email       text        NOT NULL,
  country     char(2)     NOT NULL,
  plan        text        NOT NULL,   -- free | pro | enterprise
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE perf.orders (
  id           bigint PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id  bigint      NOT NULL,
  tenant_id    int         NOT NULL,
  status       text        NOT NULL,  -- pending|paid|shipped|refunded|cancelled
  channel      text        NOT NULL,  -- web | ios | android | partner
  placed_at    timestamptz NOT NULL,
  total_cents  bigint      NOT NULL,
  ship_country char(2)     NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE perf.order_lines (
  id         bigint PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id   bigint NOT NULL,
  sku        text   NOT NULL,
  qty        int    NOT NULL,
  unit_cents bigint NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE perf.events (
  id          bigint PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id    bigint      NOT NULL,
  tenant_id   int         NOT NULL,
  kind        text        NOT NULL,
  occurred_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
  payload     jsonb       NOT NULL
);
```

Seed it deterministically — every mission in V3·B assumes these row counts
(200k customers, 2M orders, 6M lines, 5M events):

```sql
INSERT INTO perf.customers
SELECT g,
       1 + (g % 40),
       'user' || g || '@example.com',
       (ARRAY['US','GB','DE','FR','BR','JP','IN','CA'])[1 + (g % 8)],
       CASE WHEN g % 100 < 88 THEN 'free'
            WHEN g % 100 < 99 THEN 'pro' ELSE 'enterprise' END,
       timestamptz '2021-01-01' + (g % 1500) * interval '1 day'
FROM generate_series(1, 200000) g;

INSERT INTO perf.orders
SELECT g,
       1 + (g * 7919 % 200000),
       1 + (g % 40),
       CASE WHEN g % 1000 < 4   THEN 'pending'
            WHEN g % 1000 < 24  THEN 'refunded'
            WHEN g % 1000 < 44  THEN 'cancelled'
            WHEN g % 1000 < 700 THEN 'paid' ELSE 'shipped' END,
       (ARRAY['web','ios','android','partner'])[1 + (g % 4)],
       timestamptz '2023-01-01' + (g % 900) * interval '1 day'
                                + (g % 86400) * interval '1 second',
       500 + (g * 37 % 250000),
       (ARRAY['US','GB','DE','FR','BR','JP','IN','CA'])[1 + (g % 8)]
FROM generate_series(1, 2000000) g;
```

`order_lines` and `events` follow the same pattern; the lab file
`v3b_seed.sql` has all four. Then, and this matters more than anything else
you will do today:

```sql
VACUUM ANALYZE perf.customers, perf.orders, perf.order_lines, perf.events;
```

An unanalysed table gives you plans chosen from default guesses, and every
conclusion you draw from them is fiction.

## The five numbers

Take one node line:

```
->  Index Scan using orders_placed_at_idx on orders  (cost=0.43..8241.10
      rows=2600 width=61) (actual time=0.031..4.812 rows=2418 loops=3)
```

- `cost=0.43..8241.10` — startup cost, then total cost, in planner units
  where `seq_page_cost = 1.0` by definition. Startup cost is what must
  happen before the *first* row can be emitted; it is why a `LIMIT 1` on
  top of a `Sort` is expensive and a `LIMIT 1` on top of an `Index Scan` is
  free.
- `rows=2600` — the estimate. `actual ... rows=2418` — the truth.
- `actual time=0.031..4.812` — time to first row, then time to last row,
  **inclusive of every child node**, and **per loop**.
- `loops=3` — this node ran three times. Total work here is roughly
  `3 × 4.812 ms`, and the true row count is `3 × 2418`.

Two derived numbers do most of the diagnostic work:

**Exclusive time** = `(total time × loops)` minus the same product for every
child. A parent showing 900 ms whose child shows 890 ms is innocent; the
child is the suspect. Plan visualisers exist entirely to compute this column
for you, and you should be able to do it by hand for a five-node plan.

**Estimate ratio** = `actual rows ÷ estimated rows`, per node, walking
upward. The interesting node is the *lowest* one where the ratio leaves the
1/10..10 band. Above it, every bad choice is downstream of a lie, and
"fix the join" is the wrong instinct — fix the estimate (V3·B6).

## Options worth typing every time

```sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, SETTINGS) SELECT ...;
```

`BUFFERS` reports 8 KB pages: `shared hit` (found in shared_buffers),
`shared read` (not found — came from OS cache or disk), `dirtied`,
`written`, and `temp read/written` (sort or hash spill). Buffer counts are
stable across runs where timings are not, which makes them the honest metric
when you compare two plans on a laptop with a busy fan. `SETTINGS` prints
any planner GUC that is not at its default, which is how you discover the
previous engineer left `enable_nestloop = off` in the session pooler.

When you are timing a plan rather than reading it, add `TIMING OFF`:
per-node `gettimeofday()` calls can inflate a short plan's execution time by
30% or more, and the total under `SUMMARY ON` is then the number to compare.

## Mission set

Ten missions. You will compute exclusive time by hand, multiply loops,
un-average a parallel plan's per-worker rows, convert buffers to megabytes,
catch a sort spilling to disk, run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on a `DELETE` without
losing rows, and finish by parsing `FORMAT JSON` plans with the `jsonb`
operators from sector 19 to produce a ranked list of guilty nodes.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b01_plan_reading`

# Reading - sql/v3b01_plan_reading

Plan reading is arithmetic performed on a tree. The nodes tell you what
happened; only the arithmetic tells you where the time went.

## Notes

**Cost units are not milliseconds and never were.** A cost of 8241.10 means
"as expensive as reading 8241 sequential pages", because `seq_page_cost` is
pinned at 1.0 and everything else is calibrated against it:
`random_page_cost` 4.0, `cpu_tuple_cost` 0.01, `cpu_index_tuple_cost` 0.005,
`cpu_operator_cost` 0.0025. Comparing costs between two plans of the *same*
query is meaningful. Comparing a cost to a wall-clock number is not. On SSDs
the 4:1 random-to-sequential ratio is roughly a decade out of date, which is
why lowering `random_page_cost` to 1.1–2.0 is the single most common
planner-tuning change in the wild — it makes index scans look as cheap as
they actually are.

**Startup cost is a separate decision axis.** `cost=0.43..8241.10` says the
first row is nearly free. A `Sort` or a `Hash` node has a startup cost equal
to its total: nothing comes out until everything went in. When a `LIMIT`
sits on top, the planner scales the total cost by the fraction of rows
requested — but only for nodes that can stop early. This is why adding
`LIMIT 10` sometimes flips a plan to a much worse index scan: the planner
assumes it will find ten matching rows quickly, and if the matching rows all
live at the far end of the index, it will not.

**`actual time` is inclusive and per loop.** Both facts bite. Inclusive
means the top node always shows the largest number and is almost never the
problem. Per loop means `actual time=0.048..0.052 rows=1 loops=180000` is
9.4 seconds of work, printed as fifty microseconds. Exclusive time is
`(t_last × loops) − Σ(children's t_last × their loops)`; rank nodes by that
and the guilty one is at the top of the list roughly every time.

**Estimated rows are also per loop; actual rows are per loop.** So a
`rows=1` estimate against `rows=1 loops=180000` is not a misestimate at all
— the planner expected one row per invocation and got one. The misestimate,
if any, lives on the *outer* side that produced 180,000 loops.

**Parallel plans average.** Under a `Gather`, each node reports rows and
time averaged over the participating processes — workers plus the leader if
it participated. `Workers Planned: 4` with `Workers Launched: 2` means the
`max_parallel_workers` pool was exhausted and you measured a different
machine than you thought. Multiply a parallel node's `rows` by `loops` to
recover the total, and read `Workers Launched` before believing any
comparison.

**Filters have three different names, and they mean different things.**
`Rows Removed by Filter` under a scan is heap tuples fetched and discarded —
the classic missing-index signature. `Rows Removed by Index Recheck` under a
`Bitmap Heap Scan` means the bitmap went lossy (`work_mem` too small to hold
one bit per row, so it degraded to one bit per page). `Rows Removed by Join
Filter` means a join condition that could not become a hash or merge key was
evaluated per candidate pair.

**`Heap Fetches` is the honesty check on `Index Only Scan`.** A non-zero
value means the visibility map said "not all-visible" for those pages and
the executor had to visit the heap anyway. A freshly written table shows an
index-only scan with heap fetches equal to the row count, which performs
exactly like a plain index scan. `VACUUM` is what fixes it (V3·B8).

**`(never executed)`** on a subplan means the executor short-circuited — an
outer side produced zero rows, or a `LIMIT` was satisfied first. It is not
an error, and it means that branch's cost estimates were never tested.

**Two timing lines at the bottom.** `Planning Time` and `Execution Time`.
A 400 ms planning time on a 2 ms query is real and happens with wide
partitioned tables or dozens of joins; the fix is fewer partitions,
`plan_cache_mode`, or a prepared statement, not an index. `JIT:` blocks
appear when total cost exceeds `jit_above_cost` (default 100000) and can add
100+ ms of compile time to a query that then runs in 20 ms — check the JIT
timings before blaming the plan.

**`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` executes.** `EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE FROM ...` deletes.
Wrap it: `BEGIN; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) DELETE ...; ROLLBACK;`. The plan
also then reports `Trigger` timings per trigger and, with `WAL`, the WAL
bytes the statement generated — the only easy way to see that a foreign-key
trigger, not the delete, is the cost.

## Mission notes

**ex1–ex2** are pure arithmetic: exclusive time, then loops multiplication.
Do them on paper before you believe the tool.

**ex3** contrasts `TIMING ON` and `TIMING OFF` totals on the same query.
The gap is the instrument's own weight, and on short plans with millions of
node invocations it is not small.

**ex4** asks for the *lowest* misestimating node, not the worst ratio. Those
differ, and the lowest one is the cause.

**ex5–ex6** convert buffers to bytes and un-average a parallel plan.

**ex7** makes a sort spill and then fixes it with `work_mem`, which is the
first time in this volume you tune something that is not an index.

**ex8** and the challenge move to `EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON)`, where the plan
becomes a `jsonb` document you can query with sector 19's operators — the
technique behind every plan-analysis tool you have used.

**`auto_explain` is how you read plans you cannot reproduce.** Set
`auto_explain.log_min_duration = '200ms'` plus `log_analyze`,
`log_buffers`, and `log_nested_statements`, and the server logs the real
plan of the real slow execution with the real parameter values. Every
"it is fast when I test it" argument dies here. The overhead of
`log_analyze` is the same instrumentation cost `TIMING OFF` removes, so pair
it with `auto_explain.log_timing = off` on a busy system.

**Generic plans are the other reason your reproduction differs.** A prepared
statement or PL/pgSQL query replans five times with the actual parameters,
then may switch to a parameter-independent generic plan and keep it. The
plan you get from a pasted literal in psql is a custom plan. `EXPLAIN
(GENERIC_PLAN)` on a query containing `$1` placeholders shows you the other
one, without executing anything.

## Further reading

- [Using EXPLAIN](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/using-explain.html)
  — the manual's best chapter; read the cost arithmetic section slowly.
- [EXPLAIN reference](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-explain.html)
  — every option, including `WAL`, `SETTINGS`, `GENERIC_PLAN`, `MEMORY`.
- [Planner cost constants](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-query.html)
  — what `random_page_cost` and friends actually multiply.
- [auto_explain](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/auto-explain.html)
  — production plan capture with the knobs that keep it cheap.
- [explain.dalibo.com](https://explain.dalibo.com/) — paste a `FORMAT JSON`
  plan; it computes the exclusive-time and estimate-ratio columns you
  compute by hand in ex1 and ex4.

## Worked example — finding the guilty node

```
Aggregate  (cost=..) (actual time=1841.2..1841.2 rows=1 loops=1)
  ->  Nested Loop  (cost=..) (actual time=0.09..1837.4 rows=41922 loops=1)
        ->  Seq Scan on customers c  (actual time=0.01..21.4
              rows=17600 loops=1)
              Filter: (plan = 'pro')
              Rows Removed by Filter: 182400
        ->  Index Scan using orders_customer_id_idx on orders o
              (actual time=0.09..0.10 rows=2 loops=17600)
              Index Cond: (customer_id = c.id)
```

Exclusive time, computed bottom-up:

- Index Scan: `0.10 × 17600 = 1760 ms`. No children. Exclusive: **1760 ms**.
- Seq Scan: `21.4 × 1 = 21.4 ms`. Exclusive: **21.4 ms**.
- Nested Loop: `1837.4 − 1760 − 21.4 = 56 ms` of its own.
- Aggregate: `1841.2 − 1837.4 = 3.8 ms`.

95% of the query is an index scan that individually takes a tenth of a
millisecond. Nothing in this plan is "slow"; the plan is slow because it
does a fast thing 17,600 times. The fix is not a better index on `orders` —
it is a `Hash Join`, which the planner will choose on its own once it
believes 17,600 outer rows (V3·B5, V3·B6).

## Worked example — buffers tell a different story than time

```
Seq Scan on orders  (actual time=0.02..612.9 rows=2000000 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=19824 read=1176
```

21,000 pages × 8 KB = 164 MB touched, 94% of it already in
`shared_buffers`. Run the same query on a cold cache and the wall time
triples while the buffer counts stay identical. When you compare "before"
and "after" on a developer laptop, compare buffers; when you report to
someone paying for IOPS, `read` is the number that costs money.

## Common mistakes

- **Reading the top node's time as the problem.** It is inclusive. The top
  node is a summary, not a suspect.
- **Forgetting `loops`.** The single most common misreading in code review.
- **Comparing costs across different queries.** Costs are only comparable
  between candidate plans for one query on one set of statistics.
- **Trusting a first run.** The first execution warms the cache; the second
  is the number you should quote, and both should be stated.
- **Running `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on the write path without a transaction.**
- **Believing `rows=1` estimates on the inner side of a nested loop.** They
  are per loop and usually correct; the lie is upstream.
- **Ignoring `Planning Time` and the `JIT` block.** On short queries either
  can dominate execution.
- **Testing with a literal when production sends a parameter.** Custom plan
  versus generic plan; `EXPLAIN (GENERIC_PLAN)` settles it.

## Interview angle

*"You are handed a 40-node `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` and told the query takes eight
seconds. What do you do first?"*

Answer in this order and you sound like someone who has done it: compute
exclusive time per node and rank; take the top one or two nodes; on those,
compare estimated to actual rows and walk *down* to the lowest node where
the ratio breaks; classify that node as (a) missing index — look at `Rows
Removed by Filter`, (b) bad estimate — look for a correlated predicate or
stale statistics, or (c) wrong algorithm caused by (b). Then say what you
would measure to confirm, which is buffers, not time. Mentioning
`Workers Launched` and `Heap Fetches` unprompted is what separates
candidates.

## Check yourself

1. A node shows `actual time=0.4..0.9 rows=3 loops=52000`. How much wall
   time did it contribute, and how many rows did it really emit?
2. What is the difference between `Rows Removed by Filter` and `Rows
   Removed by Index Recheck`?
3. Why is comparing `cost=` values between two different queries
   meaningless?
4. `Workers Planned: 4`, `Workers Launched: 0`. What happened, and what does
   it do to your benchmark?
5. Your plan has `Heap Fetches: 1994312` on an `Index Only Scan`. What is
   the fix?
6. Which `EXPLAIN` option makes timings comparable on a noisy machine, and
   why?
7. When does `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` change the database, and how do you prevent
   it?
8. `Planning Time: 380 ms`, `Execution Time: 2.1 ms`. Name two plausible
   causes.
9. A `Sort` node prints `Sort Method: external merge Disk: 88400kB`. What is
   the knob, and what is the risk of turning it up globally?
10. What does `(never executed)` tell you about that subtree's cost
    estimate?
11. Why does adding `LIMIT 10` sometimes make a query dramatically slower?
12. How do you capture the plan of a slow query you cannot reproduce
    interactively?
lessons.fullReading:
# Reading - sql/v3b01_plan_reading

## Where the numbers come from

An `EXPLAIN` plan is not a report the database writes about itself after the
fact. It is the executor's own data structure, printed. Every node in that
tree is a C struct with a `next` method; the tree is a pull pipeline, and
`ExecProcNode` on the root repeatedly asks its children for one more tuple
until they say there are none. That single detail explains most of what
confuses people about plan output.

It explains why `actual time` is inclusive: a parent's clock is running the
entire time it sits inside its child's function call. It explains why the
figures are per loop: a node inside a nested loop is re-initialised and
drained once per outer tuple, and the instrumentation code accumulates
`ntuples` and `total` across those runs, then divides by `nloops` at print
time. It explains `(never executed)`: `nloops` is zero because nobody ever
called the node, so there is nothing to divide by. And it explains why
parallel nodes average: each worker has its own `Instrumentation` struct in
shared memory, and the leader sums them and divides.

With `ANALYZE`, every tuple that crosses every node boundary triggers two
`gettimeofday()` calls. On Linux with a fast clocksource that is roughly
25–50 ns each; on a VM that fell back to `hpet` it can be a microsecond. A
plan that moves ten million tuples across five node boundaries therefore
pays somewhere between two and twenty seconds *for the measurement*. This is
the entire reason `TIMING OFF` exists: you keep row counts, buffers, and one
honest total, and you drop the per-node breakdown. Test your instrument
before you trust it: `pg_test_timing` reports your clock's per-call cost.

## What the planner actually did

The cost numbers come from a different world than the actual numbers. Before
execution, the planner enumerated access paths for each relation, then built
join orders bottom-up with dynamic programming (`GEQO`, a genetic algorithm,
takes over past `geqo_threshold` joins — twelve by default — and its results
are not deterministic, which is a fun bug report to receive). Each path
carries a startup cost, a total cost, and a row estimate. The cheapest total
cost wins unless a `LIMIT` is present, in which case the planner
interpolates between startup and total by the fraction of rows wanted.

Costs are pure arithmetic over three inputs: table statistics
(`pg_statistic`, refreshed by `ANALYZE`), physical size (`pg_class.relpages`
and `reltuples`, adjusted at plan time by the real current size), and the
cost constants. A sequential scan costs `relpages × seq_page_cost + reltuples
× cpu_tuple_cost` plus one `cpu_operator_cost` per filter clause evaluated.
An index scan costs the index pages walked at `random_page_cost` plus heap
pages fetched, discounted by `pg_stats.correlation` — the correlation
between the index's logical order and the heap's physical order — which is
why a scan over an index on an append-only timestamp column is priced far
below one on a randomly distributed UUID with the identical selectivity.

The 4:1 default ratio between `random_page_cost` and `seq_page_cost` was
calibrated on spinning rust with a seek time measured in milliseconds. On
NVMe the true ratio is closer to 1.1:1. Leaving the default in place biases
every plan in your database toward sequential scans and hash joins. Changing
it is a one-line, whole-instance change with broad consequences: do it
deliberately, measure a representative workload before and after, and never
as a reaction to a single slow query.

## History, and why the output looks like this

Postgres has printed plans since Berkeley days, but the modern shape arrived
in stages you can still see in the text. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` — actual rows and
times — landed in 7.2 (2002). `BUFFERS` arrived in 9.0, machine-readable
`FORMAT JSON|XML|YAML` in 9.0 as well, which is what made third-party
analysers possible. `Rows Removed by Filter` came in 9.4 and quietly changed
how people hunt for missing indexes. Parallel query, with its averaged rows
and `Workers Launched` line, arrived in 9.6. `SETTINGS` came in 12, `WAL` in
13, `GENERIC_PLAN` in 16, and `MEMORY` in 17. If you read a plan on an old
server and a line you expect is missing, it is usually a version story
rather than a configuration one.

The text format is a rendering, not the source of truth. `FORMAT JSON` gives
you the same tree with stable keys — `Node Type`, `Actual Total Time`,
`Actual Loops`, `Plans` for children — and because the result is a single
`jsonb` value you can query it with the operators from sector 19. A
recursive CTE over `Plans` plus a little arithmetic reproduces the exclusive
time column that every commercial tool sells you. That is the challenge in
this sector, and once you have written it you stop needing to paste customer
plans into a website.

## Performance notes

`EXPLAIN` without `ANALYZE` costs a plan, which for a wide partitioned table
can itself be hundreds of milliseconds; it does not touch data. `EXPLAIN
ANALYZE` costs a full execution plus instrumentation. Neither is free on a
production primary, and `auto_explain` with `log_analyze = on` applies that
cost to every statement over the threshold — set the threshold high, set
`log_timing = off`, and sample with `auto_explain.sample_rate` if the
instance is hot.

Buffer numbers are the only figures stable enough to put in a pull request.
`shared hit` costs CPU and a lock; `shared read` costs an I/O that may have
been served by the OS page cache — Postgres cannot tell the difference, so a
"read" is not necessarily a disk seek. `dirtied` matters for write
amplification, and `temp read/written` is the unambiguous signature of a
sort or hash that did not fit in `work_mem`.

## When not to reach for EXPLAIN

When you do not yet know which query is slow. Plan reading is a microscope,
and pointing a microscope at a random part of a system is a waste of a good
afternoon. `pg_stat_statements` — ranked by `total_exec_time`, not
`mean_exec_time` — tells you which statement to put under the lens. A query
that takes 40 ms and runs 900 times a second outranks the 6-second report
somebody runs at midnight, and only aggregate statistics can tell you that.

Also skip it when the problem is not the plan at all: lock waits
(`pg_locks`, `pg_stat_activity.wait_event`), connection churn, a client that
fetches a million rows one round trip at a time, or an ORM issuing the same
query per row. A perfect plan executed 5,000 times per page load is still a
slow page, and `EXPLAIN` will show you five thousand innocent plans.

## Reading a plan somebody pastes at you

Ask three questions before you read a line of it. Was it captured with
`ANALYZE`, or is every number a guess? Was the cache warm, and was it the
first run? Were the parameter values representative, or did they pick the
one customer with three orders? A plan captured from a generic prepared
statement against a parameter distribution it was not planned for is the
most common source of "the plan looks fine but production is on fire", and
no amount of careful arithmetic on the printed numbers will surface it —
only knowing to ask will.

## Further reading

- [Using EXPLAIN](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/using-explain.html)
  — read the cost arithmetic section slowly, twice.
- [EXPLAIN reference](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-explain.html)
  — every option, including `WAL`, `SETTINGS`, `GENERIC_PLAN`, `MEMORY`.
- [Planner cost constants](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-query.html)
  — what `random_page_cost` and friends multiply.
- [auto_explain](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/auto-explain.html)
  — capturing production plans cheaply.
- [pg_test_timing](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/pgtesttiming.html)
  — measure your clock before trusting per-node times.
- [explain.dalibo.com](https://explain.dalibo.com/) — the visualiser whose
  exclusive-time column you rebuild in this sector's challenge.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — exclusive time

A plan node's `actual time` includes its children. Rank nodes by *exclusive*
time and the guilty one surfaces immediately.

Here is a plan from `perf`, trimmed to the lines that matter:

```
Aggregate  (actual time=902.4..902.4 rows=1 loops=1)
  ->  Hash Join  (actual time=118.7..861.2 rows=402118 loops=1)
        ->  Seq Scan on orders o  (actual time=0.02..214.9
              rows=402118 loops=1)
              Filter: (status = 'refunded')
              Rows Removed by Filter: 1597882
        ->  Hash  (actual time=118.1..118.1 rows=200000 loops=1)
              ->  Seq Scan on customers c  (actual time=0.01..38.4
                    rows=200000 loops=1)
```

Edit `ex1/solution.sql` to return **one row, four columns** of exclusive
milliseconds, rounded to one decimal, in this order:

| column | node |
| --- | --- |
| `agg_ms` | `Aggregate` |
| `join_ms` | `Hash Join` |
| `scan_orders_ms` | `Seq Scan on orders` |
| `hash_side_ms` | the `Hash` node's subtree total |

Every node here has `loops=1`, so exclusive time is the node's own total
minus the totals of its direct children.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b01_plan_reading ex1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Nothing here needs multiplying — every node ran once. The only operation is
subtraction, because a parent's printed time already contains everything its
children spent.

## Hint 2

For a two-child node, exclusive is `parent_total - child_a - child_b`. A
node at 500.0 with children at 300.0 and 150.0 kept 50.0 ms for itself.

## Hint 3

`Hash Join` is `861.2 - 214.9 - 118.1`. Then decide what `hash_side_ms`
means: the `Hash` node's total already contains the customers scan, so the
subtree total is just 118.1 — no subtraction. The largest of your four
numbers should be the join.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Predict before you compute. Only one node in this plan touched two million
rows and threw 1.6 million of them away. Guess which column will be biggest,
then check whether your arithmetic agrees; when it does not, one of the two
is wrong and finding out which is the actual skill.

## Hint 2

Sanity rule: the four exclusive numbers must sum to the top node's 902.4 ms.
If yours do not, you subtracted a child twice or skipped one.

## Hint 3

`902.4 - 861.2` is the aggregate's own share and it is tiny. That is the
shape of nearly every real plan: the top node is bookkeeping, the leaves are
the work.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b01_plan_reading / ex1 — exclusive time per node
SELECT round((902.4 - 861.2)::numeric, 1)         AS agg_ms,
       round((861.2 - 214.9 - 118.1)::numeric, 1) AS join_ms,
       round((214.9)::numeric, 1)                 AS scan_orders_ms,
       round((118.1)::numeric, 1)                 AS hash_side_ms;

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — loops multiply

Per-loop figures are the most misread numbers in `EXPLAIN`. This plan looks
harmless and is not:

```
Nested Loop  (actual time=0.11..3184.6 rows=35200 loops=1)
  ->  Seq Scan on customers c  (actual time=0.01..44.2 rows=17600 loops=1)
        Filter: (plan = 'pro')
  ->  Index Scan using orders_customer_id_idx on orders o
        (actual time=0.041..0.176 rows=2 loops=17600)
        Index Cond: (customer_id = c.id)
        Buffers: shared hit=4
```

Edit `ex2/solution.sql` to return **one row, four columns**:

1. `inner_total_ms` — wall time spent inside the inner `Index Scan` across
   all loops, one decimal.
2. `inner_rows_total` — rows the inner side really emitted in total
   (integer).
3. `inner_share_pct` — that time as a percentage of the Nested Loop's
   3184.6 ms, one decimal.
4. `inner_buffers` — total 8 KB buffers the inner side touched (integer).

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b01_plan_reading ex2`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Everything printed on the inner node is an average over 17,600 executions —
the times, the rows, and the buffer line too. Undo the averaging before you
interpret any of it.

## Hint 2

`actual time=start..end`: the number you multiply is `end`, time to the
node's *last* row. So `0.176 × loops`, never `0.041 × loops`.

## Hint 3

Three multiplications and one division. Expect the inner share to land in
the high nineties, which is the lesson: an index scan taking 0.176 ms is not
slow, and this plan is still three seconds of it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Reframe as cost per customer. Each `pro` customer costs one index descent;
there are 17,600 of them. What is 17,600 descents worth, and what would a
single hash join over the same two tables have cost instead?

## Hint 2

Buffers under a nested loop are printed per loop exactly like times. Four
each, 17,600 times, is 70,400 buffer touches — roughly 550 MB of buffer
traffic to produce 35,200 rows.

## Hint 3

`0.176 * 17600` is a shade over 3.0 seconds; divide by 3184.6 and multiply
by 100 for the share. A share above 100 means you multiplied the start time
instead of the end time.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b01_plan_reading / ex2 — undoing per-loop averaging
WITH n AS (
  SELECT 0.176::numeric AS t_last, 2::numeric AS rows_per_loop,
         17600::numeric AS loops, 4::numeric AS buffers_per_loop,
         3184.6::numeric AS parent_ms)
SELECT round(t_last * loops, 1)                   AS inner_total_ms,
       (rows_per_loop * loops)::bigint            AS inner_rows_total,
       round(t_last * loops / parent_ms * 100, 1) AS inner_share_pct,
       (buffers_per_loop * loops)::bigint         AS inner_buffers
FROM n;

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — the cost of the instrument

`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` calls `gettimeofday()` around every tuple at every node
boundary. On a plan that moves a lot of tuples that instrumentation is
itself measurable — the plan you "measured" can be slower than the query you
shipped.

Run both in the lab:

```sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING ON,  SUMMARY ON)
SELECT count(*) FROM perf.order_lines WHERE qty > 1;

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY ON)
SELECT count(*) FROM perf.order_lines WHERE qty > 1;
```

On the reference machine they report `Execution Time: 1412.8 ms` and
`Execution Time: 948.3 ms`, over a plan whose scan emitted 3,982,000 rows.

Edit `ex3/solution.sql` to return **one row, three columns**:

1. `overhead_ms` — instrumentation cost, one decimal.
2. `overhead_pct` — that as a percentage of the `TIMING ON` total, one
   decimal.
3. `ns_per_tuple` — nanoseconds of instrumentation per tuple crossing the
   scan boundary, `overhead_ms × 1e6 ÷ 3982000`, rounded to a whole number.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b01_plan_reading ex3`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The difference between the two totals is not noise, it is the measuring
apparatus. Subtract once, then express that one number two other ways.

## Hint 2

Milliseconds to nanoseconds is `× 1e6`. Divide by the tuple count for a
per-tuple figure, then compare it with what `pg_test_timing` reports for a
single clock call on your hardware; the two should be within a small
multiple.

## Hint 3

Expect roughly 460 ms of overhead, about a third of the measured total, and
a per-tuple cost in the low hundreds of nanoseconds. A `ns_per_tuple` in the
thousands means you divided by the wrong row count.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Turn the question around: which of the two totals would you put in a ticket?
Neither is production latency, but one is much closer — and knowing which
one you are quoting is the actual point of the exercise.

## Hint 2

Cast explicitly. `round(x, 1)` only exists for `numeric`; on `double
precision` you get "function round(double precision, integer) does not
exist", which is the most common error in this whole sector.

## Hint 3

`1412.8 - 948.3 = 464.5`. Divide by 1412.8 for the share; multiply by 1e6
and divide by 3982000 for the per-tuple cost, then `round(...)::bigint`.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b01_plan_reading / ex3 — instrumentation overhead
WITH m AS (
  SELECT 1412.8::numeric AS timed_ms, 948.3::numeric AS untimed_ms,
         3982000::numeric AS tuples)
SELECT round(timed_ms - untimed_ms, 1)                       AS overhead_ms,
       round((timed_ms - untimed_ms) / timed_ms * 100, 1)    AS overhead_pct,
       round((timed_ms - untimed_ms) * 1e6 / tuples)::bigint AS ns_per_tuple
FROM m;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3b01_plan_reading / ex3 — expected result
SELECT 464.5 AS overhead_ms, 32.9 AS overhead_pct, 117 AS ns_per_tuple;

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — find the lie, not the symptom

Estimates propagate. When a plan is wrong the useful node is the *lowest*
one whose estimate broke; everything above it inherited the error.

```
[1] Sort  (cost=..8801 rows=12 width=48)
        (actual time=1990.1..1991.0 rows=8791 loops=1)
  [2] ->  Nested Loop  (cost=..8799 rows=12)
            (actual time=2.9..1974.2 rows=8791 loops=1)
        [3] ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on orders o  (cost=..2210 rows=13)
                  (actual time=2.7..96.4 rows=8791 loops=1)
                  Recheck Cond: (channel = 'partner')
                  Filter: (status = 'refunded')
        [4] ->  Index Scan using customers_pkey on customers c
                  (cost=..0.42 rows=1)
                  (actual time=0.20..0.21 rows=1 loops=8791)
```

Edit `ex4/solution.sql` to return **one row, four columns**:

1. `guilty_node` — bracket number of the lowest node whose estimate is wrong
   by more than 10× (integer).
2. `ratio` — its `actual rows ÷ estimated rows`, one decimal.
3. `innocent_node` — bracket number of a node whose estimate is correct
   despite sitting inside the damage (integer).
4. `diagnosis` — exactly one of `'stale statistics'`,
   `'correlated predicates'`, `'missing index'`, explaining why node 3
   under-estimated when `channel` and `status` are each indexed and each
   freshly analysed.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b01_plan_reading ex4`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Work bottom-up. Nodes 1 and 2 both show 8791 against 12, but neither of them
computed that estimate — they inherited it from below.

## Hint 2

Node 4's `rows=1` estimate against `rows=1 loops=8791` is perfectly correct:
per loop it really does return one row. The lie is not there either.

## Hint 3

Two predicates on one table, each estimated correctly alone, multiplied as
if independent. PostgreSQL has a specific feature for that case, which you
meet in V3·B6. The ratio is `8791 / 13`.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Imagine repairing each node in turn. An index on node 3 changes nothing — it
already used one. Forcing another join changes nothing — the join was chosen
*because* the plan believed 13 rows. Only one repair sits upstream of
everything else.

## Hint 2

`refunded` is 2% of orders and `partner` is 25%. Multiplied as independent
that is 0.5%, or 10,000 rows — but the planner said 13, so it did not even
multiply the fractions you would expect. Whatever the exact arithmetic, the
column combination is not behaving independently.

## Hint 3

Answer `3` for the guilty node, `4` for the innocent one, `676.2` for the
ratio, and the diagnosis string naming dependence between columns rather
than out-of-date numbers.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b01_plan_reading / ex4 — locate the lowest broken estimate
SELECT 3                            AS guilty_node,
       round(8791::numeric / 13, 1) AS ratio,
       4                            AS innocent_node,
       'correlated predicates'      AS diagnosis;

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — buffers are the honest metric

Times move with cache state and machine load; buffer counts do not. Two runs
of the same query:

```
run A (cold):  Buffers: shared hit=1204  read=20892   Execution Time: 2841.7 ms
run B (warm):  Buffers: shared hit=22096 read=0       Execution Time: 611.3 ms
```

Edit `ex5/solution.sql` to return **one row, five columns**:

1. `pages_a`, `pages_b` — total pages touched in each run (integers).
2. `mb_read_a` — megabytes read from outside `shared_buffers` in run A, one
   decimal, using 8 KB pages and 1 MB = 1024 KB.
3. `hit_pct_a` — run A's buffer hit ratio as a percentage, one decimal.
4. `verdict` — `'same work'` if the runs touched the same number of pages,
   otherwise `'different work'`. Derive it with a `CASE` over the totals,
   not a hard-coded literal.

The point is column 5: equal page counts mean the 4.6× time difference is
cache state, and reporting run B as an improvement would be a lie.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b01_plan_reading ex5`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`hit + read` is the total logical work; `read` alone is what crossed the
`shared_buffers` boundary. Add first, convert second.

## Hint 2

A page is 8192 bytes. Working in kilobytes keeps it simple:
`20892 × 8 / 1024` megabytes.

## Hint 3

Both runs total 22,096 pages. Write the verdict as a comparison so the query
still tells the truth if you paste different numbers into the CTE.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what a reviewer should conclude from these two lines. Columns 1–4 exist
only to justify column 5; compute the totals first and let them decide the
verdict rather than deciding it yourself.

## Hint 2

`shared read` does not mean "disk". The operating system may have served it
from its own page cache. It means "not in `shared_buffers`" — the only thing
PostgreSQL can actually observe.

## Hint 3

`hit_pct_a` is `1204 / 22096 × 100`, around 5.4%; run B is 100%. Both did
the same 172 MB of logical work.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b01_plan_reading / ex5 — buffer accounting for two runs
WITH r AS (
  SELECT 1204::numeric AS hit_a, 20892::numeric AS read_a,
         22096::numeric AS hit_b, 0::numeric    AS read_b)
SELECT (hit_a + read_a)::bigint                        AS pages_a,
       (hit_b + read_b)::bigint                        AS pages_b,
       round(read_a * 8 / 1024, 1)                     AS mb_read_a,
       round(hit_a / (hit_a + read_a) * 100, 1)        AS hit_pct_a,
       CASE WHEN hit_a + read_a = hit_b + read_b
            THEN 'same work' ELSE 'different work' END AS verdict
FROM r;

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — un-average a parallel plan

Under a `Gather`, nodes report rows and times averaged across the processes
that ran them. Read them raw and you conclude the scan lost most of your
table.

```
Finalize Aggregate  (actual time=1502.9..1502.9 rows=1 loops=1)
  ->  Gather  (actual time=1499.1..1502.4 rows=3 loops=1)
        Workers Planned: 4
        Workers Launched: 2
        ->  Partial Aggregate  (actual time=1490.2..1490.2 rows=1 loops=3)
              ->  Parallel Seq Scan on order_lines  (actual
                    time=0.03..1201.8 rows=1327333 loops=3)
                    Filter: (qty > 1)
                    Rows Removed by Filter: 672667
```

`perf.order_lines` holds 6,000,000 rows.

Edit `ex6/solution.sql` to return **one row, five columns**:

1. `processes` — processes that actually scanned. The leader participates,
   so this is `Workers Launched + 1`.
2. `rows_scanned_total` — rows the scan emitted across all processes.
3. `rows_examined_total` — rows read before the filter, across all
   processes.
4. `covers_table` — a comparison expression that is `true` when
   `rows_examined_total` equals 6,000,000.
5. `worker_shortfall` — `Workers Planned − Workers Launched`, the number
   that makes this benchmark non-reproducible.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b01_plan_reading ex6`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`loops=3` under a `Gather` is not "it ran three times in sequence" — it is
"three processes each ran it once". The multiplication is identical; the
meaning is not.

## Hint 2

Rows examined per process is emitted plus removed: `1327333 + 672667`. Then
scale by the process count.

## Hint 3

Two million rows per process across three processes is exactly the table,
which confirms you un-averaged correctly. Column 4 must be a comparison, not
a literal `true`.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask why `Workers Launched` is below `Workers Planned`. The pool
(`max_parallel_workers`, `max_parallel_workers_per_gather`) was already
spent by other backends. The same query at a quieter moment divides the work
differently, so any timing here belongs to a moment, not to the query.

## Hint 2

The `Gather` node's `rows=3` is not three data rows: it is three partial
aggregates waiting for `Finalize Aggregate`. Never use that 3 as a data row
count.

## Hint 3

Put `launched`, `per_proc_rows` and `per_proc_removed` in a CTE and derive
every column from them. Hard-coded products are where this arithmetic slips.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b01_plan_reading / ex6 — recovering totals from a parallel plan
WITH p AS (
  SELECT 4::numeric AS planned, 2::numeric AS launched,
         1327333::numeric AS per_proc_rows,
         672667::numeric  AS per_proc_removed,
         6000000::numeric AS table_rows)
SELECT (launched + 1)::int                          AS processes,
       ((launched + 1) * per_proc_rows)::bigint     AS rows_scanned_total,
       ((launched + 1) * (per_proc_rows + per_proc_removed))::bigint
                                                    AS rows_examined_total,
       ((launched + 1) * (per_proc_rows + per_proc_removed) = table_rows)
                                                    AS covers_table,
       (planned - launched)::int                    AS worker_shortfall
FROM p;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3b01_plan_reading / ex6 — expected result
SELECT 3 AS processes, 3981999 AS rows_scanned_total,
       6000000 AS rows_examined_total, true AS covers_table,
       2 AS worker_shortfall;

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — a sort that fell out of memory

Run this in the lab:

```sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT customer_id, placed_at, total_cents
FROM perf.orders
WHERE placed_at >= timestamptz '2024-01-01'
ORDER BY total_cents DESC, id;
```

With the default 4 MB `work_mem` the `Sort` node reports:

```
Sort Method: external merge  Disk: 41728kB
Buffers: shared hit=9120, temp read=5216 written=5216
```

Edit `ex7/solution.sql` so that it:

1. sets a session-local `work_mem` large enough for this sort to stay in
   memory, using `SET LOCAL` inside the file, and
2. returns the same result set as the query above.

**Measurable goal:** `dojo plan v3b01_plan_reading ex7` must then show
`Sort Method: quicksort` and `temp read=0 written=0`.

Choose the value deliberately. `Disk: 41728kB` is the size of the tape data;
an in-memory sort of the same tuples needs somewhat more because of
per-tuple overhead, but not ten times more. State your reasoning in a
comment.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b01_plan_reading ex7`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`work_mem` is per sort node per connection — not per query, not per server.
That is exactly why the default is small: three sorts across 200 connections
can allocate 600 times whatever you set.

## Hint 2

```sql
SET LOCAL work_mem = '64MB';
```

`SET LOCAL` reverts at the end of the transaction, which is what you want in
a file other people will run. Plain `SET` leaks into the rest of the session
— and through a connection pooler, into somebody else's query.

## Hint 3

41728 kB is about 41 MB of tape. Round up for tuple headers and the sort
tuple array: 64 MB is the honest first guess, and the next plan's `Sort
Method` line tells you immediately whether it was enough.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Before raising anything, ask whether the sort is necessary at all. Here it
is — but in V3·B3 the same ordering comes from an index and the `Sort` node
disappears rather than being made bigger. Memory is the fix you reach for
when the order cannot come from an index.

## Hint 2

`temp read`/`written` are counted in 8 KB blocks, so 5216 blocks is the
41 MB you saw. When the sort fits, both go to zero — and that, not the
timing, is your pass condition.

## Hint 3

Two statements in the file: the `SET LOCAL`, then the `SELECT` with
`ORDER BY total_cents DESC, id`. Keep the `id` tiebreaker; without it the
row order is not deterministic and the grader's comparison drifts.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b01_plan_reading / ex7 — keep the sort in memory
-- 41728kB of tape data plus per-tuple overhead: 64MB clears it without
-- inviting every connection to allocate 64MB per sort node.
SET LOCAL work_mem = '64MB';

SELECT customer_id, placed_at, total_cents
FROM perf.orders
WHERE placed_at >= timestamptz '2024-01-01'
ORDER BY total_cents DESC, id;

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — measuring a write without performing one

`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` executes. On a `DELETE` that means the rows are gone, and
on a referenced table it means the integrity triggers ran too — frequently
where the time actually went.

You need the cost of purging one tenant's cancelled orders:

```sql
DELETE FROM perf.orders WHERE tenant_id = 7 AND status = 'cancelled';
```

Edit `ex8/solution.sql` so that it measures that statement's plan **and
leaves the table unchanged**, then reports what it learned. The file must:

1. run the measurement inside an explicit transaction that is rolled back,
   using `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, WAL)`;
2. after the rollback, return **one row, three columns** —
   `rows_to_delete` (a live `count(*)` of the matching rows),
   `measured_safely` (boolean `true`),
   `why_wal` (a sentence on what the `WAL` option adds).

**Measurable goal:** running the file twice returns the identical
`rows_to_delete` both times.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b01_plan_reading ex8`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`BEGIN; ... ROLLBACK;` around the `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`. The plan is still
printed — the rollback undoes the row changes, not the measurement.

## Hint 2

`WAL` reports `records`, `fpi` (full-page images) and `bytes`. Full-page
images spike right after a checkpoint, which is why the same delete can
generate ten times the WAL depending on when it runs.

## Hint 3

Structure: `BEGIN;`, the `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, WAL) DELETE ...;`,
`ROLLBACK;`, then the reporting `SELECT`. The count must be a real query
against the table, not a literal — that is what makes the run-it-twice check
meaningful.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

There is a second reason for the transaction beyond safety: inside it you
also get the `Trigger for constraint ...` lines printed after the plan,
which attribute time to foreign keys rather than to the delete. On a table
referenced by an unindexed child column those lines are usually the entire
cost.

## Hint 2

A trap worth naming: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` inside a transaction still takes the
locks the real statement would, and holds them until you roll back. On a
busy table this measures production and blocks it at the same time. Do it on
a replica or in a window.

## Hint 3

Keep `why_wal` to one sentence naming full-page images and the checkpoint
interaction. The grader only checks that the column is non-empty text, but
the sentence is the part you will reuse in a real review.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — build the exclusive-time column yourself

Every plan visualiser sells you one derived column: exclusive time per node,
ranked. You computed it by hand in ex1. Now compute it in SQL, for any plan,
from `EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON)` — a `jsonb` document whose `Plans` key holds
child arrays.

Capture a plan first:

```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS perf.captured_plan (label text, doc jsonb);

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, FORMAT JSON)
SELECT c.country, count(*), sum(o.total_cents)
FROM perf.orders o
JOIN perf.customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'refunded'
GROUP BY c.country;
-- then paste the returned JSON:
INSERT INTO perf.captured_plan VALUES ('refunds_by_country', '<paste>'::jsonb);
```

Edit `challenge/solution.sql` to read `perf.captured_plan` and return, for
the row labelled `refunds_by_country`, **one row per plan node**, ordered by
`exclusive_ms` descending:

| column | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `node` | `Node Type`, plus `' on ' || "Relation Name"` when present |
| `depth` | 0 at the root, incrementing per level |
| `loops` | `Actual Loops` |
| `total_ms` | `Actual Total Time × Actual Loops`, one decimal |
| `exclusive_ms` | `total_ms` minus the same product for its direct children |
| `est_ratio` | `(Actual Rows × Actual Loops) ÷ greatest(Plan Rows × Actual Loops, 1)`, one decimal |

**Measurable goal:** `sum(exclusive_ms)` must equal the root node's
`total_ms` within 0.2 ms of rounding error.

You will need a recursive CTE over `Plans`, a `jsonb_array_elements` per
level, and a synthetic path so a node can find its own children.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b01_plan_reading challenge`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The document is an array holding one object: `doc -> 0 -> 'Plan'` is the
root. Children live at `node -> 'Plans'`, absent on leaves — so use
`coalesce(node -> 'Plans', '[]'::jsonb)` instead of a null test per level.

## Hint 2

Give every node an identity as you descend. A text path works well:

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE walk AS (
  SELECT doc -> 0 -> 'Plan' AS node, 0 AS depth, '0'::text AS path
  FROM perf.captured_plan WHERE label = 'refunds_by_country'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT t.child, w.depth + 1, w.path || '.' || (t.ord - 1)::text
  FROM walk w
  CROSS JOIN LATERAL jsonb_array_elements(
         coalesce(w.node -> 'Plans', '[]'::jsonb)) WITH ORDINALITY AS t(child, ord))
SELECT * FROM walk;
```

## Hint 3

With a `path` on every node, the parent path is
`left(path, length(path) - position('.' in reverse(path)))`. Sum children's
`total_ms` per parent path in a second CTE, left-join it back, and subtract
with `coalesce(..., 0)`.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Different entry point: drop the recursion for a moment. If you already had a
table `(path, parent_path, total_ms)`, the exclusive column is one
aggregation and one subtraction. Everything else exists to produce that
table — build it first and check it by counting nodes against the text plan.

## Hint 2

Watch types. `node ->> 'Actual Total Time'` is `text`; cast to `numeric`
before arithmetic. `Actual Loops` is 0 on a `(never executed)` node, so
guard the ratio with `greatest(..., 1)` and let such a node's `total_ms`
fall out as 0.

## Hint 3

Shape: recursive CTE `walk` producing `(node, depth, path)`; a CTE `flat`
extracting the numeric fields and the parent path; a CTE `kids` doing
`SELECT parent_path, sum(total_ms) GROUP BY 1`; a final select joining
`flat` to `kids`, ordering by `exclusive_ms DESC`. Verify with
`sum(exclusive_ms)` before you submit.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b01_plan_reading / challenge — exclusive time per node from FORMAT JSON
WITH RECURSIVE walk AS (
  SELECT doc -> 0 -> 'Plan' AS node, 0 AS depth, '0'::text AS path
  FROM perf.captured_plan
  WHERE label = 'refunds_by_country'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT t.child, w.depth + 1, w.path || '.' || (t.ord - 1)::text
  FROM walk w
  CROSS JOIN LATERAL jsonb_array_elements(
         coalesce(w.node -> 'Plans', '[]'::jsonb)
       ) WITH ORDINALITY AS t(child, ord)
),
flat AS (
  SELECT path,
         CASE WHEN path = '0' THEN NULL
              ELSE left(path, length(path) - position('.' in reverse(path)))
         END AS parent_path,
         depth,
         (node ->> 'Node Type')
           || coalesce(' on ' || (node ->> 'Relation Name'), '')   AS node,
         coalesce((node ->> 'Actual Loops')::numeric, 0)           AS loops,
         coalesce((node ->> 'Actual Total Time')::numeric, 0)
           * coalesce((node ->> 'Actual Loops')::numeric, 0)       AS total_ms,
         coalesce((node ->> 'Actual Rows')::numeric, 0)
           * coalesce((node ->> 'Actual Loops')::numeric, 0)       AS act_rows,
         greatest(coalesce((node ->> 'Plan Rows')::numeric, 0)
           * coalesce((node ->> 'Actual Loops')::numeric, 0), 1)   AS est_rows
  FROM walk
),
kids AS (
  SELECT parent_path, sum(total_ms) AS child_ms
  FROM flat
  WHERE parent_path IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY parent_path
)
SELECT f.node,
       f.depth,
       f.loops::bigint                                 AS loops,
       round(f.total_ms, 1)                            AS total_ms,
       round(f.total_ms - coalesce(k.child_ms, 0), 1)  AS exclusive_ms,
       round(f.act_rows / f.est_rows, 1)               AS est_ratio
FROM flat f
LEFT JOIN kids k ON k.parent_path = f.path
ORDER BY exclusive_ms DESC, f.path;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3b01_plan_reading / challenge — the invariant the grader checks
-- sum(exclusive_ms) must equal the root node's total_ms within 0.2 ms.
-- Shape of the output (values are machine-dependent):
--   node                   | depth | loops | total_ms | exclusive_ms | est_ratio
--   Seq Scan on orders     |     2 |     1 |    214.9 |        214.9 |       1.0
--   Hash Join              |     1 |     1 |    861.2 |        528.2 |       1.0
--   Hash                   |     2 |     1 |    118.1 |         79.7 |       1.0
--   HashAggregate          |     0 |     1 |    902.4 |         41.2 |       1.0
--   Seq Scan on customers  |     3 |     1 |     38.4 |         38.4 |       1.0

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 — triage a plan cold

Nobody hands you a labelled plan in production. Here is one, unannotated,
attached to an on-call page that says "the dashboard takes nine seconds".

```
Limit  (actual time=8914.2..8914.4 rows=50 loops=1)
  ->  Sort  (actual time=8914.2..8914.3 rows=50 loops=1)
        Sort Key: (sum(o.total_cents)) DESC
        Sort Method: top-N heapsort  Memory: 33kB
        ->  GroupAggregate  (actual time=41.9..8901.7 rows=182114 loops=1)
              ->  Nested Loop  (actual time=41.6..8404.1 rows=402118 loops=1)
                    ->  Index Scan using customers_pkey on customers c
                          (actual time=0.01..91.4 rows=182114 loops=1)
                    ->  Index Scan using orders_customer_id_idx on orders o
                          (actual time=0.041..0.045 rows=2 loops=182114)
                          Index Cond: (customer_id = c.id)
                          Buffers: shared hit=4
```

Edit `review1/solution.sql` to return **one row, six columns**:

1. `hot_node` — the node type holding the most exclusive time (text).
2. `hot_exclusive_ms` — its exclusive milliseconds, one decimal.
3. `inner_buffer_touches` — total buffers the inner index scan touched.
4. `top_n_wasteful` — `true` if the plan sorts far more groups than the
   `LIMIT` needs.
5. `first_fix` — one of `'add an index'`, `'change the join strategy'`,
   `'raise work_mem'`.
6. `why` — one sentence defending column 5 with a number from the plan.

The trap is column 1: the aggregate shows 8901.7 and the nested loop 8404.1,
and neither is where the time is spent.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b01_plan_reading review1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Do the arithmetic before forming an opinion. The inner scan's 0.045 ms is
per loop and there are 182,114 loops; that product is the first number to
write down.

## Hint 2

The nested loop's exclusive time is `8404.1` minus the outer scan's `91.4`
minus the inner side's total across all loops. If that comes out near zero,
the loop is innocent and its child is your answer.

## Hint 3

`0.045 × 182114 ≈ 8195 ms`. The `top-N heapsort` used 33 kB, so memory is
not the issue, and the inner side already has its index — so "add an index"
is not it either. What remains is the strategy: 182,114 index descents where
one hash join would do.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Different entry: count round trips. This plan performs one index descent per
customer, for every customer in the table, to render fifty rows. Any answer
that leaves 182,114 descents in place is a micro-optimisation of the wrong
thing.

## Hint 2

Column 4 is about shape, not sort method. `top-N heapsort` is already the
cheap sort — but it must still receive 182,114 aggregated groups to pick
fifty, and nothing here lets the executor stop early, because the aggregate
must finish before the sort can begin.

## Hint 3

`inner_buffer_touches` is `4 × 182114 = 728456`, about 5.7 GB of buffer
traffic. Put that number in your `why` sentence; it is the most persuasive
figure in the plan.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b01_plan_reading / review1 — cold triage of a nine-second dashboard
WITH n AS (
  SELECT 182114::numeric AS loops, 0.045::numeric AS inner_t_last,
         4::numeric AS inner_buf, 50::numeric AS limit_rows,
         182114::numeric AS groups)
SELECT 'Index Scan'                     AS hot_node,
       round(inner_t_last * loops, 1)   AS hot_exclusive_ms,
       (inner_buf * loops)::bigint      AS inner_buffer_touches,
       (groups > limit_rows * 10)       AS top_n_wasteful,
       'change the join strategy'       AS first_fix,
       'The inner index scan costs 0.045 ms and 4 buffers per loop but runs '
       || loops::text || ' times, so it holds about '
       || round(inner_t_last * loops)::text || ' ms and '
       || (inner_buf * loops)::text
       || ' buffer touches; one hash join replaces all of them.' AS why
FROM n;
references.expected.sql:
-- v3b01_plan_reading / review1 — expected result
SELECT 'Index Scan' AS hot_node, 8195.1 AS hot_exclusive_ms,
       728456 AS inner_buffer_touches, true AS top_n_wasteful,
       'change the join strategy' AS first_fix;

lessons.title: V3·B2 — B-trees, selectivity and index-only scans
lessons.summary: An index is not a speed setting; it is a sorted copy of one or more columns with pointers back to the heap, and whether the planner uses it is a cost decision about selectivity and physical order. This sector measures tree height, reads selectivity straight out of pg_stats, finds the crossover where a sequential scan wins, and makes an index-only scan actually report zero heap fetches.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·B2 — B-trees, selectivity and index-only scans

V3·B1 left you able to prove where the time went. This sector is the first
of four about the instrument you reach for most often, and it starts by
dismantling two beliefs that survive far too long: that an index makes
queries fast, and that a sequential scan is a failure.

An index is a sorted, redundant copy of some columns, with a pointer to each
matching heap row. It buys you the ability to *find* rows without reading
all of them. It costs you disk, buffer cache, and work on every insert,
update and delete of the indexed columns. Whether the planner uses one is
not a preference — it is arithmetic about **selectivity** and **physical
correlation**, and when it declines to use your index it is usually right.

## The tree, concretely

A PostgreSQL B-tree is a Lehman-Yao B+ tree of 8 KB pages. Only the leaf
level holds pointers to data (`ctid`, a page-and-offset pair). Internal
pages hold separator keys, truncated to the shortest prefix that still
separates — so a `bigint` index over `perf.orders` fits roughly 400 entries
per internal page and a couple of hundred per leaf.

That fanout is why depth is small and nearly constant:

```
2,000,000 rows / ~250 entries per leaf   =   8,000 leaf pages
8,000 leaves  / ~400 separators per page =      20 internal pages
20            / 400                      =       1 root
```

Three levels. A point lookup is three page reads plus one heap read, and it
stays three levels until the table gets about a hundred times bigger. This
is the origin of the rule of thumb that a primary-key lookup costs four
buffer touches whatever the table size — check it yourself with
`EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` in ex1.

You can see the structure directly:

```sql
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pageinspect;
SELECT * FROM bt_metap('orders_pkey');       -- level = height - 1
SELECT * FROM bt_page_stats('orders_pkey', 3);
```

## Selectivity decides everything

Selectivity is the fraction of the table a predicate keeps. In `perf.orders`
(2,000,000 rows):

| predicate | rows | selectivity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id = 918273` | 1 | 0.00005% |
| `status = 'pending'` | 8,000 | 0.4% |
| `status = 'refunded'` | 40,000 | 2% |
| `channel = 'web'` | 500,000 | 25% |
| `total_cents > 500` | 2,000,000 | 100% |

An index scan pays roughly one random heap page per matching row until the
matches start sharing pages. A sequential scan pays one sequential page per
eight or so rows, whatever the predicate. Cross-multiply and the break-even
lands somewhere between 2% and 10% of the table depending on
`random_page_cost` and on how well the index order matches heap order. Above
it, `Seq Scan` is genuinely cheaper and the planner choosing it is not a
bug you should hunt with `SET enable_seqscan = off`.

The planner does not count rows to learn this. It reads `pg_stats`:

```sql
SELECT attname, n_distinct, most_common_vals, most_common_freqs
FROM pg_stats
WHERE schemaname = 'perf' AND tablename = 'orders' AND attname = 'status';
```

`most_common_freqs` gives the exact fraction for each frequent value; for
anything not in that list the planner uses
`(1 - sum(mcf)) / (n_distinct - length(mcv))`. You compute both by hand in
ex2, and once you have, "why did it think 13 rows?" stops being mysterious.

## Correlation, the hidden multiplier

`pg_stats.correlation` measures how closely a column's order matches the
heap's physical order: 1.0 for an append-only `placed_at`, near 0 for a
random UUID. An index scan over a perfectly correlated column reads heap
pages nearly sequentially, so the planner discounts it heavily; over an
uncorrelated column each matching row may be a separate random page. The
same selectivity can therefore give you an index scan on one column and a
sequential scan on another, and the difference is physical layout, not the
index.

## Index-only scans, and the promise they break

If every column a query needs lives in the index, PostgreSQL can answer
without touching the heap — except that the heap is where row visibility
lives. So it consults the **visibility map**: one bit per heap page saying
"every tuple on this page is visible to everyone". Where the bit is set, the
heap visit is skipped; where it is not, it is not.

```
Index Only Scan using orders_status_placed_idx on orders
  (actual time=0.03..41.9 rows=39987 loops=1)
  Heap Fetches: 39987          <-- the promise, unkept
```

`Heap Fetches: 39987` means the scan was an index scan wearing a costume.
The fix is `VACUUM`, which sets visibility-map bits (V3·B8). This is why a
freshly loaded table shows no benefit until it is vacuumed, and why a
heavily updated table loses the benefit again between autovacuum runs.

`INCLUDE` adds payload columns to the leaf level without making them part of
the key:

```sql
CREATE INDEX orders_cust_incl_idx
  ON perf.orders (customer_id) INCLUDE (total_cents, status);
```

They cannot be searched or sorted on, they do not participate in
uniqueness, and they make leaves fatter — but they turn a lookup plus heap
fetch into a single index read. ex5 makes one report `Heap Fetches: 0`.

## Mission set

Ten missions: measure real tree height and lookup buffers, compute
selectivity from `pg_stats` by hand, find your instance's crossover point,
repair three non-sargable predicates, earn a genuine `Heap Fetches: 0`,
prove that B-trees do index NULLs, hunt unused and redundant indexes, and
finish by choosing the smallest index set that serves a whole query mix.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b02_btree_selectivity`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - sql/v3b02_btree_selectivity

The index is not the fast part. The index is the part that lets you avoid
reading rows; whether avoiding them is cheaper than reading them is a
separate question, answered per query, by arithmetic.

## Notes

**A B-tree leaf entry is key plus `ctid`.** The `ctid` is `(block, offset)`
into the heap. Following it costs a page read that may be random, which is
the entire reason index scans are not free per row. When many matches share
a page the cost amortises; when they are scattered it does not, and
`pg_stats.correlation` is how the planner guesses which world it is in.

**Height is logarithmic and therefore boring.** Fanout of a few hundred
means three levels covers millions of rows and four covers billions. Stop
worrying about depth; worry about how many leaf entries a range predicate
sweeps and how many distinct heap pages those entries point at.

**Deduplication changed the economics of low-cardinality indexes.**
Since PostgreSQL 13, a B-tree stores repeated keys as one key with a posting
list of `ctid`s. An index on `status` over two million rows is far smaller
than it used to be — but small is not the same as useful: reading 500,000
`ctid`s to fetch 500,000 rows is still worse than a sequential scan.

**Selectivity arithmetic, in the planner's own terms.** For an equality
predicate, if the value is in `most_common_vals`, selectivity is the
matching `most_common_freqs` entry exactly. Otherwise it is
`(1 - sum(mcf)) / (n_distinct - n_mcv)`. For a range predicate, the planner
interpolates within `histogram_bounds`. Multiply selectivity by
`reltuples` and you have the `rows=` you see in the plan; when the plan's
number and your hand calculation disagree, the statistics are stale.

**`n_distinct` can be negative and that is deliberate.** A negative value is
a *ratio* to the row count: `-1` means "every row distinct, and it will stay
that way as the table grows". `ANALYZE` estimates distinctness from a
sample, so on a large table it is often badly wrong for wide-tailed columns
— you can pin it with `ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET (n_distinct =
...)` (V3·B6).

**Sargability is a property of the predicate, not the column.** An index on
`placed_at` cannot serve `WHERE date_trunc('day', placed_at) = DATE
'2024-05-01'`, because the index stores `placed_at`, not the function of it.
Rewrite to a half-open range and the same index works. The recurring
offenders: a function wrapped around the column, `LIKE '%foo'` with a
leading wildcard, `col::date = ...`, `col + interval '1 day' < now()`,
implicit collation or type coercion on the indexed side, and `OR` across
different columns, which needs either a bitmap OR or a rewrite to `UNION`.

**B-trees index NULLs.** Unlike Oracle, PostgreSQL stores NULL keys, so
`WHERE delivered_at IS NULL` can use a plain B-tree index and `ORDER BY col
NULLS LAST` can be satisfied by an index declared with a matching
`NULLS LAST`. The ordering matters: `ASC` implies `NULLS LAST` and `DESC`
implies `NULLS FIRST`, and a mismatch silently costs you the ordered scan.

**Index-only scans need the visibility map, not luck.** `Heap Fetches` is
the count of times the map said "cannot vouch for this page". After a bulk
load or a burst of updates, that number equals the row count and the plan
performs like a regular index scan. `VACUUM` sets the bits;
`pg_visibility`'s `pg_visibility_map_summary()` tells you what fraction of
pages are all-visible right now.

**`INCLUDE` columns are payload, not key.** They are stored only at the leaf
level, are not used for searching, ordering or uniqueness, and are dropped
from internal pages by suffix truncation. Their real use is turning a unique
constraint into a covering index without weakening the constraint:
`UNIQUE (email) INCLUDE (id, plan)`.

**Every index is a write tax.** Each insert adds an entry to every index;
each update writes a new heap tuple and, unless every indexed column is
unchanged *and* the page has room, new entries in every index too (HOT
updates are the exception — V3·B8). Six indexes on a hot table means an
update is roughly seven writes. `pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan = 0` after a
representative period is the strongest evidence you can have for dropping
one.

**Operator families decide whether a cast is fatal.** An `int4` column and
an `int8` literal share a B-tree operator family, so the coercion lands on
the constant and the index still works. `text` and `bigint` share nothing,
so the cast lands on the column and becomes a per-row function call. When
you are unsure, read the `EXPLAIN` line: `Index Cond` means the comparison
happened inside the index, `Filter` means it happened after fetching the
row, and no amount of reasoning beats those two words.

## Mission notes

**ex1** measures the tree you just read about — with `pageinspect` if it is
available and with buffer counts if it is not.

**ex2** makes you compute selectivity by hand from `pg_stats` and compare it
with the plan's `rows=`. Do it once and you will read every estimate
differently afterwards.

**ex3** finds the crossover on *your* instance, which depends on
`random_page_cost` and the cache. There is no universal 5%.

**ex4** repairs three non-sargable predicates; the third one is a type
coercion that looks harmless.

**ex5** earns `Heap Fetches: 0` — the vacuum matters as much as the index.

**ex6** proves NULL handling; **ex7** hunts redundant indexes with the
left-prefix rule from V3·B3 in mind; **ex8** is the type-mismatch trap in
its most common production form.

## Further reading

- [Index types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-types.html)
  — start here, then read the B-tree implementation README in the source.
- [Row estimation examples](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/row-estimation-examples.html)
  — the manual doing ex2's arithmetic in public.
- [Index-only scans and covering indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-index-only-scans.html)
- [pageinspect](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/pageinspect.html)
  — `bt_metap`, `bt_page_stats`, `bt_page_items`.
- [Use The Index, Luke](https://use-the-index-luke.com/) — the clearest
  non-vendor explanation of why predicate shape decides index usability.
