# Reading - sql/v3b03_composite_order

## What the executor does with a multicolumn index condition

When you write `WHERE a = 7 AND b >= '2024-06-01'` against an index on
`(a, b)`, the planner splits your predicate into two categories that the
plan text unhelpfully prints together. Some clauses become **scan keys** that
position the descent: they are turned into a search tuple, the tree is
walked once, and the scan begins at the first leaf entry at or after that
tuple. Other clauses become scan keys that are merely *evaluated* on each
entry the scan visits, and a third group becomes a heap `Filter` applied
after the row is fetched.

Positioning keys are what make an index fast. Everything else is a cheaper
form of scanning. The plan shows `Index Cond` for the first two categories
and `Filter` for the third, which is why two plans with identical `Index
Cond` lines can differ by an order of magnitude in buffers — the text does
not distinguish "descended on this" from "checked this per entry".

The executor also knows when to stop. With `(a, b)` and `a = 7`, the scan
ends at the first entry where `a <> 7`; it does not read to the end of the
index. That termination condition is why an equality-first index is
efficient even when the trailing columns are unconstrained, and why a
leading range predicate makes the scan open-ended in a way no trailing
predicate can fix.

## Sorted output is a resource

An index scan is one of the few nodes that emits rows already ordered, and
the planner tracks that ordering as a *pathkey* attached to the path. Pathkeys
propagate: a nested loop preserves the outer side's ordering, an append over
partitions can merge them, and a node that requires ordering — `Merge Join`,
`GroupAggregate`, `Unique`, `WindowAgg`, `Limit` under `ORDER BY` — can
consume a matching pathkey instead of inserting a `Sort`.

This is the reason composite design pays off in places the query text never
mentions. An index on `(customer_id, placed_at)` does not merely accelerate
a filter; it makes `GROUP BY customer_id` streamable, makes a merge join
against `customers` possible without sorting two million rows, and makes
`DISTINCT ON (customer_id) ... ORDER BY customer_id, placed_at DESC` a
single ordered pass. When you evaluate an index, ask what pathkeys it
supplies, not just what predicates it answers.

Pathkeys are also why direction is fussy. The planner will happily read an
index backwards to satisfy a fully-reversed ordering, because reversing
every column of a sorted list is still a sorted list. Reversing one column of
several is not, and there is no cheap operation that produces it — so the
mixed-direction case needs the index declared with those exact directions.

## The skip scan PostgreSQL does not have

Consider `SELECT DISTINCT tenant_id FROM perf.orders` with an index on
`(tenant_id, placed_at)`. Forty distinct values sit in forty contiguous
blocks of the index, and the theoretically optimal plan is forty descents:
find the smallest value, then repeatedly search for the smallest value
strictly greater than the last. Oracle calls it a skip scan, MySQL 8 calls
it loose index scan, and PostgreSQL, through version 17, does neither — it
reads all two million entries and de-duplicates.

You can write the optimal plan by hand:

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE t AS (
  SELECT min(tenant_id) AS tenant_id FROM perf.orders
  UNION ALL
  SELECT (SELECT min(o.tenant_id) FROM perf.orders o
           WHERE o.tenant_id > t.tenant_id)
  FROM t WHERE t.tenant_id IS NOT NULL)
SELECT tenant_id FROM t WHERE tenant_id IS NOT NULL;
```

Each `min()` over an indexed column is an `Index Only Scan` with `LIMIT 1`,
so the whole thing is forty-one descents — microseconds instead of hundreds
of milliseconds. The trick generalises to any "distinct leading values"
problem, including the `DISTINCT ON` top-N-per-group patterns from sector
49, and it is worth keeping in a snippets file.

## History and trade-offs

Multicolumn B-trees are as old as the access method, but two changes in the
last decade altered how you should design them. Suffix truncation
(PostgreSQL 12) stopped internal pages from carrying trailing key columns,
which made wide composites much cheaper to descend and removed most of the
argument for keeping keys narrow. Deduplication (13) collapsed repeated
leading keys into posting lists, which made low-cardinality leading columns
— exactly the `(status, ...)` and `(tenant_id, ...)` shapes you want for
equality-first design — dramatically smaller on disk.

`INCLUDE` (11) completed the picture by separating "columns I search by"
from "columns I return". Before it, covering an extra column meant putting
it in the key, which enlarged every internal page and, on a unique index,
broke the constraint you were trying to enforce. The modern idiom —
`UNIQUE (tenant_id, external_id) INCLUDE (id, status)` — was simply not
expressible.

The trade-offs are unchanged, though. Every added key column widens leaf
entries and shrinks fanout; every added index multiplies write cost and
vacuum time; and an index designed for a query that later changes shape
becomes pure overhead that nobody dares delete. The discipline that keeps
this manageable is not cleverness in design — it is periodically running the
audit from V3·B2 and actually dropping what it flags.

## When not to reach for a composite

When the predicate combinations are genuinely unpredictable — an admin
search screen with twelve optional filters — several single-column indexes
and `BitmapAnd` degrade gracefully, where a set of composites would need
2^12 of them to cover the space. When one of the columns is very low
cardinality and always constrained to the same value, a partial index is
smaller and faster (V3·B4). When the leading column is a timestamp used only
for retention, partitioning may be the better tool. And when the table is
small, none of this matters: 5,000 rows fit in fifty pages and the planner
will scan them faster than it can descend a tree.

## Reading the design out of the query log

The design method that survives contact with production is mechanical.
Take the top twenty statements from `pg_stat_statements` by
`total_exec_time`, normalise each into the triple (equality columns, range
or ordering column, returned columns), and write the triples in a list. Then
merge: two statements whose equality sets are identical and whose ordering
columns agree can share an index; a statement whose equality set is a subset
of another's can ride on that other index as a left prefix. What remains
after merging is your index set, usually a third the size of what a
per-query design would produce.

The step teams skip is the last one — checking the merged set against the
write path. Every index on `orders` is written on every insert, and an
index over a column that `UPDATE` touches also blocks HOT updates for that
table, which turns a cheap in-page update into a new heap tuple plus one
entry in every index. If the table takes 5,000 inserts a second and serves
twenty analytical queries an hour, the analytical indexes need to justify
themselves against 18 million writes an hour, and often they cannot: the
right answer is a replica, a materialised view (sector 46), or a
periodically refreshed rollup table rather than a fourth index.

Do this once with real numbers and the abstract advice in this sector turns
into a procedure you can run in an afternoon and defend in a review.

## Further reading

- [Multicolumn indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-multicolumn.html)
- [Indexes and ORDER BY](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-ordering.html)
- [Combining multiple indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-bitmap-scans.html)
- [Loose indexscan](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Loose_indexscan) — the
  recursive CTE above, with variants for multiple columns.
- [Use The Index, Luke — concatenated keys](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/where-clause/the-equals-operator/concatenated-keys)
  — the phone-book model, at length and with pictures.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — what does this index actually serve?

One index exists on `perf.orders`:

```sql
CREATE INDEX orders_tcs_idx ON perf.orders (tenant_id, channel, placed_at);
```

Six queries arrive:

```
Q1  WHERE tenant_id = 7
Q2  WHERE channel = 'ios'
Q3  WHERE tenant_id = 7 AND channel = 'ios'
Q4  WHERE tenant_id = 7 AND placed_at >= '2024-06-01'
Q5  WHERE tenant_id = 7 AND channel = 'ios' AND placed_at >= '2024-06-01'
Q6  WHERE tenant_id > 30 AND channel = 'ios'
```

Edit `ex1/solution.sql` to return **one row per query**, ordered by label,
with columns:

| column | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `q` | the label, `'Q1'`..`'Q6'` |
| `key_cols_used` | how many leading key columns position the descent (0–3) |
| `usable` | `'index cond'`, `'index cond + per-entry check'`, or `'no descent'` |
| `note` | one clause explaining the classification |

Rules: a column positions the descent only if every column to its left is
constrained by equality and it is itself constrained. A column constrained
but not positioned is still checked per entry (that is the second verdict).

**Measurable goal:** exactly one query scores `key_cols_used = 0`, and
exactly one scores 3.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b03_composite_order ex1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Walk each query left to right through `(tenant_id, channel, placed_at)` and
stop at the first column that is either unconstrained or constrained by a
range. That stopping point is `key_cols_used`.

## Hint 2

Q4 is the interesting one: `tenant_id` positions, `channel` is unconstrained
so the descent stops at one column, and `placed_at` is still pushed into the
`Index Cond` and checked on every entry of tenant 7's block.

## Hint 3

Build it as a `VALUES` list with your four columns and just `ORDER BY q` —
the exercise is the classification, not the SQL. Q2 is the zero; Q5 is the
three.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Try predicting the buffer counts instead of the categories, then classify.
Q3 touches one tenant-and-channel block, Q4 touches one tenant block (twenty
times bigger), Q2 touches the entire index. The categories are just names
for those three magnitudes.

## Hint 2

Q6 is the trap. `tenant_id > 30` is a range on the *leading* column, so it
positions the start of the scan but leaves everything after it open —
`channel` is then interleaved through ten tenants' worth of entries and can
only be checked per entry.

## Hint 3

Be careful not to write `'no descent'` for Q6. It does descend, to
`tenant_id = 31`; what it cannot do is narrow further. Reserve `'no
descent'` for the query that constrains nothing in the leading position at
all.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b03_composite_order / ex1 — which queries the composite serves
SELECT *
FROM (VALUES
  ('Q1', 1, 'index cond',
   'equality on the leading column positions the descent; rest unconstrained'),
  ('Q2', 0, 'no descent',
   'channel is not a left prefix, so there is no starting tuple to descend to'),
  ('Q3', 2, 'index cond',
   'equality on both leading columns narrows to a single contiguous block'),
  ('Q4', 1, 'index cond + per-entry check',
   'tenant_id positions; channel is unconstrained so placed_at is checked '
   'on every entry of the tenant block'),
  ('Q5', 3, 'index cond',
   'two equalities then one range: the ideal shape, every entry swept is a hit'),
  ('Q6', 1, 'index cond + per-entry check',
   'a range on the leading column positions the start but leaves channel '
   'interleaved across ten tenants')
) AS v(q, key_cols_used, usable, note)
ORDER BY q;

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — fix the column order, prove it in buffers

The monthly tenant report:

```sql
SELECT count(*), sum(total_cents)
FROM perf.orders
WHERE tenant_id = 7
  AND placed_at >= timestamptz '2024-06-01'
  AND placed_at <  timestamptz '2024-07-01';
```

The table has exactly one usable index:

```sql
CREATE INDEX orders_placed_tenant_idx ON perf.orders (placed_at, tenant_id);
```

Measure it with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`, then write
`ex2/indexes.sql` with a better index and `ex2/solution.sql` with the
unchanged query.

**Measurable goal:** buffers for this query drop by at least 10×, and the
plan is an `Index Only Scan` with `Heap Fetches: 0`. Record the before and
after buffer counts in a comment in `indexes.sql`.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b03_composite_order ex2`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The query has one equality and one range. The rule says which goes first,
and the existing index has it backwards.

## Hint 2

You also need `total_cents` for the `sum`. Adding it as an `INCLUDE` column
turns the index scan into an index-only scan; adding it to the key would
enlarge the tree for no benefit, since nothing searches by amount.

## Hint 3

```sql
CREATE INDEX orders_tenant_placed_sum_idx
  ON perf.orders (tenant_id, placed_at) INCLUDE (total_cents);
VACUUM (ANALYZE) perf.orders;
```

The vacuum is not optional if you want `Heap Fetches: 0`.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Predict the ratio before measuring. There are 40 tenants; one month is about
3.3% of 900 days of data. The wrong-order index sweeps a whole month across
all tenants; the right one sweeps one tenant's month. So expect roughly
fortyfold, and buffers to fall from a couple of hundred to a dozen.

## Hint 2

Do not drop the old index yet — the comparison is the exercise. Keep both,
force each with `SET enable_indexscan`/`enable_indexonlyscan` toggles or
just read which the planner picks once both exist. It will pick yours.

## Hint 3

If your buffer improvement is small, check whether the planner used your new
index at all. `ANALYZE` after creating it; a brand-new index with no
statistics on a table whose `reltuples` is stale can lose to a plan the
planner already believes in.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b03_composite_order / ex2 — the query is unchanged; the index is not
SELECT count(*), sum(total_cents)
FROM perf.orders
WHERE tenant_id = 7
  AND placed_at >= timestamptz '2024-06-01'
  AND placed_at <  timestamptz '2024-07-01';

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — the sort that came back

The support console lists a tenant's orders, worst status first, newest
first within a status:

```sql
SELECT id, status, placed_at
FROM perf.orders
WHERE tenant_id = 7
ORDER BY status ASC, placed_at DESC
LIMIT 50;
```

With `CREATE INDEX ON perf.orders (tenant_id, status, placed_at)` the plan
still contains a `Sort` node over about 50,000 rows.

Write `ex3/indexes.sql` with an index that removes the sort, and
`ex3/solution.sql` with the query.

**Measurable goal:** no `Sort` node in the plan, and the `Index Scan` node
reports `rows=50` — not fifty thousand.

Then add, as a second statement in `solution.sql`, **one row, three
columns**: `works_backwards` (boolean — can a single B-tree scan satisfy
`ORDER BY status DESC, placed_at ASC` with your index?), `needs_own_index`
(boolean — does `ORDER BY status ASC, placed_at ASC` need a different
index?), and `rule` (one sentence).

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b03_composite_order ex3`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A B-tree can be read forwards or backwards, which reverses *every* column at
once. Your `ORDER BY` reverses one of two. Declare the index to match.

## Hint 2

```sql
CREATE INDEX ... ON perf.orders (tenant_id, status, placed_at DESC);
```

`tenant_id` is an equality so its direction is irrelevant; the two ordering
columns must match the `ORDER BY` exactly, or be exactly its reverse.

## Hint 3

For the second statement: reversing your index gives `status DESC, placed_at
ASC` — so the first boolean is true. `status ASC, placed_at ASC` is neither
your order nor its reverse, so the second boolean is true as well.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what "sorted" means for a tuple list. `(a, b DESC)` is one total order.
Reading it backwards gives `(a DESC, b ASC)`. Those are the only two orders
a single scan can produce, out of the four combinations of directions —
which is exactly why mixed `ORDER BY` needs a matching declaration.

## Hint 2

Notice the `LIMIT`'s role. Without it, a sort over 50,000 rows costs maybe
30 ms and nobody notices. With it, the sorted index scan can stop after
fifty entries and the difference is three orders of magnitude. Ordering
indexes pay off in proportion to how early you stop.

## Hint 3

Watch for `NULLS` if you generalise this. `ASC` means `NULLS LAST` and
`DESC` means `NULLS FIRST` by default, so an `ORDER BY placed_at DESC NULLS
LAST` needs the index declared `placed_at DESC NULLS LAST` — the default
would put them first and the sort returns.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b03_composite_order / ex3 — mixed-direction ordering from the index
SELECT id, status, placed_at
FROM perf.orders
WHERE tenant_id = 7
ORDER BY status ASC, placed_at DESC
LIMIT 50;

SELECT true  AS works_backwards,   -- reversed scan gives status DESC, placed_at ASC
       true  AS needs_own_index,   -- status ASC, placed_at ASC is neither
       'A single B-tree scan produces exactly two orders: the declared one '
       || 'and its full reverse, so any mixed ASC/DESC ordering must be '
       || 'declared on the index itself.' AS rule;

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — a GROUP BY that never sorts and never hashes

Finance runs this hourly over the whole table:

```sql
SELECT tenant_id, count(*) AS orders, sum(total_cents) AS revenue
FROM perf.orders
WHERE status IN ('paid', 'shipped')
GROUP BY tenant_id
ORDER BY tenant_id;
```

Today it is a `Seq Scan` feeding a `HashAggregate` that holds 40 groups —
fine — but reads 164 MB to do it.

Write `ex4/indexes.sql` and `ex4/solution.sql` so that the query is answered
entirely from an index.

**Measurable goal:** the plan contains `Index Only Scan` with
`Heap Fetches: 0` and no `Seq Scan`; buffers drop below a quarter of the
original.

Record in a comment which aggregate node you ended up with
(`HashAggregate` or `GroupAggregate`) and why the choice is reasonable
either way at 40 groups.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b03_composite_order ex4`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

An index-only scan needs every referenced column: `status` (predicate),
`tenant_id` (grouping), `total_cents` (aggregate). Decide which are keys and
which are payload.

## Hint 2

`status` is the equality-ish predicate — an `IN` list of two values — so it
leads. `tenant_id` follows because it supplies grouping order.
`total_cents` is summed only, so it is `INCLUDE`.

## Hint 3

```sql
CREATE INDEX ... ON perf.orders (status, tenant_id) INCLUDE (total_cents);
```

With the `IN` list the scan descends twice, once per status, so the output
is ordered within each descent but not across them — the planner may still
choose `HashAggregate`, which at 40 groups is entirely reasonable.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it from the data volume. The index carries three narrow columns for
1.9 million qualifying rows: roughly 60 MB against the table's 164 MB, and
the scan touches only the qualifying part of it. The win here is not the
algorithm, it is reading a third of the bytes.

## Hint 2

If you want to see `GroupAggregate` instead, try the single-status version
of the query: one descent gives a single ordered stream, the planner has a
pathkey on `tenant_id`, and it can stream groups without building a hash
table. That comparison is worth running.

## Hint 3

Do not put `total_cents` in the key "to be safe". It would sit between
nothing and nothing in the sort order, enlarge every internal page, and
prevent deduplication from collapsing the repeated `(status, tenant_id)`
pairs — which on this data is a real difference in index size.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b03_composite_order / ex4 — revenue per tenant, entirely from the index
SELECT tenant_id, count(*) AS orders, sum(total_cents) AS revenue
FROM perf.orders
WHERE status IN ('paid', 'shipped')
GROUP BY tenant_id
ORDER BY tenant_id;

-- Plan uses HashAggregate over an Index Only Scan: the IN list means two
-- descents, so the stream is not globally ordered by tenant_id. At 40 groups
-- the hash table is a few kilobytes, so streaming would buy nothing.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — BitmapAnd versus a composite

Two single-column indexes exist:

```sql
CREATE INDEX orders_status_only_idx  ON perf.orders (status);
CREATE INDEX orders_channel_only_idx ON perf.orders (channel);
```

The query:

```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM perf.orders
WHERE status = 'refunded' AND channel = 'partner';
```

`EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` shows a `BitmapAnd` combining both.

Edit `ex5/solution.sql` to return **one row, six columns** comparing that
plan with the composite alternative you build in `ex5/indexes.sql`:

| column | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `bitmap_buffers` | measured buffers for the BitmapAnd plan |
| `composite_buffers` | measured buffers with your composite |
| `bitmap_index_mb` | combined size of the two single-column indexes, one decimal, from `pg_relation_size` |
| `composite_index_mb` | size of your composite, one decimal, live |
| `keep_singles` | boolean: would you keep the two single-column indexes? |
| `why` | one sentence defending `keep_singles` |

**Measurable goal:** the two size columns must be computed live from
`pg_relation_size`, and `composite_buffers` must be smaller than
`bitmap_buffers`.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b03_composite_order ex5`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The composite is `(status, channel)` or `(channel, status)` — both are two
equalities, so either order positions fully. Pick the one that also serves
some other query you have already written, and say so.

## Hint 2

`pg_relation_size('perf.orders_status_only_idx'::regclass)` gives bytes;
sum the two and convert. Getting the buffer numbers means running the
`EXPLAIN` twice and pasting the two figures into a CTE — that part is
measurement, not derivation.

## Hint 3

For `keep_singles`, think about what else queries `channel` alone. If
nothing does, the single-column indexes are pure write cost once the
composite exists. If an ad-hoc admin screen filters on `channel` with no
`status`, they are your hedge.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Approach it as a hedging question rather than a performance one. `BitmapAnd`
is the planner's way of handling combinations nobody designed for. A
composite is a bet that this specific combination is the one that matters.
Both are defensible; the mistake is holding both bets without noticing you
are paying for them.

## Hint 2

Look at the bitmap plan's `Rows Removed by Index Recheck` line. If it is
non-zero, the bitmap went lossy — `work_mem` could not hold one bit per row
— and the heap scan had to recheck every tuple on every matching page. That
detail is why bitmap plans degrade unpredictably as tables grow.

## Hint 3

Notice what the composite gives you that the bitmap cannot: ordered output.
Add `ORDER BY placed_at LIMIT 20` to the query and the bitmap plan grows a
`Sort` while `(status, channel, placed_at)` does not. If the real workload
has that shape, the decision is already made.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b03_composite_order / ex5 — bitmap intersection versus one composite
WITH m AS (SELECT 512::numeric AS bitmap_buffers, 46::numeric AS composite_buffers)
SELECT m.bitmap_buffers::bigint    AS bitmap_buffers,
       m.composite_buffers::bigint AS composite_buffers,
       round((pg_relation_size('perf.orders_status_only_idx'::regclass)
            + pg_relation_size('perf.orders_channel_only_idx'::regclass))::numeric
             / 1024 / 1024, 1)     AS bitmap_index_mb,
       round(pg_relation_size('perf.orders_status_channel_idx'::regclass)::numeric
             / 1024 / 1024, 1)     AS composite_index_mb,
       false                       AS keep_singles,
       'Nothing in this workload filters on channel alone, and status alone '
       || 'is served by the composite as a left prefix, so the two singles '
       || 'are write cost with no read benefit.' AS why
FROM m;

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — hand-roll the skip scan

`perf.orders` has 2,000,000 rows and 40 distinct `tenant_id` values, and an
index on `(tenant_id, placed_at)`.

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT tenant_id FROM perf.orders ORDER BY tenant_id;
```

PostgreSQL has no loose index scan, so this reads every index entry.

Edit `ex6/solution.sql` to return the same 40 rows using a recursive CTE
that performs one index descent per distinct value.

**Measurable goal:** the plan's total buffers must be under 200 (against
several thousand for the naive query), and the result must be identical —
40 rows, ascending.

Then, as a second statement, return **one row, three columns**:
`descents` (40), `naive_entries_read` (2000000), and `speedup_shape` — the
text `'O(distinct * log n) instead of O(n)'`.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b03_composite_order ex6`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The seed is `SELECT min(tenant_id) FROM perf.orders`, which the planner
answers with an `Index Only Scan` plus `LIMIT 1` — one descent. Every step
after it is the same query with `WHERE tenant_id > <previous>`.

## Hint 2

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE t AS (
  SELECT min(tenant_id) AS tenant_id FROM perf.orders
  UNION ALL
  SELECT (SELECT min(o.tenant_id) FROM perf.orders o
          WHERE o.tenant_id > t.tenant_id)
  FROM t
  WHERE t.tenant_id IS NOT NULL)
SELECT tenant_id FROM t WHERE tenant_id IS NOT NULL ORDER BY tenant_id;
```

## Hint 3

Two details make it terminate: the scalar subquery returns `NULL` when
nothing is greater, and the `WHERE t.tenant_id IS NOT NULL` in the recursive
arm stops the recursion one step later. Filtering the `NULL` out again in
the final select is what keeps the result clean.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Different framing: this is a "next greater value" loop, the same shape as
paginating by key (V3·B7). If you have written keyset pagination, you have
already written this — the only difference is that here each step advances
to the next *distinct* value rather than the next row.

## Hint 2

Aggregates with `min()`/`max()` over an indexed column are special-cased by
the planner into `Result` + `Limit` + `Index Only Scan Backward/Forward`.
That rewrite is what makes each recursion step a descent instead of a scan —
check for it in the plan before trusting the buffer count.

## Hint 3

A recursive CTE cannot reference itself inside an aggregate, which is why
the `min()` lives in a scalar subquery in the select list rather than in the
`FROM`. If you get "recursive reference to query t must not appear within an
aggregate function", that is the rule you hit, and this is the workaround.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b03_composite_order / ex6 — a loose index scan, by hand
WITH RECURSIVE t AS (
  SELECT min(tenant_id) AS tenant_id FROM perf.orders
  UNION ALL
  SELECT (SELECT min(o.tenant_id)
          FROM perf.orders o
          WHERE o.tenant_id > t.tenant_id)
  FROM t
  WHERE t.tenant_id IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT tenant_id
FROM t
WHERE tenant_id IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY tenant_id;

SELECT 40      AS descents,
       2000000 AS naive_entries_read,
       'O(distinct * log n) instead of O(n)' AS speedup_shape;

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — a unique index that also covers the read

Orders arrive from partners with an idempotency key:

```sql
ALTER TABLE perf.orders
  ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS external_id text;
UPDATE perf.orders SET external_id = 'ext-' || tenant_id || '-' || id;
```

Two access paths need serving:

- the ingest upsert, `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, external_id) DO
  NOTHING`, thousands per minute;
- the partner status check, `SELECT id, status, placed_at FROM perf.orders
  WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND external_id = $2`, also thousands per minute.

Write `ex7/indexes.sql` with **one** index serving both, and
`ex7/solution.sql` with the status-check query plus a second statement
returning `constraint_intact` (boolean `true`) and `covers_read` (boolean
`true`).

**Measurable goal:** the status check plans as `Index Only Scan` with
`Heap Fetches: 0`, and an attempt to insert a duplicate
`(tenant_id, external_id)` still fails.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b03_composite_order ex7`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, external_id)` requires a unique index on exactly
those two columns, in that key. The read wants three more columns back.
Before PostgreSQL 11 those requirements were in conflict.

## Hint 2

```sql
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... ON perf.orders (tenant_id, external_id)
  INCLUDE (id, status, placed_at);
```

`INCLUDE` columns are not part of the key, so uniqueness is still over the
two columns and `ON CONFLICT` still matches the index.

## Hint 3

`Heap Fetches: 0` needs a vacuum after the bulk `UPDATE` that populated
`external_id` — that update rewrote every row in the table and cleared the
visibility map completely.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about what would break if you put the read columns in the key instead.
`(tenant_id, external_id, status)` is unique over three columns, which means
two rows with the same external id and different statuses would both be
accepted — the constraint you actually needed is gone, and the bug appears
months later as duplicate orders.

## Hint 2

Consider the write cost you just accepted. Every insert now writes an index
entry carrying five columns instead of two, and every update to `status`
changes an `INCLUDE` column, which means the update cannot be HOT and must
write a new index entry. For a status column that changes several times per
order, that is a real trade — worth making here, worth naming out loud.

## Hint 3

Test the constraint rather than asserting it:
`INSERT INTO perf.orders (id, tenant_id, external_id, ...) VALUES (...)`
with an existing pair should raise `duplicate key value violates unique
constraint`. Do it inside a transaction you roll back.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b03_composite_order / ex7 — the partner status check, answered from the index
SELECT id, status, placed_at
FROM perf.orders
WHERE tenant_id = 7
  AND external_id = 'ext-7-918273';

SELECT true AS constraint_intact,  -- uniqueness is still over (tenant_id, external_id)
       true AS covers_read;        -- id, status, placed_at ride along as payload
references.indexes.sql:
-- v3b03_composite_order / ex7 — one unique index that also covers the read
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS orders_tenant_external_uidx
  ON perf.orders (tenant_id, external_id)
  INCLUDE (id, status, placed_at);

-- The bulk UPDATE that populated external_id rewrote every row, so the
-- visibility map is empty until this runs.
VACUUM (ANALYZE) perf.orders;

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — the IN list that loses your ordering

The multi-tenant admin view:

```sql
SELECT id, tenant_id, placed_at
FROM perf.orders
WHERE tenant_id IN (3, 7, 9, 21)
ORDER BY placed_at DESC
LIMIT 20;
```

With `(tenant_id, placed_at DESC)` the plan descends four times — and then
sorts, because the four ordered streams are not one ordered stream.

Edit `ex8/solution.sql` with a rewrite that returns the identical 20 rows
**without a full sort of all four tenants' orders**, using the same index.

**Measurable goal:** the plan reads at most a few hundred rows total (four
partial scans of ~20 each plus the merge), not the ~200,000 rows those four
tenants own. `LIMIT`-per-branch is the trick; state in a comment why 20 per
branch is sufficient and 19 would not be.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b03_composite_order ex8`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The index gives you each tenant's orders already sorted. What you need is
the twenty newest across four sorted streams — and you only ever need
twenty from each stream to guarantee the global top twenty.

## Hint 2

`UNION ALL` four `LIMIT 20` subqueries, then order and limit again:

```sql
(SELECT ... WHERE tenant_id = 3 ORDER BY placed_at DESC LIMIT 20)
UNION ALL
(SELECT ... WHERE tenant_id = 7 ORDER BY placed_at DESC LIMIT 20)
...
ORDER BY placed_at DESC LIMIT 20;
```

## Hint 3

`LATERAL` is the tidier form: put the tenant list in a `VALUES` clause and
join laterally to a per-tenant `LIMIT 20`. Same plan shape, one place to
change the list.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Prove the bound to yourself instead of taking it on faith. If the global top
twenty contained 21 rows from one tenant, that tenant's own top twenty would
have to be missing one of them — impossible, since it is sorted. So twenty
per branch is exactly enough, and nineteen is not: all twenty could come
from one tenant.

## Hint 2

This is the manual version of a `MergeAppend`, which PostgreSQL does build
automatically over *partitions* of a partitioned table. If these four
tenants were four partitions, the planner would merge the ordered streams
for you and stop after twenty rows. Recognising when a rewrite is really a
missing physical design is worth as much as the rewrite.

## Hint 3

Keep the outer `ORDER BY` and `LIMIT`. Without them you return up to eighty
rows in an undefined order, which passes a careless eye and fails the
grader.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b03_composite_order / ex8 — merge four ordered streams instead of sorting
-- 20 per branch is exactly sufficient: if the global top 20 held 21 rows from
-- one tenant, that tenant's own ordered top 20 would be missing one of them.
-- 19 per branch is not: all 20 winners can come from a single tenant.
SELECT o.id, o.tenant_id, o.placed_at
FROM (VALUES (3), (7), (9), (21)) AS t(tenant_id)
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT id, tenant_id, placed_at
  FROM perf.orders
  WHERE tenant_id = t.tenant_id
  ORDER BY placed_at DESC
  LIMIT 20
) o
ORDER BY o.placed_at DESC
LIMIT 20;

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — three queries that want three different orders

The reporting service issues these against `perf.orders`:

```sql
-- R1  tenant timeline, 3000/min
SELECT id, status, total_cents FROM perf.orders
WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND placed_at BETWEEN $2 AND $3
ORDER BY placed_at DESC LIMIT 100;

-- R2  global refund queue, 200/min
SELECT id, tenant_id, placed_at FROM perf.orders
WHERE status = 'refunded' AND placed_at >= $1
ORDER BY placed_at DESC LIMIT 50;

-- R3  per-tenant status rollup, 20/min
SELECT tenant_id, status, count(*), sum(total_cents)
FROM perf.orders
WHERE placed_at >= $1
GROUP BY tenant_id, status;
```

Write `challenge/indexes.sql` with **at most two** new indexes, and
`challenge/solution.sql` returning your design as a result set: one row per
query label with columns `q`, `index_used`, `positions` (how many key
columns position the descent), `sort_avoided` (boolean), `index_only`
(boolean), and `why` (one sentence).

Constraints, all checkable in a plan:

- R1 and R2 must each avoid a `Sort` node entirely.
- At least one of the three must plan as `Index Only Scan` with
  `Heap Fetches: 0`.
- Total added index size under 250 MB (`pg_relation_size`).
- You may not create an index whose key is a left prefix of another index
  you create.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b03_composite_order challenge`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Write the three shapes out as (equality columns | range/order column |
returned columns) triples first. R1 is (tenant_id | placed_at DESC | status,
total_cents). R2 is (status | placed_at DESC | tenant_id). R3 has no
equality at all.

## Hint 2

R3 is the one to solve last, and possibly not at all. It runs 20 times a
minute over a date range and groups by two columns — it may be perfectly
happy scanning one of the indexes you built for R1 or R2, or even the heap.
Deciding not to add an index is a legitimate answer if you defend it.

## Hint 3

Two candidates: `(tenant_id, placed_at DESC) INCLUDE (status, total_cents)`
for R1, and `(status, placed_at DESC)` for R2. Then check whether R3 can ride
on the first one — it can, as an index-only scan, because that index carries
tenant, time, status and amount, which is every column R3 touches.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the frequencies. R1 runs 150 times more often than R3. If one
index can serve R1 perfectly and R3 adequately, that is a better outcome
than three perfect indexes, because the third index taxes every insert for
twenty queries a minute.

## Hint 2

Check the prefix constraint against your own answer before submitting: is
`(status, placed_at DESC)` a prefix of your other index, or the other way
around? Neither, if you chose the pair above — but if you were tempted to
add `(tenant_id)` for something, that one *is* a prefix and the rule bites.

## Hint 3

For `positions`, count honestly. R3 has no equality predicate, so if it uses
the R1 index at all it positions on nothing and scans the whole index —
which is still a win if the index is a third of the table's size and the
scan is index-only. Write that in `why` rather than pretending it descends.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b03_composite_order / challenge — two indexes, three queries
SELECT *
FROM (VALUES
  ('R1', 'orders_tenant_placed_cover_idx', 2, true, true,
   'Equality on tenant_id then placed_at DESC positions and orders; status '
   'and total_cents ride along as INCLUDE, so the 3000/min query is an '
   'index-only scan that stops after 100 entries.'),
  ('R2', 'orders_status_placed_desc_idx', 2, true, false,
   'Equality on status then placed_at DESC gives both the filter and the '
   'ordering; LIMIT 50 stops the scan after fifty entries, and the two '
   'returned columns are cheap heap fetches at that volume.'),
  ('R3', 'orders_tenant_placed_cover_idx', 0, false, true,
   'No equality predicate, so it scans the whole index - but that index '
   'carries every column R3 touches, so it is an index-only scan over a '
   'third of the bytes the heap would cost, at 20 queries per minute.')
) AS v(q, index_used, positions, sort_avoided, index_only, why)
ORDER BY q;

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 — read four indexes, predict six plans

A table you have just inherited:

```sql
CREATE TABLE perf.shipments (
  id           bigint PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id     bigint      NOT NULL,
  tenant_id    int         NOT NULL,
  carrier      text        NOT NULL,
  status       text        NOT NULL,
  shipped_at   timestamptz NOT NULL,
  delivered_at timestamptz
);

CREATE INDEX s1 ON perf.shipments (tenant_id, shipped_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX s2 ON perf.shipments (carrier, status);
CREATE INDEX s3 ON perf.shipments (order_id) INCLUDE (status, delivered_at);
CREATE INDEX s4 ON perf.shipments (tenant_id);
```

Six queries:

```
A  WHERE order_id = $1
B  WHERE tenant_id = $1 ORDER BY shipped_at DESC LIMIT 20
C  WHERE status = 'in_transit'
D  WHERE carrier = 'dhl' AND status = 'in_transit' ORDER BY shipped_at
E  WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND shipped_at >= $2 AND carrier = 'dhl'
F  WHERE delivered_at IS NULL AND tenant_id = $1
```

Edit `review1/solution.sql` to return **one row per query**, ordered by
label: `q`, `index` (the index the planner should choose, or `'none'`),
`sort_needed` (boolean), `index_only_possible` (boolean), and `note`.

Then add a second statement returning **one row, two columns**:
`drop_me` (the name of the one index that is pure overhead) and `reason`.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b03_composite_order review1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Go query by query and ask only two things: is there a left prefix that this
predicate constrains, and does the index's declared order match any `ORDER
BY` the query has?

## Hint 2

C constrains `status` alone, which is the *second* column of `s2` — no
descent. D constrains both of `s2`'s columns but orders by a column `s2`
does not carry, so it descends and then sorts.

## Hint 3

For the drop: `s4` is `(tenant_id)`, and `s1` is `(tenant_id, shipped_at
DESC)`. Every query `s4` can serve, `s1` serves as a left prefix, at the
cost of a slightly wider tree. That is the textbook redundancy.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Different entry point: for each index, list the queries it serves, rather
than for each query listing the indexes. Two of the four indexes will turn
out to serve exactly one query each, one serves several, and one serves
nothing that another does not already serve. That view makes the drop
obvious and also tells you which index is load-bearing.

## Hint 2

F is the interesting one. `delivered_at IS NULL` is indexable — B-trees
store NULLs — but no index here leads with it, so `s1` descends on
`tenant_id` and the NULL test becomes a per-entry check. Note in the `note`
column what index would serve F properly, and notice that the honest answer
is a *partial* index, which is V3·B4.

## Hint 3

`index_only_possible` depends on the select list as much as the predicate.
A is the clean case: `s3` carries `status` and `delivered_at` as payload, so
a query returning only those columns never touches the heap — provided the
table has been vacuumed.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b03_composite_order / review1 — six queries against four indexes
SELECT *
FROM (VALUES
  ('A', 's3',   false, true,
   'equality on the leading key column; status and delivered_at are INCLUDE '
   'payload, so a query returning only those never visits the heap'),
  ('B', 's1',   false, false,
   'equality on tenant_id positions, shipped_at DESC supplies the order, '
   'LIMIT 20 stops the scan after twenty entries'),
  ('C', 'none', false, false,
   'status is the second column of s2, so there is no left prefix to descend '
   'to; expect a sequential scan'),
  ('D', 's2',   true,  false,
   'both s2 columns are equalities so the descent is exact, but shipped_at '
   'is not in s2 and the ordering must be sorted afterwards'),
  ('E', 's1',   false, false,
   'tenant_id positions and shipped_at narrows; carrier is not in s1 so it '
   'becomes a per-entry check or a heap filter'),
  ('F', 's1',   false, false,
   'descends on tenant_id and checks delivered_at IS NULL per entry; a '
   'partial index WHERE delivered_at IS NULL would serve it properly')
) AS v(q, index, sort_needed, index_only_possible, note)
ORDER BY q;

SELECT 's4' AS drop_me,
       'Its key (tenant_id) is a strict left prefix of s1 (tenant_id, '
       || 'shipped_at DESC), so every query it can serve is served by s1 at '
       || 'the cost of a slightly wider tree; keeping it only taxes writes.'
         AS reason;

lessons.title: V3·B4 — Partial, expression, GIN and GiST indexes
lessons.summary: B-trees index whole column values for ordered comparisons. The other index shapes cover what is left: a partial index over the 0.4% of rows anyone queries, an expression index over a value you compute rather than store, GIN for containment inside documents and arrays, GiST for ranges and exclusion constraints. This sector builds all four, and shows the predicate-proof and immutability traps that make them silently useless.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·B4 — Partial, expression, GIN and GiST indexes

Three sectors of B-trees have taught you one shape of index: whole column
values, sorted, compared with `<`, `=`, `>`. Most schemas contain at least
one query that shape cannot serve well, and reaching for a bigger B-tree is
the wrong reflex. This sector covers the four alternatives you will actually
use, and — more usefully — the specific ways each one silently fails to be
used at all.

## Partial indexes: index the rows anyone asks about

`perf.orders` has 2,000,000 rows, of which 8,000 are `pending`. The order
processor polls them every second:

```sql
SELECT id, customer_id FROM perf.orders
WHERE status = 'pending'
ORDER BY placed_at
LIMIT 100;
```

A full index on `(status, placed_at)` is 60 MB, of which 59.8 MB describes
rows this query will never look at. The partial version:

```sql
CREATE INDEX orders_pending_idx ON perf.orders (placed_at)
WHERE status = 'pending';
```

is about 250 kB, stays entirely in cache, and — the part people miss — is
only written when a row *enters or leaves* the pending state, not on every
insert of a shipped order. Queue tables are the canonical case, and the
smaller the hot subset, the more absurd the win.

The catch is that the planner must **prove** your query's predicate implies
the index's. It does that with a limited theorem prover over
constant-folded expressions, not by understanding your domain. So:

```sql
WHERE status = 'pending'                       -- proved, index used
WHERE status = 'pending' AND tenant_id = 7     -- proved, index used
WHERE status <> 'shipped'                      -- NOT proved, index ignored
WHERE status = $1                              -- NOT proved at plan time
                                               -- unless $1 folds to 'pending'
```

The third line is the one that ruins afternoons. It is logically true that
your data only ever holds five statuses, so `<> 'shipped'` overlaps
`= 'pending'` — but the planner cannot know that, and it will not guess.
Write the predicate the index expects, or index a wider condition.

Two more rules: the predicate must be immutable, so `WHERE created_at >
now() - interval '7 days'` is rejected — a "recent rows" index has to be
rebuilt on a fixed boundary; and a **partial unique** index gives you
conditional uniqueness, which is how soft deletes are done properly:

```sql
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX customers_email_live_uidx
  ON perf.customers (lower(email)) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;
```

## Expression indexes: index what you compare

An index stores what you told it to store. If your query compares
`lower(email)`, index `lower(email)`:

```sql
CREATE INDEX customers_lower_email_idx ON perf.customers (lower(email));
SELECT id FROM perf.customers WHERE lower(email) = 'user4711@example.com';
```

The expression must be `IMMUTABLE`: same input, same output, forever. That
rules out anything touching the session time zone or the current time, which
is why `CREATE INDEX ... ((placed_at::date))` is rejected — casting
`timestamptz` to `date` depends on `TimeZone`. The fix is to be explicit
about the zone, which makes the expression immutable again:

```sql
CREATE INDEX orders_day_utc_idx
  ON perf.orders ((date_trunc('day', placed_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')));
```

A quiet bonus: `ANALYZE` collects statistics *on the expression itself* and
stores them in `pg_stats` under the index name, so an expression index also
fixes the row estimates for that expression — sometimes the larger win.

## GIN: one entry per element, not per row

GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) indexes the *contents* of a value: every
key of a `jsonb` document, every element of an array, every lexeme of a
`tsvector`, every trigram of a string. The posting list under each key holds
the rows containing it, which makes containment questions cheap:

```sql
CREATE INDEX events_payload_gin ON perf.events USING gin (payload);
SELECT * FROM perf.events WHERE payload @> '{"kind": "refund"}';
```

Two operator classes matter. The default `jsonb_ops` indexes keys *and*
values separately and supports `?`, `?|`, `?&` as well as `@>`.
`jsonb_path_ops` hashes whole key-value paths: roughly a third the size,
noticeably faster for `@>`, and unable to answer key-existence questions.
Pick `jsonb_path_ops` unless you actually use `?`.

GIN's costs are real. Inserts are expensive, so GIN buffers them in a
"pending list" (`fastupdate`, on by default) that is flushed when it exceeds
`gin_pending_list_limit` — which means one unlucky insert pays for
everybody's, and a query may have to scan the unsorted pending list. GIN
also cannot supply ordering, and it cannot answer inequality.

Trigram search is the same machinery applied to text:

```sql
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm;
CREATE INDEX customers_email_trgm ON perf.customers
  USING gin (email gin_trgm_ops);
SELECT id FROM perf.customers WHERE email ILIKE '%4711%';
```

That is the only practical way to index a leading-wildcard `LIKE`.

## GiST: for things that overlap

GiST is a framework for indexes over data with no total order — geometry,
ranges, `tsvector` for weighted search, and nearest-neighbour ordering with
`<->`. Its most valuable feature in ordinary schemas is the exclusion
constraint, which enforces "these two rows must not overlap":

```sql
ALTER TABLE perf.reservations
  ADD CONSTRAINT no_double_booking
  EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during WITH &&);
```

That is a correctness feature you cannot express with a unique constraint,
and it is backed by an index that also serves range queries. `btree_gist`
supplies the `WITH =` operator for scalar columns; `btree_gin` does the
equivalent for GIN, letting one index combine `tenant_id = 7` with
`payload @> '...'`.

## Mission set

Ten missions: build a queue index two hundred times smaller than the naive
one, hit the predicate-proof wall and get past it, add conditional
uniqueness for soft deletes, index an expression and inherit its statistics,
break and repair an immutability error, compare `jsonb_ops` with
`jsonb_path_ops` in bytes and buffers, make a leading-wildcard search fast,
and enforce non-overlap with a GiST exclusion constraint.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b04_partial_expression_gin`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - sql/v3b04_partial_expression_gin

Four index shapes, four failure modes. The shapes are easy; the failure
modes are what this sector is for, because each one produces a valid index
that the planner then declines to use, with no error and no warning.

## Notes

**A partial index is a normal index over a subset of rows.** Everything you
know about B-trees still applies inside it — column order, `INCLUDE`,
ordering. What changes is size, write cost, and usability: it is written
only when a row enters, leaves, or moves within the predicate, and it can
only be used when the planner proves your predicate implies the index's.

**The proof is syntactic and shallow.** `predicate_implied_by()` works over
constant-folded clauses using operator properties and a small set of rules.
`x = 'pending'` implies `x = 'pending'`; `x = 'pending' AND y = 7` implies
`x = 'pending'`; `x > 10` implies `x > 5`. It does not know that your five
statuses are exhaustive, does not reason across `OR` well, and cannot see
the value of a parameter at plan time unless the plan is a custom plan for
those parameters. When your partial index is ignored, the first thing to
check is whether the query text contains the index's predicate literally.

**Partial unique indexes are the correct soft-delete pattern.** `UNIQUE
(email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL` allows any number of deleted rows with the
same email and exactly one live one. There is no way to express that with a
table constraint, which is why it is a bare `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` rather
than an `ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT` — and consequently why
`ON CONFLICT` needs the *inferred* form with a matching `WHERE` clause:
`ON CONFLICT (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL DO UPDATE ...`.

**Expression indexes need `IMMUTABLE`, and the check is about the function's
declaration, not its behaviour.** `lower(text)` is immutable; `lower(citext)`
is not, because collation. `timestamptz::date` is `STABLE` because the
answer depends on `TimeZone`. `now()`, `random()`, `current_user` are all
`VOLATILE`. If you must index a stable expression, pin the variable part:
`placed_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC'` is immutable because the zone is a literal.

**Expression statistics come free with the index.** `ANALYZE` samples the
expression's values and stores them as if the expression were a column,
which you can read back from `pg_stats` filtered on the index name. This is
occasionally worth creating an index *for* — a badly estimated
`date_trunc('month', ...)` group key can produce a plan that is wrong by a
factor of thirty, and the index fixes the estimate as a side effect.

**GIN stores keys, not rows, and answers only containment-shaped
questions.** `@>`, `?`, `?|`, `?&`, `@@`, `&&` — never `<`, never `ORDER BY`.
A GIN scan produces a bitmap, so a GIN plan is always a `Bitmap Heap Scan`
and always unordered. When your query needs both containment and ordering,
you need the ordering to come from somewhere else, usually a small `LIMIT`
over a re-sorted bitmap or a second B-tree.

**`fastupdate` trades insert latency for query latency and predictability.**
New entries go to an unsorted pending list; queries must scan it in addition
to the tree; and when it exceeds `gin_pending_list_limit` (4 MB default) the
unlucky transaction that crosses the line pays to merge it. On a
write-heavy table where p99 latency matters, `ALTER INDEX ... SET
(fastupdate = off)` makes every insert slower and none of them catastrophic.

**GiST is a template, not an index type.** It supplies a page layout and a
search algorithm and asks the opclass for `consistent`, `union`, `penalty`
and `picksplit`. That is why `btree_gist` can exist at all, and why GiST is
lossy in general: `consistent` may return "maybe", so the heap recheck is
part of the design rather than a degradation. It is also why GiST supports
`ORDER BY col <-> point` — nearest-neighbour search as an index scan, which
no B-tree can do.

**Exclusion constraints are the feature nobody knows they need.** Anything
of the form "no two rows may both X and overlap in Y" — room bookings,
employee shifts, price validity windows, IP allocations — is one
`EXCLUDE USING gist` away, enforced by the database rather than by
application code that forgets under concurrency. The cost is a GiST index
and a slower insert path.

**BRIN is the fifth shape, and it is not in this sector's missions.** For a
table physically ordered by a column — append-only time series being the
whole use case — a BRIN index storing min/max per 128-page range is
kilobytes where a B-tree is gigabytes. It is only ever as good as the
physical correlation, so it is brittle in exactly the way partial indexes
are not, but on a 500 GB append-only log it is the difference between
possible and not.

## Mission notes

**ex1–ex3** are the partial-index arc: build one, hit the proof wall, then
use partial uniqueness for a soft delete.

**ex4–ex5** are expressions: index one, then break the immutability rule and
repair it, which is the error message everyone meets eventually.

**ex6** measures `jsonb_ops` against `jsonb_path_ops` in bytes and buffers,
so the choice stops being folklore.

**ex7** makes `ILIKE '%...%'` fast with trigrams and asks what it cost.

**ex8** enforces non-overlap with an exclusion constraint and proves it by
trying to violate it.

## Further reading

- [Partial indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-partial.html)
  — including the implication rules, with examples.
- [Indexes on expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-expressional.html)
- [GIN](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/gin.html) and
  [jsonb indexing](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/datatype-json.html#JSON-INDEXING)
- [pg_trgm](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/pgtrgm.html) — trigram
  similarity and the operator classes for `LIKE`/`ILIKE`/`~`.
- [Exclusion constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-constraints.html#DDL-CONSTRAINTS-EXCLUSION)
  and [range types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/rangetypes.html).
