# V3·B5 — Nested loop, hash, merge: why the planner picks one

Four sectors of index work have been building toward this one. An index
changes what a scan costs; the join strategy decides how many times that
scan happens. Get the strategy wrong and the fastest index in the world runs
180,000 times.

PostgreSQL has three join algorithms and no others. Every join you have ever
run was one of them.

## Nested loop

For each row of the outer input, scan the inner input for matches.

```
Nested Loop  (actual rows=41800 loops=1)
  ->  Seq Scan on customers c   (rows=17600 loops=1)
  ->  Index Scan using orders_customer_id_idx on orders o
        (rows=2 loops=17600)
```

Cost is `outer_rows × inner_cost_per_lookup`. That is linear in the outer
side and completely dominated by whether the inner side has an index on the
join key. With one, each lookup is three or four buffers; without one, each
lookup is a full scan of the inner table and the plan is quadratic.

Nested loop is the only strategy that can start returning rows immediately,
so it wins whenever the outer side is small — a handful of rows from a
selective filter — or when a `LIMIT` means you will stop early. It is the
right answer far more often than its reputation suggests, and it is also the
single most common cause of a query that was fast in staging and is not in
production, because "small outer side" is an estimate.

**Memoize** (PostgreSQL 14) fixed the worst case. When the outer side
repeats join keys, a `Memoize` node caches inner results:

```
->  Memoize  (actual rows=2 loops=17600)
      Cache Key: c.id
      Hits: 15200  Misses: 2400  Evictions: 0  Memory Usage: 1904kB
```

Read the hit ratio the way you would read a cache in any other system. High
hits mean the loop is much cheaper than its `loops` count suggests; high
misses with evictions mean `work_mem` is too small and the node is pure
overhead.

## Hash join

Build a hash table from the smaller input, then stream the larger one past
it.

```
Hash Join  (actual rows=402118 loops=1)
  Hash Cond: (o.customer_id = c.id)
  ->  Seq Scan on orders o  (rows=2000000)
  ->  Hash  (rows=200000)
        Buckets: 262144  Batches: 1  Memory Usage: 14336kB
        ->  Seq Scan on customers c
```

Cost is `build_rows + probe_rows` — linear in both, with a large constant
for building. It needs no indexes and no ordering, which makes it the
workhorse for analytical queries that touch most of both tables. It requires
an equality condition: there is no such thing as a hash join on `<`.

The line to read is `Batches`. When the build side does not fit in
`work_mem`, PostgreSQL partitions both inputs by hash into batches, spills
them to temporary files, and processes one batch at a time. `Batches: 8`
means both sides were written to disk and read back. Worse, the planner
decided the batch count *before* it saw the data, so a skewed key
distribution can produce one enormous batch and seven empty ones.

## Merge join

Sort both inputs on the join key — or take them already sorted from indexes
— and walk them in step, like merging two sorted lists.

```
Merge Join  (actual rows=402118 loops=1)
  Merge Cond: (o.customer_id = c.id)
  ->  Index Scan using orders_customer_id_idx on orders o
  ->  Index Scan using customers_pkey on customers c
```

Cost is `sort_a + sort_b + a + b`, and the sorts are free when indexes
supply the order. Merge join is the specialist: it wins on large joins where
both sides are already sorted, it is the only strategy whose memory use is
bounded regardless of input size, and it handles inequality conditions in
range joins. When you see one, look for whether the sorts are real `Sort`
nodes — if they are, the planner chose to sort two million rows, and it
believed that was cheaper than hashing them.

## How the choice is actually made

The planner enumerates join orders and, for each pair, prices all three
algorithms with the same cost model you have been reading since V3·B1. The
inputs to that arithmetic are row estimates. So:

> Almost every "the planner chose a stupid join" is really "the planner had
> a wrong row estimate". Fix the estimate (V3·B6) before you fight the
> strategy.

The `enable_*` flags — `enable_nestloop`, `enable_hashjoin`,
`enable_mergejoin` — are diagnostic tools, not fixes. Turning one off adds a
cost penalty of 10^10 rather than forbidding the plan, which makes them
perfect for asking "what would the second-best plan have been, and how much
worse did the planner think it was?".

Join *order* is a separate search. Up to `join_collapse_limit` (8) relations
the planner considers all orderings by dynamic programming; beyond
`geqo_threshold` (12) it switches to a genetic algorithm whose output is not
deterministic. A twelve-table report that plans differently on Tuesday is
usually this, and the fix is fewer joins in one statement — or, occasionally,
`join_collapse_limit = 1` plus explicit `JOIN` order that you have measured.

## Mission set

Ten missions: read a hash join's build side and batch count, compute the
break-even point between nested loop and hash by hand, cure a spilling hash
join, turn a bad nested loop into a good one, measure a Memoize hit ratio,
earn a merge join without a sort, tell semi joins from anti joins from
`LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL`, and watch planning time explode past
`join_collapse_limit`.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b05_join_strategies`

## Worked example — the break-even, computed

Joining `customers` (200,000 rows) to `orders` (2,000,000 rows) on
`customer_id`, with an index on the inner side. What outer row count makes a
hash join cheaper than a nested loop?

- Nested loop: `outer × 4 buffers × random_page_cost` ≈ `outer × 16` cost
  units, plus the outer scan.
- Hash join: build 200,000 rows (`200000 × cpu_tuple_cost` plus the scan of
  customers, ~1,400 pages) plus probe 2,000,000 rows. Call it 25,000 cost
  units before the outer side is even considered.

`outer × 16 = 25000` gives an outer side of about 1,500 rows. Below that,
loop; above it, hash. Now look at what a bad estimate does: the planner
thinks the filter yields 12 rows, so it loops — and the filter actually
yields 8,791, so the join costs 140,000 units instead of 25,000. Nothing
about the algorithm was wrong; the input to the arithmetic was.

## Worked example — a hash join that spilled

```
Hash Join  (actual time=891.2..4120.7 rows=1980114 loops=1)
  ->  Seq Scan on order_lines l  (rows=6000000)
  ->  Hash  (actual time=884.9..884.9 rows=2000000 loops=1)
        Buckets: 65536 (originally 262144)  Batches: 32 (originally 1)
        Memory Usage: 4224kB
        ->  Seq Scan on orders o  (rows=2000000)
  Buffers: shared hit=71040, temp read=41200 written=41200
```

Three tells. `Batches: 32 (originally 1)` means the planner expected the
build side to fit and it did not, so the executor re-partitioned at runtime.
`Buckets ... (originally 262144)` is the same story from the other side.
`temp read/written` is the physical cost: 41,200 blocks, 320 MB, written and
read back.

Two fixes, in order of preference. Reduce the build side — this query
selects three columns but the hash table stores whole tuples, so projecting
early can halve it. Then, if that is not enough, raise `work_mem` for this
statement only, with `SET LOCAL`. Raising it globally multiplies by every
concurrent sort and hash in the system.

## Common mistakes

- **Blaming the join algorithm for an estimate problem.** Check the row
  estimates on both inputs before you touch anything.
- **Using `enable_nestloop = off` as a fix.** It is a diagnostic. Shipping
  it means every join in that session, including good nested loops, is
  penalised.
- **Ignoring `loops` on the inner side.** V3·B1 exists for this.
- **Reading `Batches: 1` as "fine" without checking `Memory Usage`.** A hash
  table at 90% of `work_mem` is one data-growth event from spilling.
- **Raising `work_mem` globally to cure one query.** It is per node per
  connection.
- **Writing `NOT IN (SELECT ...)` over a nullable column.** No anti join,
  and wrong-looking results when a NULL appears.
- **Assuming an ORM's `IN` list is a semi join.** A literal `IN (1,2,3)` is
  an array condition, not a join at all.
- **Fighting a twelve-table join's plan instability** instead of splitting
  the query.

## Interview angle

*"When would a nested loop beat a hash join on a million-row table?"*

The strong answer inverts the question: the size of the *inner* table is
almost irrelevant, what matters is how many times you probe it. Give the
two cases. First, a small outer side — a filter yielding a few hundred rows
joined to an indexed inner table costs a few hundred descents, while a hash
join must build a table from something. Second, an early `LIMIT` — a nested
loop streams, so `LIMIT 10` stops after ten matches, where a hash join must
build the entire hash table before it can emit a single row.

Then name the failure mode without being asked: nested loops are the plan
that punishes bad estimates most harshly, because the error multiplies by
the loop count instead of adding. That is why a plan flip from hash to
nested loop after a data change is the classic 3 a.m. incident, and why
`Memoize`, `pg_stat_statements` and honest statistics are the real
mitigations rather than a hint.

## Check yourself

1. Name the cost formula for each of the three join algorithms.
2. Which strategy can return its first row without reading all of its
   inputs? Why does that matter under `LIMIT`?
3. What does `Batches: 8 (originally 1)` tell you happened at runtime?
4. Why does `SELECT *` make a hash join more likely to spill?
5. What does `Memoize` cache, and what does `Evictions: 41200` mean?
6. Which join algorithm handles a `<` join condition, and why can the other
   two not?
7. What is the difference between a semi join and an anti join in the plan?
8. Why is `NOT IN` over a nullable column both slow and semantically
   surprising?
9. What do the `enable_*` flags actually do to the cost model?
10. At how many relations does the planner switch to GEQO, and what symptom
    does that produce?
11. Your join's inner side shows `rows=1 loops=180000`. Where is the
    misestimate, and where is it not?
12. Give two ways to fix a spilling hash join that are not "raise
    `work_mem`".
13. When is a merge join the right answer?
lessons.fullReading:
# Reading - sql/v3b05_join_strategies

## The executor, one tuple at a time

All three join nodes implement the same interface — "give me your next
tuple" — and differ only in what they do between calls. A nested loop keeps
a pointer into the outer scan and re-scans the inner side per outer tuple.
A merge join keeps a position in each sorted input and advances whichever is
behind, with a small buffer for duplicate keys on the inner side. A hash
join does something structurally different: on its first call it drains its
entire inner input into a hash table, and only then does it start pulling
outer tuples. That asymmetry is the whole reason hash joins have a startup
cost equal to building the table, and the reason a `LIMIT 1` over a hash
join still reads a whole relation.

The hash table itself is an array of buckets sized to the next power of two
above the estimated inner row count, holding whole `MinimalTuple`s. That
detail explains an otherwise mysterious tuning trick: projecting away
columns *before* the join, with a subquery or by not writing `SELECT *`,
directly shrinks the hash table, because the tuples stored are the tuples
produced by the input node.

When the table will not fit in `work_mem`, the executor partitions on the
high bits of the hash. Both inputs are written to per-batch temporary files,
and batches are processed one at a time. Two properties of that scheme
matter: it doubles the batch count dynamically when a batch turns out too
big (`Batches: 32 (originally 1)`), and it cannot split a single key across
batches. A join key where one value covers 30% of rows therefore produces
one batch that is 30% of the data no matter how many batches exist, which is
why PostgreSQL keeps a special in-memory "skew bucket" for the most common
values of the outer side — a partial mitigation, not a cure.

## Memoize, and the rehabilitation of the nested loop

Before PostgreSQL 14, a nested loop over a repeating outer key re-executed
the inner scan every time: 17,600 outer rows with 40 distinct keys meant
17,600 index descents to answer 40 distinct questions. Memoize interposes a
hash table keyed by the parameters of the inner path, with LRU eviction
bounded by `work_mem`. It is only chosen when the planner's estimate of
distinct outer values is much smaller than the outer row count — an estimate
that comes from `n_distinct`, and is therefore only as good as V3·B6 makes
it.

Read the four counters as one story. `Hits` versus `Misses` is the ratio
you expect from `n_distinct`. `Evictions` above zero means the working set
exceeded the memory budget, and a Memoize that evicts constantly is worse
than none at all, because it pays hashing costs and still re-executes. The
node also refuses to cache anything containing volatile functions, so a
parameterised inner path calling `random()` or `now()` silently loses the
optimisation.

## Where the estimates come from, and where they break

The row estimate for a join is
`outer_rows × inner_rows × selectivity(join condition)`. For an equijoin on
`a.x = b.y`, selectivity is derived from the two columns' `n_distinct` and
their most-common-value lists: PostgreSQL matches MCVs on both sides
explicitly, then assumes uniformity over the rest. This works well for
foreign keys with even distributions and badly for skew — a join key where
one value dominates produces an estimate that is right on average and wrong
for every actual execution.

Since 9.6 the planner also uses foreign key constraints as a hint that a
join's selectivity is exactly `1/outer_rows` per row, which fixed a whole
class of multi-column join misestimates. It is one of the strongest
practical arguments for declaring foreign keys even in systems where the
application "already guarantees" integrity: the constraint is information
the planner uses.

Errors compound upward. A two-table join off by 10× feeds a three-table
join that is off by 100×, and by the fifth relation the plan is being chosen
by noise. This is the mechanism behind the folklore that "big joins are
unpredictable" — they are not unpredictable, they are compounding a
measurable error, and the fix is at the bottom of the tree.

## Join order: a search, not a rule

Given `n` relations, the number of possible join trees grows super
exponentially. PostgreSQL builds the cheapest plan bottom-up: all single
relations, then all pairs, then triples, keeping only the cheapest path (and
the cheapest *ordered* path, since ordering may pay off later) for each
subset. That is exponential in memory but tractable to about a dozen
relations, which is what `join_collapse_limit` and `from_collapse_limit`
govern — they control how many `FROM` items and explicit `JOIN`s the planner
is allowed to flatten into one search problem.

Past `geqo_threshold`, a genetic algorithm takes over: random plans, fitness
by cost, crossover, mutation. It is fast and it is *not deterministic*, so a
report with fourteen joins can plan well today and badly tomorrow with
unchanged data. If you have such a query, the options in order are: split it,
reduce the joins, materialise part of it, or — as a last resort — set
`join_collapse_limit = 1` and write the joins in the exact order you want,
accepting that you have now taken responsibility for a decision the planner
used to make.

## Reading a join you did not expect

Three signatures come up often enough to memorise. A `Nested Loop` whose
inner node shows `loops` in the tens of thousands and whose outer estimate
is a single-digit `rows=` is the classic misestimate flip: the fix is
upstream, at the scan. A `Hash Join` whose `Hash` node shows
`Batches: N (originally 1)` is a runtime spill: the fix is a narrower build
side or more memory for that statement. A `Merge Join` sitting above two
explicit `Sort` nodes means the planner paid to sort both inputs and still
thought it was winning, which usually means the alternative was a hash join
it expected to spill — check `work_mem` before you touch anything else.

There is a fourth signature that is not a problem at all: a `Materialize`
node under the inner side of a nested loop. It caches the inner input's rows
so that re-scanning does not re-execute the child, and it is the planner
doing exactly the right thing for a small inner relation. People see it and
assume something has gone wrong; nothing has.

Finally, note that the plan tells you the strategy but not the *reason*. To
get the reason you need the costs of the alternatives, and the only way to
see those is to disable the chosen strategy and re-plan. Two `EXPLAIN`s
and a subtraction is a complete answer to "why did it choose this?" — and it
is a much better habit than reasoning about what the planner ought to have
done.

## When not to touch any of this

When the query runs 40 ms and is called twice an hour. When the estimates are
already correct and the plan is simply the cost of the work — some joins are
expensive because they join a lot of rows, and no strategy fixes that; the
answer is a rollup table or a materialised view (sector 46). And when the
real problem is the number of statements: a nested loop inside the database
is thousands of times cheaper than the same loop in application code issuing
one query per row, so a plan you dislike may still be the best thing
happening in that request.

## Further reading

- [Planner/optimizer overview](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/planner-optimizer.html)
- [Controlling the planner with GUCs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-query.html)
- [`nodeHashjoin.c`](https://github.com/postgres/postgres/blob/master/src/backend/executor/nodeHashjoin.c)
  and [`nodeMemoize.c`](https://github.com/postgres/postgres/blob/master/src/backend/executor/nodeMemoize.c)
- [Genetic query optimizer](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/geqo.html)
- [Row estimation examples](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/row-estimation-examples.html)
  — the join-selectivity arithmetic, worked.

## Hint 1

The `Hash` node always sits above the build input. Everything printed on it
— buckets, batches, memory — describes the table built from its child.

## Hint 2

`Batches: 32 (originally 1)` means the planner expected one batch and the
executor had to re-partition 32 ways at runtime. The parenthesised number is
always the plan-time expectation.

## Hint 3

`Memory Usage: 4224kB` is what one batch used, so the whole table is roughly
`4224 × 32` kB — about 132 MB. Round that up when you propose a
`work_mem`, and remember the setting is per node per connection.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask which side *should* have been the build side. `orders` has two million
rows, `order_lines` six million — so the planner did choose the smaller one.
The problem is not the choice, it is that two million rows do not fit in
4 MB, and the plan-time estimate said they would.

## Hint 2

For `cheaper_fix`, the strongest answer is projection. The hash table stores
whole tuples from its input, so a build side that selects three narrow
columns instead of the whole row can be several times smaller — and unlike
`work_mem`, that fix costs nothing anywhere else in the system.

## Hint 3

Convert carefully: `temp written` is in 8 KB blocks, and both inputs are
written, so the 41,200 blocks cover both sides. 41,200 × 8 / 1024 is about
322 MB of temporary I/O for one join.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b05_join_strategies / ex1 — reading a spilled hash join
WITH h AS (
  SELECT 2000000::numeric AS build_rows, 32::numeric AS batches,
         4224::numeric AS mem_kb, 41200::numeric AS temp_blocks)
SELECT 'orders'                                  AS build_side,
       build_rows::bigint                        AS build_rows,
       (batches > 1)                             AS spilled,
       round(temp_blocks * 8 / 1024, 1)          AS temp_mb,
       round(mem_kb * batches / 1024, 1)         AS est_workmem_needed_mb,
       'Project the build side down to the columns the join actually needs; '
       || 'the hash table stores whole tuples, so a narrower input shrinks '
       || 'it without touching a global setting.' AS cheaper_fix
FROM h;

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — where the loop stops winning

Joining a filtered `perf.customers` to `perf.orders` on `customer_id`, with
`orders_customer_id_idx` present.

Cost inputs, using the planner's own units:

- one index descent plus heap fetch on the inner side: 4 pages at
  `random_page_cost = 4.0`, so 16 cost units per outer row;
- building a hash table from all 200,000 customers: scanning `customers`
  costs 1,400 pages (1,400 units) and hashing costs
  `200000 × cpu_tuple_cost (0.01)`, so 2,000 units;
- probing it with 2,000,000 orders: the `orders` scan is 20,000 pages, plus
  `2000000 × 0.01` for the probe.

Edit `ex2/solution.sql` to return **one row, five columns**:

1. `hash_fixed_cost` — build cost only (scan + hash), a whole number.
2. `loop_cost_per_outer_row` — 16.
3. `breakeven_outer_rows` — where nested-loop cost equals the hash join's
   fixed cost, rounded to a whole number.
4. `verdict_at_1200` — `'nested loop'` or `'hash join'` for an outer side of
   1,200 rows.
5. `verdict_at_8791` — the same for 8,791 rows.

**Measurable goal:** the two verdicts differ, and `breakeven_outer_rows`
lands between 100 and 1,000.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b05_join_strategies ex2`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Ignore the probe side for the break-even: both plans must scan `orders`
somehow, so the comparison is between "build a hash table" and "descend the
index once per outer row".

## Hint 2

`breakeven = hash_fixed_cost / loop_cost_per_outer_row`. Everything else is
a comparison against that threshold.

## Hint 3

Write the verdict columns as `CASE` expressions over the computed break-even
rather than typing the answers — that way the query still tells the truth
when you change `random_page_cost` in the CTE.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Different framing: this is the arithmetic behind every plan flip you will
ever debug. When an estimate says 12 outer rows and reality is 8,791, the
planner is not being stupid — it is applying this formula to a false input,
and the error is multiplied by 16 cost units per row.

## Hint 2

Try recomputing with `random_page_cost = 1.1` instead of 4.0: the per-row
loop cost drops to about 4.4 and the break-even moves out past 700 rows.
That single setting moves the boundary between two whole plan families,
which is why changing it is a whole-instance decision.

## Hint 3

Note what the model omits. Caching means the second and subsequent descents
into the same inner pages are buffer hits, which the planner accounts for
only crudely — real nested loops over a small hot inner table beat this
arithmetic, which is part of why `Memoize` exists.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b05_join_strategies / ex2 — the nested-loop / hash-join break-even
WITH c AS (
  SELECT 1400::numeric AS build_scan_cost,
         200000::numeric * 0.01 AS build_hash_cost,
         16::numeric AS loop_per_row)
SELECT round(build_scan_cost + build_hash_cost)::bigint      AS hash_fixed_cost,
       loop_per_row::bigint                                  AS loop_cost_per_outer_row,
       round((build_scan_cost + build_hash_cost) / loop_per_row)::bigint
                                                             AS breakeven_outer_rows,
       CASE WHEN 1200 * loop_per_row < build_scan_cost + build_hash_cost
            THEN 'nested loop' ELSE 'hash join' END           AS verdict_at_1200,
       CASE WHEN 8791 * loop_per_row < build_scan_cost + build_hash_cost
            THEN 'nested loop' ELSE 'hash join' END           AS verdict_at_8791
FROM c;

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — cure the spill without touching the server

The reconciliation join:

```sql
SELECT o.id, o.placed_at, l.sku, l.qty
FROM perf.orders o
JOIN perf.order_lines l ON l.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.status = 'refunded';
```

runs with `Batches: 16` and 300 MB of temporary I/O on the default 4 MB
`work_mem`.

Edit `ex3/solution.sql` to produce the same rows with `Batches: 1` and
`temp read=0 written=0`, under these constraints:

- you may use **one** `SET LOCAL` and it may not exceed `'32MB'`;
- you may restructure the query;
- you may not create an index.

**Measurable goal:** `dojo plan v3b05_join_strategies ex3` shows
`Batches: 1` and no `temp` buffers, with `work_mem` at 32 MB or less.

State in a comment how much of the improvement came from the restructuring
and how much from the memory.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b05_join_strategies ex3`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The build side is whichever input the planner thinks is smaller — here the
filtered `orders`. Its hash table stores whole tuples from that input, so
what it costs depends on how wide those tuples are.

## Hint 2

Filter and project *before* the join, in a subquery or CTE, so the hash
table holds two narrow columns instead of eight:

```sql
WITH r AS (SELECT id, placed_at FROM perf.orders WHERE status = 'refunded')
SELECT ...
```

## Hint 3

40,000 refunded orders at roughly 30 bytes per hashed tuple is about 1.2 MB
— comfortably inside even the default. The `SET LOCAL work_mem = '32MB'` is
then a safety margin rather than the fix, which is exactly the point of the
comment you have to write.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Approach it by asking what is in the hash table. People reach for
`work_mem` because the plan mentions memory, but the memory is a consequence
of tuple width times row count, and you control both. Reducing either is a
local fix; raising `work_mem` is a global one applied locally.

## Hint 2

Beware of a CTE that the planner materialises when you did not want it to.
Since PostgreSQL 12 a plain `WITH` is inlined when referenced once and not
recursive; adding `MATERIALIZED` forces a temporary result. Here inlining is
what you want, so do not add the keyword.

## Hint 3

Verify with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` twice, and compare `temp
read/written` rather than time. On a warm cache the timing difference can be
smaller than the noise while the temp blocks go cleanly to zero.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b05_join_strategies / ex3 — narrow the build side, then add a margin
-- Restructuring did the work: projecting refunded orders down to two columns
-- takes the hash table from ~130 MB of full rows to about 1.2 MB. The 32 MB
-- work_mem is headroom for growth, not the fix.
SET LOCAL work_mem = '32MB';

WITH refunded AS (
  SELECT id, placed_at
  FROM perf.orders
  WHERE status = 'refunded'
)
SELECT r.id, r.placed_at, l.sku, l.qty
FROM refunded r
JOIN perf.order_lines l ON l.order_id = r.id;

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — make the nested loop good

A new table arrives with no indexes:

```sql
CREATE TABLE perf.returns (
  id       bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id bigint      NOT NULL,
  reason   text        NOT NULL,
  filed_at timestamptz NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO perf.returns (order_id, reason, filed_at)
SELECT id, 'damaged', placed_at + interval '5 days'
FROM perf.orders WHERE status = 'refunded';
```

The support query:

```sql
SELECT r.id, r.reason, o.total_cents
FROM perf.returns r
JOIN perf.orders o ON o.id = r.order_id
WHERE r.filed_at >= timestamptz '2024-06-01'
ORDER BY r.filed_at
LIMIT 25;
```

The planner picks a nested loop — correctly, because of the `LIMIT` — but
each inner lookup is against a table with no usable path, and the query
takes seconds.

Write `ex4/indexes.sql` with **exactly two** indexes and `ex4/solution.sql`
with the unchanged query.

**Measurable goal:** the plan is a `Nested Loop` whose outer side is an
index scan producing 25 rows, whose inner side is an index scan with
`loops=25`, and total buffers under 200.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b05_join_strategies ex4`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two indexes, two jobs. One makes the outer side both filtered and ordered so
the `LIMIT` can stop early. The other makes each inner lookup a descent
rather than a scan.

## Hint 2

The inner side joins on `o.id`, which is already the primary key — so that
index exists. Look again at which table is inner: with a `LIMIT` and an
`ORDER BY` on `returns`, the planner wants `returns` as the outer side.

## Hint 3

`CREATE INDEX ON perf.returns (filed_at)` gives the outer side its ordered,
filtered scan. The second index is the one the *insert* left missing —
`perf.returns(order_id)` — which matters for the reverse join direction and
for the foreign-key checks any future `DELETE` on `orders` will perform.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Count the loops you expect before you build anything. `LIMIT 25` with an
ordered outer side means 25 inner lookups, each four buffers: about a
hundred buffers total. If your plan shows `loops` in the thousands, the
outer side is not ordered by the index and the executor is fetching rows it
will throw away.

## Hint 2

Notice why this is a nested loop rather than a hash join, and why that is
right: a hash join would have to build a table from one of the inputs before
returning a single row, and the query only wants twenty-five. Streaming
beats bulk whenever you stop early.

## Hint 3

Check the second index's real justification. Nothing in *this* query needs
`returns(order_id)`, but an unindexed foreign-key column makes every
`DELETE` or key-update on the parent table scan the child — the classic
missing index that only shows up as `Trigger for constraint` time in a
plan.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b05_join_strategies / ex4 — the query is fine; the access paths were not
SELECT r.id, r.reason, o.total_cents
FROM perf.returns r
JOIN perf.orders o ON o.id = r.order_id
WHERE r.filed_at >= timestamptz '2024-06-01'
ORDER BY r.filed_at
LIMIT 25;

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — did Memoize earn its place?

```sql
SELECT o.id, c.plan
FROM perf.orders o
JOIN perf.customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.tenant_id = 7 AND o.placed_at >= timestamptz '2024-06-01';
```

On PostgreSQL 14+ the plan contains:

```
->  Memoize  (actual time=0.001..0.001 rows=1 loops=41200)
      Cache Key: o.customer_id
      Cache Mode: logical
      Hits: 39180  Misses: 2020  Evictions: 0  Overflows: 0
      Memory Usage: 289kB
```

Edit `ex5/solution.sql` to return **one row, five columns**:

1. `hit_rate_pct` — hits ÷ (hits + misses) × 100, one decimal.
2. `descents_saved` — lookups avoided (integer).
3. `healthy` — boolean: `true` when evictions are zero *and* hit rate is
   above 50.
4. `distinct_keys_seen` — what `Misses` tells you about the number of
   distinct customers in this tenant's June orders.
5. `how_to_measure_benefit` — one sentence naming the setting you would
   toggle to quantify what Memoize saved.

**Measurable goal:** every column except the last is derived from the four
counters, not hard-coded.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b05_join_strategies ex5`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`Misses` is exactly the number of distinct cache keys the node ever saw —
each miss is the first time that key appeared, and every later occurrence is
a hit.

## Hint 2

Put the four counters in a CTE and derive everything: hit rate, saved
lookups (hits), health (a boolean expression over evictions and rate), and
distinct keys (misses).

## Hint 3

`SET LOCAL enable_memoize = off;` and re-run with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE,
BUFFERS)`. The difference in buffers between the two runs is what the cache
bought — which is a number rather than an opinion.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask when this node would be actively harmful. If the outer side's keys were
all distinct, every probe is a miss, and you pay hashing plus memory for
zero reuse. The planner avoids that using `n_distinct` — so a wrong
`n_distinct` (V3·B6) can produce a Memoize that is pure overhead.

## Hint 2

`Overflows` is the counter people miss: it counts entries too large for the
cache's per-entry limit, which happens when one key matches many inner rows.
A join where one customer has 50,000 orders can overflow constantly while
the hit rate still looks respectable.

## Hint 3

Note `Cache Mode: logical` versus `binary`. Logical mode compares keys with
the type's equality operator, binary compares raw bytes; binary is faster
but only valid when equality implies bitwise identity, which is not true for
`numeric`, `citext` or anything with a collation.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b05_join_strategies / ex5 — auditing a Memoize node
WITH m AS (
  SELECT 39180::numeric AS hits, 2020::numeric AS misses,
         0::numeric AS evictions)
SELECT round(hits / (hits + misses) * 100, 1)                AS hit_rate_pct,
       hits::bigint                                          AS descents_saved,
       (evictions = 0 AND hits / (hits + misses) * 100 > 50) AS healthy,
       misses::bigint                                        AS distinct_keys_seen,
       'Re-run with SET LOCAL enable_memoize = off and compare BUFFERS; the '
       || 'difference is what the cache actually saved.' AS how_to_measure_benefit
FROM m;

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — a merge join with no sorts

Merge join is the specialist: bounded memory, streams, and free when both
inputs arrive sorted.

The join:

```sql
SELECT o.id, o.total_cents, l.sku
FROM perf.orders o
JOIN perf.order_lines l ON l.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.placed_at >= timestamptz '2024-06-01';
```

Write `ex6/indexes.sql` so that a merge join is available **without any
`Sort` node**, and `ex6/solution.sql` with the query plus a second statement
returning **one row, four columns**: `sorts_in_plan` (0),
`memory_bounded` (boolean `true`), `beats_hash_when` (one sentence), and
`loses_to_hash_when` (one sentence).

You may add `SET LOCAL enable_hashjoin = off;` in `solution.sql` to see the
merge plan — say in a comment why that is a diagnostic and not a fix.

**Measurable goal:** with hash joins disabled, the plan shows `Merge Join`
over two index scans and zero `Sort` nodes.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b05_join_strategies ex6`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A merge join needs both inputs ordered by the join key: `orders` by `id`
(the primary key already provides it) and `order_lines` by `order_id`.

## Hint 2

```sql
CREATE INDEX order_lines_order_id_idx ON perf.order_lines (order_id);
```

That gives the second input its ordering. Whether the planner *chooses*
merge is a separate question — hence the diagnostic flag.

## Hint 3

For `beats_hash_when`: both inputs already sorted, both large, and memory
tight — merge streams and cannot spill the way a hash join does. For
`loses_to_hash_when`: either input needs a real sort, or one side is small
enough that building a hash table is trivial.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Watch what the `placed_at` predicate does to the ordering. Filtering
`orders` by date while scanning by `id` means either an index scan on the
primary key with a filter (ordered, but reads everything) or a scan on a
date index (selective, but ordered by date, not by `id`). That tension is
exactly why the planner often prefers hashing here, and noticing it is worth
more than the index.

## Hint 2

Merge join has one more property worth knowing: it can handle non-equality
conditions in a range join, which hash join cannot. If you ever join on
`a.ts BETWEEN b.start AND b.end`, merge and nested loop are your only
options.

## Hint 3

Be precise in the comment about `enable_hashjoin = off`. It does not forbid
hash joins; it adds a cost of 10^10, so the plan can still contain one if
nothing else is possible. Its use is comparative: read both costs and you
learn what the planner thought the alternative was worth.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b05_join_strategies / ex6 — a merge join fed by two ordered index scans
-- enable_hashjoin = off is a microscope, not a fix: it adds a 1e10 cost
-- penalty so we can see and price the second-best plan.
SET LOCAL enable_hashjoin = off;

SELECT o.id, o.total_cents, l.sku
FROM perf.orders o
JOIN perf.order_lines l ON l.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.placed_at >= timestamptz '2024-06-01';

SELECT 0    AS sorts_in_plan,
       true AS memory_bounded,
       'Both inputs are already ordered by the join key and both are large: '
       || 'merge streams them in one pass with bounded memory and cannot '
       || 'spill.'                                        AS beats_hash_when,
       'Either side needs a real Sort node, or one side is small enough that '
       || 'building a hash table costs less than the ordering does.'
                                                          AS loses_to_hash_when;

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — semi, anti, and the NOT IN trap

Three questions about customers who have never ordered:

```sql
-- (a)
SELECT count(*) FROM perf.customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM perf.orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);
-- (b)
SELECT count(*) FROM perf.customers c
LEFT JOIN perf.orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;
-- (c)
SELECT count(*) FROM perf.customers c
WHERE c.id NOT IN (SELECT o.customer_id FROM perf.orders o);
```

Edit `ex7/solution.sql` to return **one row per variant**, ordered by label,
with columns `variant` (`'a'`,`'b'`,`'c'`), `plan_node` (the join node type
you expect, text), `same_result` (boolean — does it return the same count as
(a)?), and `note` (one clause).

Then add a second statement: a single query returning the **correct** count
of customers with no orders, written the way you would ship it, plus a
comment naming why you chose that form.

**Measurable goal:** exactly one variant has `same_result = false` in the
general case, and your `note` for it names NULLs.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b05_join_strategies ex7`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

(a) and (b) both become `Anti Join` — the planner recognises the
`LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL` idiom and rewrites it. Check with `EXPLAIN` that
both say `Hash Anti Join`.

## Hint 2

(c) is different. If `orders.customer_id` is nullable, a single NULL in the
subquery makes `x NOT IN (...)` evaluate to NULL for every row, so the
result is zero — silently.

## Hint 3

Even when the column is `NOT NULL`, the planner often cannot use an anti
join for `NOT IN` and falls back to a materialised subplan with a per-row
scan. So (c) can be both slower and, in general, wrong.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Different entry: write down the three-valued logic by hand for one row.
`5 NOT IN (1, 2, NULL)` is `NOT (5=1 OR 5=2 OR 5=NULL)` = `NOT (false OR
false OR unknown)` = `NOT unknown` = unknown, which fails the `WHERE`. That
is the whole bug, and it is not a PostgreSQL quirk — it is the SQL standard.

## Hint 2

For the semi-join side of the coin, note that `EXISTS` and `IN` (not `NOT
IN`) usually produce identical plans: both become `Semi Join`, which stops
at the first match per outer row. Preferring `EXISTS` is about readability
and about avoiding the `NOT IN` trap by habit, not about performance.

## Hint 3

For the shipped version, `NOT EXISTS` is the answer, and the reason to write
in the comment is that it is null-safe, index-friendly, and expresses the
intent directly — three properties `LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL` only has by
accident of the planner recognising it.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b05_join_strategies / ex7 — three spellings, two plans, one trap
SELECT *
FROM (VALUES
  ('a', 'Hash Anti Join', true,
   'NOT EXISTS is the canonical anti join and is null-safe'),
  ('b', 'Hash Anti Join', true,
   'the planner recognises LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL and rewrites it to an anti join'),
  ('c', 'Subplan / Materialize', false,
   'NOT IN returns unknown for every row once the subquery yields a single NULL, '
   'so the count collapses to zero and no anti join is possible')
) AS v(variant, plan_node, same_result, note)
ORDER BY variant;

-- Shipped form: null-safe, becomes an anti join, and says what it means.
SELECT count(*) AS customers_without_orders
FROM perf.customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM perf.orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
);

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — when planning becomes the cost

Build a wide join. In the lab:

```sql
CREATE TABLE perf.dim1 (id int PRIMARY KEY, label text);
-- ... repeat through dim10, each seeded with 1000 rows
INSERT INTO perf.dim1 SELECT g, 'l' || g FROM generate_series(1, 1000) g;
```

Then time the planner, not the executor:

```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT count(*)
FROM perf.orders o
JOIN perf.dim1  d1  ON d1.id  = o.tenant_id
JOIN perf.dim2  d2  ON d2.id  = o.tenant_id
-- ... through d10
;
```

Edit `ex8/solution.sql` to return **one row per configuration**, with
columns `relations` (2, 6, 9, 11), `search` (`'dynamic programming'` or
`'genetic (GEQO)'`), `planning_ms` (your measured `Planning Time`, one
decimal), and `deterministic` (boolean).

Then add a second statement returning **one row, two columns**: `first_fix`
(one of `'split the query'`, `'raise join_collapse_limit'`,
`'set join_collapse_limit = 1'`) and `why` (one sentence).

**Measurable goal:** `planning_ms` must rise by at least 10× between 2 and
11 relations, and `deterministic` must be `false` exactly where GEQO
applies.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b05_join_strategies ex8`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`SHOW join_collapse_limit;` (8) and `SHOW geqo_threshold;` (12). The first
controls how many `FROM`/`JOIN` items are flattened into one search; the
second is where the genetic algorithm takes over.

## Hint 2

`EXPLAIN` alone — no `ANALYZE` — is enough: it plans without executing, and
`Planning Time` is printed at the bottom.

## Hint 3

GEQO is seeded randomly (`geqo_seed`), so two identical `EXPLAIN`s past the
threshold can return different plans. That is what `deterministic = false`
means, and it is the symptom behind "the report was fast last week".
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it from the incident report. A dashboard query that takes 400 ms,
of which 380 ms is planning, cannot be fixed by any index — and every
profiler you point at it will show the database as slow. Knowing to read
`Planning Time` first is the entire lesson.

## Hint 2

Consider prepared statements as a mitigation before restructuring: a
generic plan is computed once and reused, turning per-execution planning
into a one-off. It is not free — a generic plan is chosen without knowing
your parameters — but for a stable twelve-way join it is often the right
trade.

## Hint 3

For `first_fix`, prefer `'split the query'`. Raising `join_collapse_limit`
makes planning slower still; setting it to 1 hands you responsibility for
the join order forever. Splitting reduces the search space to something the
planner handles well, which is the only option that gets better with time.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b05_join_strategies / ex8 — planning cost as a function of join count
SELECT *
FROM (VALUES
  (2,  'dynamic programming', 0.4,   true),
  (6,  'dynamic programming', 3.1,   true),
  (9,  'dynamic programming', 46.8,  true),
  (11, 'genetic (GEQO)',      118.2, false)
) AS v(relations, search, planning_ms, deterministic)
ORDER BY relations;

SELECT 'split the query' AS first_fix,
       'Raising join_collapse_limit makes planning slower still and setting '
       || 'it to 1 makes you the optimiser forever; splitting the statement '
       || 'shrinks the search space and keeps the planner useful.' AS why;

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — nine seconds, one wrong number

The nightly settlement query:

```sql
SELECT c.country,
       count(*)              AS orders,
       sum(o.total_cents)    AS revenue
FROM perf.orders o
JOIN perf.customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'refunded'
  AND o.channel = 'partner'
  AND o.placed_at >= timestamptz '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY c.country;
```

Its plan:

```
HashAggregate  (actual time=9014.1..9014.3 rows=8 loops=1)
  ->  Nested Loop  (actual time=3.1..8998.2 rows=8791 loops=1)
        ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on orders o  (cost=..2210 rows=13)
                (actual time=2.9..102.4 rows=8791 loops=1)
```

## Hint 1

Start from the diagnosis, not the menu. The scan node estimated 13 rows and
produced 8,791 — a 676× error — and the join strategy was chosen on that
number. Which of the three fixes changes the number?

## Hint 2

F2 gives the scan a better access path but the same estimate: `status` and
`channel` are still assumed independent, so the planner still predicts a
handful of rows and still chooses a nested loop. A faster scan of 8,791 rows
does not stop 8,791 index descents.

## Hint 3

```sql
CREATE STATISTICS orders_status_channel_stx (dependencies, mcv)
  ON status, channel FROM perf.orders;
ANALYZE perf.orders;
```

With a correct estimate the planner prices the loop at 8,791 descents,
compares it with building a hash table from `customers`, and switches on its
own. V3·B6 is entirely about this object.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Different entry point: ask what you would have to believe for each fix to
work. F1 requires that the SQL is expressing the intent badly — read it
again; it is not. F2 requires that the scan is the cost — it is 102 ms of a
9,000 ms query. Only F3 addresses the 676× number that chose the plan.

## Hint 2

Be honest about F2's residual value. The index is not useless: after the
estimate is fixed, a plan that reads 8,791 rows by index instead of by
bitmap-plus-filter is still cheaper, and you may well want both. The
exercise is about which one is *the* fix, not about forbidding the other.

## Hint 3

Measure the estimate directly rather than eyeballing the plan:
`EXPLAIN SELECT ...` and read the scan node's `rows=`, or query
`pg_statistic_ext_data` after analysing to see the dependency degree the
statistics object recorded. Put that number in `est_rows_after`.

-- v3b05_join_strategies / challenge — fix the estimate, the strategy follows
SELECT c.country,
       count(*)           AS orders,
       sum(o.total_cents) AS revenue
FROM perf.orders o
JOIN perf.customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'refunded'
  AND o.channel = 'partner'
  AND o.placed_at >= timestamptz '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY c.country;

SELECT 'F3'          AS chosen,
       'Hash Join'   AS expected_strategy,
       13            AS est_rows_before,
       8600          AS est_rows_after,
       'F1 is empty because the SQL already expresses the intent, and F2 '
       || 'speeds up a 102 ms scan inside a 9 s query while leaving the 676x '
       || 'estimate error - and therefore the nested loop - untouched.'

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 — match the strategy to the situation

Six situations, no plans given. For each, name the join strategy you would
expect PostgreSQL to choose, and the one change that would flip it.

```
J1  50 rows from a filtered lookup table joined to a 2M-row table
    on an indexed key, no LIMIT.
J2  The same, but the 2M-row table has no index on the join key.
J3  Two 2M-row tables joined on a key both have B-tree indexes on,
    all rows needed, work_mem = 4MB.
J4  200k-row table joined to 6M-row table on an unindexed key,
    all rows needed, work_mem = 512MB.
J5  A join whose outer side has 500k rows but only 40 distinct join
    keys, inner side indexed.
J6  A range join: b.ts BETWEEN a.start_ts AND a.end_ts.
```

Edit `review1/solution.sql` to return **one row per situation**, ordered by
label, with columns `j`, `strategy` (`'nested loop'`, `'nested loop +
memoize'`, `'hash join'`, `'merge join'`), `reason` (one clause), and
`flips_when` (one clause naming the change that would make the planner pick
something else).

Then add a second statement returning **one row, three columns**:
`most_fragile` (the label whose plan is most sensitive to a bad row
estimate), `blast_radius` (one sentence on what goes wrong), and
`mitigation` (one clause).

**Measurable goal:** all four strategy values appear at least once.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b05_join_strategies review1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

J1 and J2 are the same query with and without an inner index — which is
exactly the difference between a linear nested loop and a quadratic one, and
the planner knows it.

## Hint 2

J3 is the merge join's home ground: both inputs sorted by indexes, both
large, and memory tight enough that a hash table would spill.

## Hint 3

J5 is Memoize: 500,000 probes for 40 distinct answers. J6 cannot be a hash
join at all — hashing requires equality.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Approach `flips_when` as the more interesting column. Every one of these
choices is a threshold, and naming the threshold is what proves you
understand the mechanism: outer row count, presence of an index, `work_mem`,
`n_distinct`, or the operator in the join condition.

## Hint 2

For `most_fragile`, the answer is the nested loop family. The error in a
hash join's estimate costs you a badly sized hash table; the same error in a
nested loop multiplies by the loop count, which is how a 20 ms query becomes
a nine-second one without anything else changing.

## Hint 3

`mitigation` should be concrete and boring: extended statistics on
correlated predicates, a larger `default_statistics_target` on skewed
columns, and `auto_explain` so you can see the plan that actually ran rather
than the one you can reproduce.

-- v3b05_join_strategies / review1 — six situations, four strategies
SELECT *
FROM (VALUES
  ('J1', 'nested loop',
   '50 outer rows x one indexed descent each is far below the cost of building any hash table',
   'the filter starts yielding thousands of rows instead of fifty'),
  ('J2', 'hash join',
   'without an inner index each lookup would be a full scan, so the loop is quadratic',
   'an index appears on the inner join key'),
  ('J3', 'merge join',
   'both inputs arrive sorted from indexes and 4MB of work_mem cannot hold a 2M-row hash table',
   'work_mem grows enough that hashing one side beats streaming both'),
  ('J4', 'hash join',
   'no ordering, no indexes, plenty of memory: build from the 200k side and stream the 6M side',
   'memory shrinks until the build spills into many batches'),
  ('J5', 'nested loop + memoize',
   '500k probes resolve to 40 distinct cache keys, so nearly every lookup is a hit',
   'n_distinct is estimated badly and the planner stops expecting reuse'),
  ('J6', 'nested loop',
   'a BETWEEN condition is not an equality, so hashing is impossible and only loop or merge apply',
   'the condition becomes an equality, or a range index makes a merge cheaper')
) AS v(j, strategy, reason, flips_when)
ORDER BY j;

SELECT 'J1' AS most_fragile,
       'A nested loop multiplies its estimate error by the loop count: if '
       || 'the outer side yields 50,000 rows instead of 50, the plan does '
       || '50,000 index descents and the query goes from 5 ms to minutes.'
            AS blast_radius,
       'extended statistics on correlated predicates, a higher statistics '
       || 'target on skewed columns, and auto_explain to capture the real plan'
            AS mitigation;

lessons.title: V3·B6 — Statistics, n_distinct and bad row estimates
lessons.summary: Every plan is the cheapest route given what the planner believes, and what it believes is a few kilobytes of sampled statistics per column. This sector opens pg_stats and reproduces the estimates by hand, then fixes the three ways they go wrong: a sample too small for a skewed column, an n_distinct the estimator cannot get right, and columns that are correlated when the planner assumes independence.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·B6 — Statistics, n_distinct and bad row estimates

Every sector so far has ended in the same place. The index was fine, the
join algorithm was fine, and the plan was still wrong — because the number
the planner reasoned from was wrong. This sector is about that number.

The planner never looks at your data. It looks at a sample of it,
summarised into a few kilobytes per column by `ANALYZE`, and everything
downstream — scan choice, join strategy, join order, hash table size,
whether a sort spills — is arithmetic over that summary.

## What ANALYZE actually collects

For each column, into `pg_statistic`, readable through `pg_stats`:

| field | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `null_frac` | fraction of rows where the column is NULL |
| `avg_width` | average bytes, used to size hash tables and sorts |
| `n_distinct` | distinct values; **negative means a ratio to row count** |
| `most_common_vals` / `most_common_freqs` | the MCV list, exact frequencies |
| `histogram_bounds` | equal-frequency buckets for everything not in the MCV list |
| `correlation` | how closely column order matches physical row order |

The sample size is `300 × statistics_target` rows —
30,000 at the default target of 100. That sample is *not* proportional to
the table: 30,000 rows out of 2,000,000 and out of 2,000,000,000 alike. It
is enough for frequencies and histograms, and it is famously not enough for
`n_distinct`, which cannot be estimated well from a sample at all.

## The three ways estimates break

**1. The sample is too coarse for a skewed column.** With 100 buckets and
100 MCVs, a column whose interesting values are the 101st through 400th most
common gets lumped into "everything else" and estimated uniformly. The fix
is per-column:

```sql
ALTER TABLE perf.orders ALTER COLUMN status SET STATISTICS 500;
ANALYZE perf.orders;
```

More buckets, more MCVs, a bigger sample, a slower `ANALYZE`, and a slightly
slower planner. Raise it on the handful of columns that need it, not
globally.

**2. `n_distinct` is estimated, badly.** PostgreSQL uses the Haas-Stokes
estimator over the sample; for a column with many rare values it can be off
by orders of magnitude, and it always is on a column like `customer_id`
where most values appear once or twice. A wrong `n_distinct` poisons
`GROUP BY` estimates, `Memoize` decisions and join selectivity. When you
know the truth, tell it:

```sql
ALTER TABLE perf.orders ALTER COLUMN customer_id SET (n_distinct = 200000);
ANALYZE perf.orders;
```

Negative values are ratios: `-1` means "distinct in every row, forever",
which is what you want for a serial or a UUID, and which survives the table
growing by a factor of a thousand.

**3. Columns are assumed independent, and are not.** This is the big one.
`status = 'refunded'` is 2% and `channel = 'partner'` is 25%, so the planner
multiplies: 0.5%. If, in reality, partner orders are refunded five times as
often as web orders, the true figure is 2.5% and the estimate is off by
five — or, when three such predicates stack, by a hundred. Extended
statistics fix it:

```sql
CREATE STATISTICS orders_status_channel_stx (dependencies, mcv)
  ON status, channel FROM perf.orders;
ANALYZE perf.orders;
```

Three kinds, each solving a different problem:

- `dependencies` — functional dependencies, "knowing `channel` tells you
  something about `status`", expressed as a degree between 0 and 1. Fixes
  equality-on-both-columns estimates.
- `ndistinct` — the number of distinct *combinations*. Fixes `GROUP BY a, b`
  estimates, which otherwise multiply the two `n_distinct`s and predict more
  groups than the table has rows.
- `mcv` — a multi-column most-common-values list. The most powerful and the
  most expensive; it handles inequalities and non-uniform combinations that
  `dependencies` cannot.

Since PostgreSQL 14 you can also collect statistics on expressions:
`CREATE STATISTICS ... ON (lower(email)) FROM ...`, which does for an
expression what an expression index does, without building the index.

## Reading the damage

The diagnostic is always the same: compare `rows=` with `actual rows=` per
node, walk to the *lowest* node where the ratio breaks, and classify.

```
->  Bitmap Heap Scan on orders  (cost=.. rows=13) (actual rows=8791)
```

676× on a single scan node. Everything above it — the nested loop, the join
order, the hash table sizes — was chosen from that 13. No index and no
rewrite fixes a plan chosen from a false premise; only the premise does.

Two more things worth knowing before the missions. Autovacuum runs
`ANALYZE` when roughly `autovacuum_analyze_threshold + 0.1 ×
reltuples` rows have changed, so a 2,000,000-row table waits for 200,000
changes — which after a bulk load means your statistics can be stale for
hours. And a freshly attached partition or a newly restored table has *no*
statistics at all, which is why `ANALYZE` belongs in every load script and
every migration that moves a lot of rows.

## The order to try things in

When an estimate is wrong, work through this list and stop at the first one
that moves the number:

1. **Is it stale?** `pg_stat_user_tables.last_analyze` and
   `last_autoanalyze`. Run `ANALYZE` and re-plan before theorising.
2. **Is it one column with a long tail?** Raise that column's statistics
   target and re-analyse.
3. **Is it several predicates on one table?** Extended statistics —
   `dependencies` for equalities, `mcv` when inequalities are involved.
4. **Is it a `GROUP BY`?** `ndistinct` over the grouping columns.
5. **Is it an expression?** Expression statistics, or the expression index
   that collects them as a side effect.
6. **Is it a join?** Check for a missing foreign key and for a skewed join
   key; per-table statistics cannot fix a join's selectivity.

Notice what is not on the list: rewriting the query, adding an index, and
turning off a planner feature. Those are answers to different problems, and
reaching for them while the estimate is wrong is how afternoons disappear.

## Mission set

Ten missions: read `pg_stats` and reproduce three kinds of estimate by hand,
pin an `n_distinct` the estimator cannot get right, fix a correlated pair
with `dependencies`, fix a `GROUP BY` with `ndistinct`, fix a skewed
inequality with `mcv`, raise a statistics target and measure what it bought,
compute when autoanalyze will next fire, and finish with an estimate-error
report you can run against any workload.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b06_statistics_estimates`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - sql/v3b06_statistics_estimates

Statistics are the input to every decision the planner makes. Most
"optimiser bugs" are statistics bugs, and most statistics bugs are one of
three specific, fixable things.

## Notes

**`ANALYZE` samples, it does not scan.** It reads `300 ×
statistics_target` rows chosen by a two-stage block sampling algorithm
(Vitter's reservoir sampling over randomly chosen blocks). At the default
target that is 30,000 rows regardless of table size, which is why `ANALYZE`
on a billion-row table takes seconds and why its `n_distinct` is a guess.

**Block sampling has a bias you should know about.** Rows are sampled by
first choosing blocks, then rows within them. Values clustered on the same
pages — which is exactly what a correlated column looks like — are
over-represented relative to a true random sample. It rarely matters, but it
is the reason two `ANALYZE` runs on the same static table can produce
slightly different MCV lists.

**The MCV list is exact; the histogram is not.** Values in
`most_common_vals` carry their measured frequency, so equality estimates on
common values are usually excellent. Everything else falls into the
histogram, which has `statistics_target` equal-frequency buckets, and range
estimates interpolate linearly inside a bucket — so a range that lands
entirely inside one bucket is estimated as a fraction of that bucket, which
is where "off by five" range estimates come from.

**`n_distinct` cannot be estimated well from a sample, in principle.** This
is a known statistical result, not a PostgreSQL limitation: distinguishing
"a million values each appearing twice" from "two million values each
appearing once" requires seeing most of the table. The estimator is
conservative and tends to *underestimate* distinctness on large tables,
which produces over-large group estimates in some plans and over-eager
`Memoize` in others. Pinning it with `ALTER TABLE ... SET (n_distinct =
-0.9)` is a legitimate, durable fix when you know the shape of your data.

**The independence assumption is the largest single source of error.**
Selectivity of `a AND b` is computed as `sel(a) × sel(b)`. Two correlated
predicates therefore compound, and three make the estimate a rounding error.
Every extended statistics kind exists to break this assumption in a
particular way.

**`dependencies` records a degree, not a rule.** For each column pair it
stores a number between 0 and 1 saying how strongly `a` determines `b`; the
planner then blends the independent estimate with the dependent one. You can
read the recorded degrees:

```sql
SELECT stxname, stxddependencies
FROM pg_statistic_ext JOIN pg_statistic_ext_data USING (oid);
```

**`ndistinct` fixes grouping, not filtering.** Without it, `GROUP BY
tenant_id, status` is estimated as `n_distinct(tenant_id) ×
n_distinct(status)` = 40 × 5 = 200 groups, and that multiplication is fine
here — but `GROUP BY customer_id, country` would predict 200,000 × 8 = 1.6
million groups when there are only 200,000, and a `HashAggregate` sized for
that will be planned away in favour of something worse.

**`mcv` is the heavy artillery.** It stores actual combinations and their
frequencies, so it handles inequalities, `OR`s, and combinations that
`dependencies` cannot express. It costs more to build and to store, and it
is limited to eight columns.

**Statistics objects do not survive being ignored.** `CREATE STATISTICS`
collects nothing until the next `ANALYZE`. Every mission in this sector that
creates one also runs `ANALYZE`, and every production change that adds one
should too.

**Autoanalyze arithmetic is worth memorising.** The threshold is
`autovacuum_analyze_threshold` (50) plus
`autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor` (0.1) times `reltuples`. On two million
rows that is 200,050 changed rows before statistics refresh. For a large
append-only table this is far too lax, and the standard fix is a per-table
override: `ALTER TABLE ... SET (autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor = 0.02)`.

**Estimates are clamped, which hides errors.** The planner never predicts
fewer than one row for a scan, and never more than the relation's row count
for a grouping. Both clamps mean a wildly wrong estimate can print as a
plausible number: `rows=1` may mean "one" or may mean "0.000003, rounded
up", and those two have very different consequences when multiplied by a
loop count.

**Join estimates come from per-column statistics, not from extended
statistics.** `CREATE STATISTICS` describes one table. For a join, the
planner uses both columns' `n_distinct` and MCV lists, plus — since 9.6 —
any validated foreign key, which lets it conclude that each child row
matches exactly one parent row. That is the strongest practical argument for
declaring foreign keys even when the application "already guarantees"
integrity.

**Statistics are per-relation, and partitions are relations.** A
partitioned table has statistics on the parent (used for plans that scan
the whole hierarchy) and on each partition. A newly attached partition has
neither until analysed, so the first queries after an attach are planned
from nothing.

**Correlation is a statistic too, and it decays differently.** It is
recomputed by every `ANALYZE`, and it changes when the physical order
changes — after a `CLUSTER`, after a bulk delete and reinsert, or slowly as
updates move rows to the end of the heap. An index that was cheap when the
table was append-ordered can become expensive without anything in the query
or the index changing at all.

## Mission notes

**ex1–ex2** reproduce equality and range estimates by hand from `pg_stats`,
including the histogram interpolation nobody ever does manually until they
have to.

**ex3** pins an `n_distinct` and measures what changes.

**ex4–ex6** are the three extended statistics kinds, each on a case where it
is the right one and the others are not.

**ex7** raises a statistics target and quantifies the improvement, including
the cost.

**ex8** computes when autoanalyze will next fire, which is the arithmetic
behind "why are my stats stale".

## Further reading

- [How the planner uses statistics](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/planner-stats.html)
  and [row estimation examples](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/row-estimation-examples.html).
- [Extended statistics](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/planner-stats.html#PLANNER-STATS-EXTENDED)
- [`CREATE STATISTICS`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createstatistics.html)
- [`ANALYZE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-analyze.html) —
  sampling behaviour and the per-column target.
- [Routine vacuuming: autoanalyze](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/routine-vacuuming.html)

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b06_statistics_estimates`

## Worked example — a range estimate, by hand

```sql
SELECT histogram_bounds::text::numeric[]
FROM pg_stats
WHERE tablename = 'orders' AND attname = 'total_cents';
-- {500,2980,5460,...,247520,250499}   -- 101 bounds, 100 buckets
```

Each bucket holds 1% of the rows. For `WHERE total_cents < 4000`:

- bounds 500 and 2980 are entirely below 4000: that is one full bucket, 1%.
- 4000 falls inside the bucket `[2980, 5460)`; linear interpolation gives
  `(4000 - 2980) / (5460 - 2980)` = 0.41 of that bucket.

Selectivity = `(1 + 0.41) / 100` = 1.41%, so `rows ≈ 28,200` on two million.
Run the `EXPLAIN` and you will see a number within a percent or two of that.

Now note the assumption: linear interpolation *inside* a bucket. If your
data has a spike at 3,900 that is not big enough to reach the MCV list, the
estimate is wrong by however much that spike weighs — and the fix is a
higher statistics target, which makes the buckets narrower.

## Worked example — dependencies, before and after

```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM perf.orders
WHERE status = 'refunded' AND channel = 'partner';
-- before:  rows=13
-- actual:  8791

CREATE STATISTICS orders_sc (dependencies) ON status, channel
  FROM perf.orders;
ANALYZE perf.orders;
-- after:   rows=8600
```

Read the object it built:

```sql
SELECT stxddependencies FROM pg_statistic_ext_data d
JOIN pg_statistic_ext s ON s.oid = d.stxoid WHERE stxname = 'orders_sc';
-- {"2 => 5": 0.964000, "5 => 2": 0.213000}
```

Those are attribute numbers and dependency degrees: knowing `channel`
determines `status` 96% of the time in this data. The planner uses the
degree to blend between "fully independent" and "fully dependent", which is
why the corrected estimate is close but not exact — and close is entirely
enough to change the join strategy.

## Common mistakes

- **Creating a statistics object and not running `ANALYZE`.** It collects
  nothing until then, and the plan does not change, and you conclude the
  feature does not work.
- **Raising `default_statistics_target` globally to 1000.** Every `ANALYZE`
  gets ten times slower and every plan gets a little slower to produce. Set
  it per column.
- **Pinning `n_distinct` to an absolute number on a growing table.** Use a
  negative ratio so it scales.
- **Assuming autoanalyze has run.** Check `pg_stat_user_tables.last_analyze`
  and `last_autoanalyze` before you draw conclusions from any plan.
- **Forgetting `ANALYZE` after a bulk load, a restore, or attaching a
  partition.** New relations have no statistics at all.
- **Using `dependencies` for a `GROUP BY` problem.** That is what
  `ndistinct` is for.
- **Expecting extended statistics to fix a join estimate.** They describe
  one table; join selectivity comes from per-column statistics and foreign
  keys.
- **Dropping foreign keys "for performance".** The planner uses them for
  join selectivity.

## Interview angle

*"A query is slow. The plan shows `rows=1` where the truth is 200,000. Walk
me through it."*

The structure that impresses: first, locate the *lowest* node where estimate
and actual diverge, because everything above it inherited the error. Then
classify. If it is a single-column equality on a value that should be in the
MCV list, the statistics are stale or the target is too low. If it is two or
more predicates on the same table, it is the independence assumption and the
fix is extended statistics — `dependencies` for equalities, `mcv` when
inequalities or skew are involved. If it is a `GROUP BY`, it is `ndistinct`.
If it is an expression, it is expression statistics or an expression index.
If it is a join, look for a missing foreign key or a skewed join key.

Finish with the operational half: `ANALYZE` after bulk loads, per-table
`autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor` on large tables, and `auto_explain` so the
next occurrence is diagnosed from the plan that actually ran.

## Check yourself

1. How many rows does `ANALYZE` sample at the default target, and does that
   scale with table size?
2. What does `n_distinct = -0.4` mean, and why is a negative value usually
   the better thing to pin?
3. Reproduce the selectivity of `col = 'x'` when `x` is in the MCV list; and
   when it is not.
4. How is a range predicate estimated inside a histogram bucket?
5. Which extended statistics kind fixes `GROUP BY a, b`?
6. Which one handles inequalities and skewed combinations?
7. Why does creating a statistics object change nothing until you run
   something else?
8. Compute when autoanalyze fires on a 5,000,000-row table at default
   settings.
9. Why can `correlation` change an index scan's cost by an order of
   magnitude?
10. What happens to statistics when you attach a new partition?
11. Your `GROUP BY customer_id, country` estimates 1.6 million groups on a
    200,000-row table. Explain the arithmetic and the fix.
12. When is raising a per-column statistics target the wrong fix?
13. Name two things the planner learns from a foreign key constraint.
lessons.fullReading:
# Reading - sql/v3b06_statistics_estimates

## How the sample is taken, and what that costs you

`ANALYZE` does not read your table. It picks a target sample size of
`300 × statistics_target` rows — 30,000 by default — and collects them with
a two-stage algorithm: choose blocks at random with reservoir sampling, then
choose rows within those blocks. The constant 300 comes from a 1993 paper by
Chaudhuri, Motwani and Narasayya on the sample size needed to bound the
error of an equal-frequency histogram; it is a statistical result about
histograms, and it says nothing about distinct-value estimation, which is the
source of most of the trouble in this sector.

From the sample, PostgreSQL computes the most common values and their
frequencies, then builds a histogram from what remains, then computes
`n_distinct` with the Haas-Stokes estimator, then computes `correlation` by
comparing the sampled values' order with their physical positions. All of it
goes into one row of `pg_statistic` per column per relation, a few kilobytes
at most, and that row is what the planner consults for every plan until the
next `ANALYZE`.

Two consequences follow. First, the sample is absolute, not proportional: a
billion-row table gets the same 30,000 rows as a million-row one, so the
statistics on very large tables are proportionally much thinner, which is
exactly when you raise the per-column target. Second, `ANALYZE` on a huge
table is fast — seconds, not hours — which means there is almost never a
good reason to skip it after a load.

## Why n_distinct is the hard one

Estimating the number of distinct values from a sample is a genuinely hard
statistical problem: no estimator is unbiased across all distributions, and
the error can be unbounded. Consider two tables of a billion rows: one with
500 million values each appearing twice, one with a billion values each
appearing once. A 30,000-row sample looks nearly identical in both cases —
almost every sampled value is unique — yet the answers differ by a factor of
two, and worse cases differ by a factor of thousands.

PostgreSQL uses Haas and Stokes' estimator, which is reasonable and
conservative and still routinely wrong on large tables with long tails. The
downstream effects are specific: `GROUP BY` cardinality is
`n_distinct`-driven, so a bad value produces a `HashAggregate` sized for the
wrong number of groups (and possibly a spill, or a plan that avoids hashing
altogether); `Memoize` is chosen when distinct outer keys are far fewer than
outer rows, so a bad value creates or destroys that node; and join
selectivity for non-MCV values is `1/max(n_distinct)`, so it shifts join
estimates directly.

When you know the truth — and for a foreign key column, a tenant id, or a
natural key, you usually do — pinning it is not a hack. `ALTER TABLE ...
ALTER COLUMN ... SET (n_distinct = -1)` is a *declaration*, stored in
`pg_attribute.attoptions`, that survives `ANALYZE` and scales with the
table. The risk is the ordinary one for any declaration: if the data changes
shape and nobody revisits it, you have pinned a lie.

## Extended statistics, and what each kind computes

`dependencies` computes, for every subset of the listed columns, the degree
to which one determines another: sample the pairs, count how often equal `a`
implies equal `b`, store the ratio. At plan time, a conjunction of
equalities on those columns is estimated as a blend between the independent
product and the fully-dependent minimum, weighted by the degree. It is cheap
to store and handles the most common case — several equality filters on
correlated columns — very well. It does nothing for inequalities.

`ndistinct` computes the number of distinct combinations for each subset of
the listed columns, which is what `GROUP BY` needs. The independent
multiplication that it replaces is not merely inaccurate but often absurd:
multiply three columns' distinct counts and you routinely predict more groups
than the table has rows, and the planner clamps that to the row count, which
means "wrong" and "clamped" look the same in the plan.

`mcv` stores actual value combinations with their frequencies, up to
`statistics_target` of them, over up to eight columns. Because it holds real
combinations it can answer inequalities, `OR`s and mixtures — the estimate
for `status = 'refunded' AND channel <> 'web'` comes from summing the
matching entries. It is the most accurate and the most expensive, and it is
the one to reach for when `dependencies` alone did not move the estimate.

Since PostgreSQL 14, a statistics object may also list expressions:
`CREATE STATISTICS s ON (lower(email)), tenant_id FROM customers` gives the
planner a histogram and MCV list for the expression, which previously only an
expression index could supply. If you were creating an index purely for its
statistics side effect, this is now the cheaper option.

## The operational half

Statistics decay. Autovacuum's analyse threshold is
`50 + 0.1 × reltuples` changed rows, which on a large table is a long time,
and after a bulk load the plans in that window are chosen from a summary of
the *old* data. The remedies are all boring: `ANALYZE` explicitly at the end
of every load and migration; lower
`autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor` per table for big, fast-moving relations;
and check `pg_stat_user_tables.last_analyze` before you believe any plan
during an incident.

Partitioned tables deserve a separate paragraph. A newly attached partition
has no statistics until it is analysed, and `ANALYZE parent` does collect
per-partition statistics but only analyses the parent's own inheritance
statistics if you ask. Partition-wise plans depend on both. The rule that
saves you: analyse the partition immediately after attaching it, in the same
script, before any traffic sees it.

## When not to touch statistics

When the estimate is already right. A plan can be slow because the work is
genuinely large, and adding statistics objects to a correctly-estimated
query is superstition with a maintenance cost. Check the ratio first; if it
is within an order of magnitude, look elsewhere — at the index, the
strategy, or the amount of data the query asks for.

Also resist the global knob. `default_statistics_target = 1000` makes every
`ANALYZE` ten times slower, every planning pass slower, and every
`pg_statistic` row ten times bigger, to fix a handful of columns. Per-column
targets and per-table statistics objects are the surgical version, and they
document *which* columns were a problem — which the next engineer will thank
you for.

## The report that keeps it honest

The practice worth building is a periodic estimate-error report, which is
what this sector's challenge constructs. Capture plans with
`auto_explain` (`log_analyze`, `log_format = json`, a threshold high
enough to be cheap), load the JSON into a table, and walk it comparing
`Plan Rows × Actual Loops` against `Actual Rows × Actual Loops` per node.
Rank by the ratio, keep only the lowest offending node per plan, and you have
a weekly list of the specific statistics your database is missing.

Two properties make this better than fixing plans one at a time. It finds
problems before they become incidents, because a node estimating 13 rows
instead of 8,791 is a nested loop waiting for the table to grow. And it
tells you which fixes actually worked: the same report a week later either
shows the ratio back near 1.0 or shows that your statistics object was the
wrong kind, which is information you otherwise only get from the next
outage.

## Further reading

- [How the planner uses statistics](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/planner-stats.html)
- [Row estimation examples](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/row-estimation-examples.html)
- [`CREATE STATISTICS`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createstatistics.html)
- [Haas & Stokes, "Estimating the number of classes in a finite population"](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/276304.276331)
  — the estimator PostgreSQL uses, and its limits.
- [Routine vacuuming and autoanalyze](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/routine-vacuuming.html)
