# Reading - sql/v3b07_pagination_and_counting

## What the executor does with OFFSET

`OFFSET` is implemented in the `Limit` node, and its implementation is three
lines of logic: pull tuples from the child, discard the first `offset` of
them, then emit `limit` of them. There is no mechanism by which it could do
otherwise, because "the hundred-thousandth row in this ordering" is not a
thing the storage layer knows — ordering is a property of the query, not of
the heap, and even an index scan must walk entries one at a time to count
them.

That has a consequence people find surprising: an index does not save you.
With a perfectly matched index the plan avoids the sort, so the work per
skipped row drops from "fetch, sort" to "read one index entry" — often a
20× improvement — but it is still linear. The curve gets flatter and it does
not stop being a curve, which is why "we added an index and deep pages are
still slow" is such a common ticket.

The stability problem is separate and, in a sense, more serious. A page
query runs in its own snapshot; between page 3 and page 4 the table has
changed, and the *offset* of a given row in the new ordering has changed
with it. A row inserted above the current position pushes every later row
down by one, so the row that was last on page 3 is now first on page 4 and
the user sees it twice. Deleting a row does the reverse and a row is never
displayed. Nothing about the query is wrong; the identity "row number 61" is
simply not stable. Keyset pagination replaces that identity with a value
from the row itself, which is stable by construction.

## Why the row-value comparison is the right tool

`(placed_at, id) < ($1, $2)` is a row constructor comparison, defined by the
SQL standard to compare lexicographically: compare the first elements, and
only if equal move to the second. PostgreSQL's planner recognises the form
and, given an index on `(placed_at, id)` with matching directions, converts
it into a single index condition — the scan descends directly to the cursor
tuple and reads forward.

Write the same logic as `placed_at < $1 OR (placed_at = $1 AND id < $2)` and
you have given the planner a disjunction. It may produce a `BitmapOr` over
two index scans, or fall back to a filter on a wider scan. It is not always
worse, and it is never better, and the row-value form also happens to be
shorter and easier to review. The only reason to expand it is a database or
an ORM that cannot express row constructors — in which case the expanded
form with an explicit index hint on the composite is the fallback.

There is one wrinkle worth knowing: the comparison requires every column to
sort in the same direction. A cursor over `ORDER BY status ASC, placed_at
DESC` cannot be expressed as a single row-value comparison, because there is
no total order on the tuple that matches. The workaround is to make the
descending column ascending by negating it — `(status, -extract(epoch from
placed_at))` in an expression index — or to paginate within each `status`
group separately and merge, which is the `LATERAL` pattern from V3·B3 ex8.

## Counting under MVCC

There is no row count to read because there is no single answer. Each
transaction sees a different set of rows, depending on its snapshot, so a
count is a property of a snapshot rather than of a table. That is the whole
reason PostgreSQL cannot do what MySQL's MyISAM did, and it is a consequence
of the concurrency model rather than an oversight.

What the system does keep is `pg_class.reltuples`, updated by `VACUUM` and
`ANALYZE` — an estimate, from the last time either ran, of the live row
count. For most "N results" displays it is entirely adequate, and it costs a
catalog lookup. For a filtered count, the equivalent is the planner's own
estimate, which you can extract by running `EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON)`
dynamically and reading `Plan Rows`; that number is exactly as good as the
statistics from V3·B6, which is another argument for keeping them fresh.

When the count must be exact, the cheapest exact count is an index-only scan
over the narrowest index that answers the predicate — a partial index over a
small subset is astonishingly effective here, because counting 8,000 index
entries in a 240 kB index is a different operation from counting them in a
164 MB table. And when even that is too slow because the number is on every
page, you maintain it: a trigger-updated counter, or a periodic rollup, with
the sharding discussed below.

## Counters, contention, and sharding

A single counter row updated on every insert is a lock convoy. Every writer
takes a row lock, and writers serialise behind it, so a table that could
absorb 20,000 inserts a second on eight cores absorbs a few thousand on one.
The standard fix is to spread the counter across `N` rows — keyed by
`hashtext(...) % N`, by tenant, or by backend pid — and sum them on read.
Writes distribute across `N` locks; reads cost `N` rows instead of one, and
`N` in the low hundreds is usually the sweet spot.

The other approach is to stop counting on the write path entirely: insert
into a small delta table and roll it up periodically, which trades freshness
for throughput and removes the contention completely. Both are ordinary
engineering trades, and both are better than the third option, which is
running `count(*)` on every request and adding a cache in front of it that
nobody can invalidate correctly.

## When the cliffs do not matter

On a table of ten thousand rows, offset pagination is fine, `count(*)` is a
fraction of a millisecond, and a keyset paginator is unnecessary complexity
with a cursor-encoding scheme to maintain. The cliffs in this sector are
about tables that grow without bound, and the engineering judgement is
knowing which of your tables those are: an audit log, an events table, an
orders table in a growing business — versus a table of countries, plans or
feature flags that will never exceed a few thousand rows.

The useful habit is to decide once, per table, at design time. If the table
is unbounded, its list endpoints get keyset pagination and its counts get
estimates, from the first commit — not because it is slow today, but because
retrofitting cursors into an API that promised page numbers is a
compatibility problem rather than an optimisation.

## The API shape that avoids all of this

Design the endpoint, not just the query. A list endpoint that returns
`{items, next_cursor}` and takes `{cursor, limit}` can be backed by a
keyset scan forever, can change its sort key behind an opaque cursor, and
never promises a total it cannot afford. An endpoint that takes
`{page, per_page}` and returns `{items, total_pages}` has promised two
things that both cost O(n), in a contract that clients now depend on.

The migration path between them is the expensive part, which is the real
argument for choosing early. If you must support both, the workable
compromise is to serve page numbers within a bounded window — the first
fifty pages, say — and switch to cursors beyond it, or to cap the reported
total ("999+") so that the count query can carry a `LIMIT`. Both are
compromises a product owner can understand, and both are cheaper than
retrofitting cursors into a public API a year later.

There is one more habit worth adopting: put a `LIMIT` on everything, even
queries you believe return few rows. A missing limit is the difference
between a slow endpoint and an out-of-memory application server, and the
row count you were sure about is a property of today's data.

## Further reading

- [Use The Index, Luke — "No Offset"](https://use-the-index-luke.com/no-offset)
- [Row-wise comparison](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-comparisons.html#ROW-WISE-COMPARISON)
- [`LIMIT`/`OFFSET`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/queries-limit.html)
- [Count estimate](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Count_estimate)
- [`DECLARE` and cursors](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-declare.html)

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — measure the cliff

Before replacing offset pagination, quantify it.

In the lab, run `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` on this query for offsets 0,
1000, 10000, 100000 and 900000:

```sql
SELECT id, placed_at FROM perf.orders
ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20 OFFSET :n;
```

with `CREATE INDEX orders_placed_id_desc_idx ON perf.orders
(placed_at DESC, id DESC);` in place.

Edit `ex1/solution.sql` to return **one row per offset**, ordered by offset,
with columns:

| column | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `page_offset` | the offset |
| `rows_produced` | rows the child node actually produced: `offset + 20` |
| `measured_ms` | the `Execution Time` you observed |
| `ms_per_1k_rows` | `measured_ms ÷ rows_produced × 1000`, three decimals |
| `growth` | `'linear'` if `ms_per_1k_rows` is roughly constant across rows, else `'other'` |

**Measurable goal:** `ms_per_1k_rows` varies by less than a factor of three
across all five offsets — which is the proof that cost is linear in the
offset.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b07_pagination_and_counting ex1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Read `rows_produced` off the plan rather than assuming it: the node under
`Limit` reports `actual rows = offset + limit`. That line is the entire
lesson.

## Hint 2

Generate the offsets with `unnest(ARRAY[0,1000,10000,100000,900000])` and
join your measured times from a `VALUES` list so the arithmetic is done in
SQL, not in your head.

## Hint 3

`ms_per_1k_rows` is the normalisation that makes the point: if the cost were
constant per *page*, this number would fall as the offset grows. It does
not, because the cost is per *row produced*.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Predict the shape first. At offset 900,000 the database walks 900,020 index
entries and fetches 900,020 rows to return twenty. If your measured time at
that offset is not roughly a thousand times the time at offset 1,000,
something else — caching, a different plan — is interfering, and finding out
what is more valuable than the table.

## Hint 2

Run each measurement twice and take the second. The first run on a cold
cache measures your disk; the second measures the query. State which you
recorded.

## Hint 3

Try one extra experiment the exercise does not ask for: drop the index and
re-measure offset 0. The sort of two million rows makes even page one slow,
which shows that the index and the pagination strategy are two independent
fixes.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b07_pagination_and_counting / ex1 — the OFFSET cost curve
-- Times are second runs, warm cache, on the reference machine.
SELECT m.page_offset,
       (m.page_offset + 20)::bigint                             AS rows_produced,
       m.measured_ms,
       round(m.measured_ms / (m.page_offset + 20) * 1000, 3)    AS ms_per_1k_rows,
       'linear'                                                 AS growth
FROM (VALUES
  (0,      0.42::numeric),
  (1000,   1.90),
  (10000,  14.10),
  (100000, 96.40),
  (900000, 812.30)
) AS m(page_offset, measured_ms)
ORDER BY m.page_offset;

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — keyset pagination

Replace the paginator. The client sends the last row it saw:
`:last_placed_at = '2024-03-14 09:12:41+00'`, `:last_id = 1420318`.

Write `ex2/indexes.sql` with the index the cursor needs, and
`ex2/solution.sql` with a query returning the next 20 rows —
`id`, `placed_at`, `total_cents` — in the same order as ex1.

Use a **row-value comparison**, not an expanded `OR`.

**Measurable goal:** the plan shows an `Index Scan` (or index-only scan)
with `Index Cond` containing `ROW(...) <` and `actual rows=20`; total
buffers under 30, at any cursor position.

Then add a second statement returning **one row, three columns**:
`buffers_page_1`, `buffers_page_45000` (both measured), and
`complexity` — the text `'O(1) per page'`.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b07_pagination_and_counting ex2`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

```sql
WHERE (placed_at, id) < (timestamptz '2024-03-14 09:12:41+00', 1420318)
ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;
```

## Hint 2

The index must be `(placed_at DESC, id DESC)` or its exact reverse
`(placed_at, id)` — either can serve this ordering, because a B-tree scan
runs both ways and both columns reverse together.

## Hint 3

Check the plan for `Index Cond: (ROW(placed_at, id) < ROW(...))`. If you see
`Filter` instead, you expanded the comparison into `OR`s or the index does
not match the ordering.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about what the client has to remember. Keyset pagination moves state
from "page number" to "the last row's sort key", which means your API
returns a cursor, not a page index. That is a contract change, and it is
the reason to do it before the first release rather than after.

## Hint 2

Consider the boundary carefully: `<` versus `<=`. With a strict `<` on the
full row value and a unique tiebreaker, the cursor row itself is excluded
exactly once — no duplicates, no gaps. Using `<=` returns the cursor row
again on every page.

## Hint 3

Verify stability, not just speed: insert a row with a very recent
`placed_at` between two page fetches and confirm the second page is
unaffected. That is the property offset pagination cannot give you, and it
is worth seeing once.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b07_pagination_and_counting / ex2 — cursor-based page fetch
SELECT id, placed_at, total_cents
FROM perf.orders
WHERE (placed_at, id) < (timestamptz '2024-03-14 09:12:41+00', 1420318)
ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;

SELECT 24              AS buffers_page_1,
       25              AS buffers_page_45000,
       'O(1) per page' AS complexity;

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — a cursor over a nullable column

The delivery console pages by `delivered_at`, which is NULL for undelivered
orders, newest first, with undelivered rows shown last:

```sql
ORDER BY delivered_at DESC NULLS LAST, id DESC
```

A naive row-value cursor breaks here, because `(NULL, id) < (x, y)` is NULL,
not true.

Write `ex3/indexes.sql` and `ex3/solution.sql` implementing a correct
cursor for this ordering. The client sends `:last_delivered_at` (which may
be NULL) and `:last_id`.

**Measurable goals:**

- pages never skip or repeat a row across the NULL boundary;
- the plan contains no `Sort` node;
- the query works both when the cursor is inside the non-NULL region and
  when it is inside the NULL region.

Add a second statement returning **one row, three columns**:
`null_boundary_handled` (`true`), `technique` (short text naming your
approach), and `why_row_value_fails` (one sentence).

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b07_pagination_and_counting ex3`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The index must declare the same NULL placement as the query:
`(delivered_at DESC NULLS LAST, id DESC)`. Without it, the ordering cannot
come from the index and a sort appears.

## Hint 2

One workable technique is a sort-key expression that has no NULLs — for
example `coalesce(delivered_at, '-infinity')` — indexed and used
consistently in the `ORDER BY`, the cursor and the predicate. Then the plain
row-value comparison works again.

## Hint 3

The alternative is an explicit two-branch predicate:

```sql
WHERE (:last_delivered_at IS NOT NULL
       AND (delivered_at IS NULL
            OR (delivered_at, id) < (:last_delivered_at, :last_id)))
   OR (:last_delivered_at IS NULL AND delivered_at IS NULL AND id < :last_id)
```

Correct, and harder to keep index-friendly — which is why the expression
approach is usually preferred.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from three-valued logic. `NULL < anything` is unknown, and unknown
fails a `WHERE`, so a cursor row with a NULL sort key can never match a
plain comparison — which is why the naive version silently returns an empty
page instead of an error.

## Hint 2

Ask whether the NULL is really a sort key at all. "Undelivered" is a
different section of the list, not a later date, and modelling it as one
section — two queries, or a `UNION ALL` with the non-NULL page first — is
often clearer than encoding it as `-infinity`. Say which you chose and why.

## Hint 3

If you take the `coalesce` route, remember it must appear identically in the
index, the `ORDER BY` and the cursor predicate, and that `'-infinity'` is a
real `timestamptz` value — so a genuine row with that timestamp would sort
into the NULL group. Given seeded data from 2023 onward, that is safe here;
in a real system, say so in a comment.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b07_pagination_and_counting / ex3 — a cursor that crosses the NULL boundary
-- Technique: sort on an expression with no NULLs, used identically in the
-- index, the ORDER BY and the cursor predicate. '-infinity' is safe here
-- because no real delivered_at can precede the 2023 seed data.
SELECT id, delivered_at, placed_at
FROM perf.orders
WHERE (coalesce(delivered_at, timestamptz '-infinity'), id)
      < (coalesce(timestamptz '2024-06-02 08:00:00+00',
                  timestamptz '-infinity'), 1832991)
ORDER BY coalesce(delivered_at, timestamptz '-infinity') DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;

SELECT true                                          AS null_boundary_handled,
       'coalesce sort key + row-value cursor'        AS technique,
       'A row-value comparison containing NULL evaluates to unknown rather '
       || 'than true, so the cursor silently matches nothing once it reaches '
       || 'the NULL group.'                          AS why_row_value_fails;

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — three answers to "how many"

The list screen displays a total. Build all three answers and price them.

Edit `ex4/solution.sql` to define a helper function and then return **one
row per method**, ordered by `cost_ms`:

| column | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `method` | `'exact'`, `'reltuples'`, `'explain estimate'` |
| `value` | the number that method produces, live |
| `cost_ms` | the time you measured, one decimal |
| `error_pct` | absolute difference from the exact value, as a percentage, two decimals |
| `use_when` | one clause |

The `'explain estimate'` method must be produced by a function that runs
`EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON)` on a passed-in query text and returns `Plan Rows`.

**Measurable goal:** `reltuples` and the explain estimate are both within 5%
of exact on a freshly analysed table, and both cost under 2 ms.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b07_pagination_and_counting ex4`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION perf.est_rows(q text) RETURNS bigint
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE doc jsonb;
BEGIN
  EXECUTE 'EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON) ' || q INTO doc;
  RETURN (doc -> 0 -> 'Plan' ->> 'Plan Rows')::bigint;
END $$;
```

## Hint 2

`reltuples` is a `real` in `pg_class`; cast it to `bigint` for display and
to `numeric` for arithmetic, or your percentages will come out with float
noise.

## Hint 3

Structure the result as a `VALUES` list of method names joined laterally to
scalar subqueries, so each `value` is computed live rather than pasted.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Approach it as an interface decision. The interesting output is `use_when`:
exact when the number is the product (an invoice count), `reltuples` when it
is decoration ("about 2 million"), the explain estimate when the count is
filtered and decoration. Getting that mapping right matters more than the
milliseconds.

## Hint 2

Be careful with `EXPLAIN` on user-supplied text: the function executes
whatever it is given, so it must never be reachable from untrusted input.
Mark it `SECURITY INVOKER` (the default), keep it out of any role's default
grants, and say so in a comment — a helper that runs arbitrary SQL deserves
a warning label.

## Hint 3

Compare the two estimates against each other, not just against exact. They
come from the same statistics but different paths — `reltuples` is the
stored row count, the explain estimate is the planner's prediction after
applying predicates — so they diverge exactly when your statistics are
stale, which makes their disagreement a useful staleness alarm.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b07_pagination_and_counting / ex4 — exact, stored estimate, planner estimate
-- WARNING: est_rows executes the SQL text it is given inside EXPLAIN. Never
-- expose it to untrusted input.
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION perf.est_rows(q text) RETURNS bigint
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE doc jsonb;
BEGIN
  EXECUTE 'EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON) ' || q INTO doc;
  RETURN (doc -> 0 -> 'Plan' ->> 'Plan Rows')::bigint;
END $$;

WITH exact AS (
  SELECT count(*)::numeric AS v FROM perf.orders
),
vals AS (
  SELECT 'exact' AS method, (SELECT v FROM exact) AS value, 172.0::numeric AS cost_ms,
         'the number is part of the product, e.g. an invoice count' AS use_when
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 'reltuples',
         (SELECT reltuples::numeric FROM pg_class
           WHERE oid = 'perf.orders'::regclass),
         0.2,
         'the number is decoration: display it as "about N"'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 'explain estimate',
         perf.est_rows($$SELECT * FROM perf.orders$$)::numeric,
         0.6,
         'a filtered count that only needs to be roughly right'
)
SELECT v.method,
       v.value::bigint                                          AS value,
       v.cost_ms,
       round(abs(v.value - e.v) / e.v * 100, 2)                 AS error_pct,
       v.use_when
FROM vals v CROSS JOIN exact e
ORDER BY v.cost_ms;

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — stop counting, answer the real question

The UI shows "Showing 20 of 412,338" and a Next button. Product agrees the
total can go.

Edit `ex5/solution.sql` to return a page of 20 refunded orders **and** a
`has_more` flag, in one query, without any `count`, and without
materialising more than 21 rows.

Requirements:

- columns `id`, `placed_at`, `total_cents`, `has_more`;
- exactly 20 data rows returned;
- `has_more` is `true` when a 21st row exists.

Then add a second statement returning **one row, three columns** comparing
approaches: `rows_touched_limit21` (21),
`rows_touched_count_over` (a live `count(*)` of the filtered set), and
`ratio` — the second divided by the first, rounded to a whole number.

**Measurable goal:** the page query's plan produces at most 21 rows from its
scan node.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b07_pagination_and_counting ex5`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Fetch 21 rows in a subquery, then use a window function over those 21 rows
to compute `has_more`, and return only the first 20 in the outer query.

## Hint 2

```sql
WITH page AS (
  SELECT id, placed_at, total_cents
  FROM perf.orders WHERE status = 'refunded'
  ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC
  LIMIT 21
)
SELECT id, placed_at, total_cents,
       (count(*) OVER ()) > 20 AS has_more
FROM page
ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;
```

## Hint 3

Note that `count(*) OVER ()` is safe *here* precisely because it runs over
the 21-row CTE, not over the table. The same construct applied to the base
table is the anti-pattern from the briefing — the difference is what it
counts.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Frame it as a product question first. "412,338 results" is almost never
information the user acts on; "there is more" is. Removing the total is the
single largest performance change available on most list screens, and it
costs a conversation rather than an index.

## Hint 2

Watch the interaction with the cursor from ex2. `has_more` composes
perfectly with keyset pagination: fetch `n+1` rows after the cursor, return
`n`, and hand back the last returned row's key as the next cursor. That is
the entire API contract, and it never touches an offset or a count.

## Hint 3

If product insists on a number, offer a bounded one: `SELECT count(*) FROM
(SELECT 1 FROM ... LIMIT 1000) x` gives "999+" semantics at a fixed cost.
It is the compromise that satisfies most UIs, and it is worth having in your
pocket.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b07_pagination_and_counting / ex5 — a page plus has_more, no count over the table
WITH page AS (
  SELECT id, placed_at, total_cents
  FROM perf.orders
  WHERE status = 'refunded'
  ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC
  LIMIT 21
)
SELECT id, placed_at, total_cents,
       (count(*) OVER ()) > 20 AS has_more
FROM page
ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;

WITH f AS (
  SELECT count(*)::numeric AS filtered FROM perf.orders WHERE status = 'refunded'
)
SELECT 21                              AS rows_touched_limit21,
       f.filtered::bigint              AS rows_touched_count_over,
       round(f.filtered / 21)::bigint  AS ratio
FROM f;

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — an exact count that is actually cheap

Sometimes the number must be exact: the operations dashboard shows the exact
size of the pending queue, and it refreshes every second.

```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM perf.orders WHERE status = 'pending';   -- 8,000 rows
```

Today this scans the table or, with the composite index, walks 8,000 entries
inside a 60 MB index.

Write `ex6/indexes.sql` and `ex6/solution.sql` making this count as cheap as
it can be without maintaining a counter.

**Measurable goal:** the plan is an `Index Only Scan` with
`Heap Fetches: 0`, total buffers under 40, and the count is exact.

Add a second statement returning **one row, four columns**:
`index_kb` (live size in kB, one decimal), `rows_counted` (live),
`buffers` (measured), and `beats_counter_when` — one sentence naming the
condition under which this is preferable to a maintained counter.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b07_pagination_and_counting ex6`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The cheapest thing to count is the smallest structure that contains exactly
the rows you are counting. That is a partial index — V3·B4 ex1 built one.

## Hint 2

```sql
CREATE INDEX orders_pending_count_idx ON perf.orders (id)
WHERE status = 'pending';
VACUUM (ANALYZE) perf.orders;
```

The key column barely matters; the predicate is what makes the index small.

## Hint 3

`Heap Fetches: 0` requires the vacuum. Without it every counted entry costs
a heap visit and the index-only scan is index-only in name only.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what "cheap" means here. 8,000 entries in a 240 kB index is about thirty
pages, all of them permanently in cache. At one query per second that is
nothing; at ten thousand queries per second it is 300,000 buffer touches a
second, and the answer changes to a maintained counter. Name the threshold
rather than the technique.

## Hint 2

Note the maintenance property that makes this attractive: nothing to keep in
sync. A counter table can drift if a trigger is dropped, a bulk load
bypasses it, or a rollback is mishandled; a partial index is maintained by
the same machinery as every other index and cannot disagree with the table.

## Hint 3

Test the exactness claim under concurrency: run the count in one session
while another inserts pending rows. You will get a consistent snapshot, not
a torn number — which is exactly what a naively implemented counter cannot
promise.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b07_pagination_and_counting / ex6 — exact queue depth from a tiny index
SELECT count(*) FROM perf.orders WHERE status = 'pending';

SELECT round(pg_relation_size('perf.orders_pending_count_idx'::regclass)::numeric
             / 1024, 1)                                       AS index_kb,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM perf.orders WHERE status = 'pending')::bigint
                                                              AS rows_counted,
       32                                                     AS buffers,
       'Prefer this while the counted subset stays small and the query rate '
       || 'is modest; past a few thousand counts per second the buffer '
       || 'traffic justifies a maintained, sharded counter.' AS beats_counter_when;

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — a counter that survives concurrency

The events table takes 20,000 inserts a second and the dashboard needs an
exact total per tenant. A single counter row per tenant is a lock convoy:
every insert for tenant 7 waits behind every other insert for tenant 7.

Build the sharded version. Write `ex7/indexes.sql` with:

```sql
CREATE TABLE perf.event_counts (
  tenant_id int  NOT NULL,
  shard     int  NOT NULL,
  n         bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, shard)
);
```

plus the trigger (or the statement pattern) that maintains it, seeded with
`N = 16` shards per tenant.

Write `ex7/solution.sql` with:

1. the read query — exact total per tenant, ordered by `tenant_id`;
2. a statement returning **one row, four columns**: `shards` (16),
   `write_contention` (`'1/16 of a single-row counter'`),
   `read_cost_rows` (16 per tenant), and `drift_risk` — one sentence naming
   how a counter table can disagree with the table it counts.

**Measurable goal:** the read is an index-only scan over
`perf.event_counts` touching 16 rows per tenant, and two concurrent inserts
for the same tenant do not block each other unless they hash to the same
shard.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b07_pagination_and_counting ex7`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Choose the shard from something that spreads writers, not rows:
`(hashint4(pg_backend_pid()) & 15)` gives each backend a stable shard, so
concurrent sessions rarely collide.

## Hint 2

The maintenance statement is an upsert:

```sql
INSERT INTO perf.event_counts (tenant_id, shard, n)
VALUES (NEW.tenant_id, (hashint4(pg_backend_pid()) & 15), 1)
ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, shard) DO UPDATE SET n = perf.event_counts.n + 1;
```

## Hint 3

The read is `SELECT tenant_id, sum(n) FROM perf.event_counts GROUP BY
tenant_id ORDER BY tenant_id` — sixteen rows per tenant, which for forty
tenants is 640 rows and entirely in cache.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Be honest about what a trigger costs. A row-level `AFTER INSERT` trigger
fires per row, so a 10,000-row `COPY` performs 10,000 upserts. A
statement-level trigger with a transition table, or an explicit counter
update in the same transaction as a batch insert, is dramatically cheaper —
and naming that trade is more valuable than the sharding itself.

## Hint 2

For `drift_risk`, the concrete answers: a bulk load that disables triggers,
a `TRUNCATE` (which does not fire row triggers), a replica promotion mid
transaction, or a logical-replication apply path that skips triggers by
default. All of them are real, all of them have bitten people, and all of
them argue for a periodic reconciliation job.

## Hint 3

Consider the alternative shape before committing: an append-only delta table
(`INSERT INTO perf.event_deltas VALUES (tenant_id, 1)`) rolled up on a
schedule has no update contention at all, at the cost of freshness and a
background job. It is often the better answer above a certain write rate.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b07_pagination_and_counting / ex7 — reading a sharded counter
SELECT tenant_id, sum(n)::bigint AS events
FROM perf.event_counts
GROUP BY tenant_id
ORDER BY tenant_id;

SELECT 16                                    AS shards,
       '1/16 of a single-row counter'        AS write_contention,
       16                                    AS read_cost_rows,
       'Triggers do not fire for TRUNCATE, are skipped by loads that disable '
       || 'them, and are off by default on the logical-replication apply '
       || 'path, so a counter table needs a periodic reconciliation job.'
                                             AS drift_risk;

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — the duplicate row the user sees

Offset pagination is not only slow; it is wrong over a changing table. Prove
it, and prove the cursor version is not.

Edit `ex8/solution.sql` to run this experiment inside one transaction that
rolls back:

1. take "page 1" with `ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 5 OFFSET 0`
   into a temporary table `p1`;
2. insert one new order whose `placed_at` is newer than everything;
3. take "page 2" with the same ordering and `OFFSET 5` into `p2`;
4. take the keyset equivalent of page 2 — rows after `p1`'s last row — into
   `p3`;
5. roll back and return **one row, four columns**: `offset_duplicates`
   (count of ids appearing in both `p1` and `p2`), `keyset_duplicates`
   (same for `p1` and `p3`), `verdict` (`'offset is unstable'`), and
   `mechanism` — one sentence.

**Measurable goal:** `offset_duplicates` is 1 and `keyset_duplicates` is 0.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b07_pagination_and_counting ex8`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Use `CREATE TEMP TABLE p1 AS SELECT ...` so the pages persist inside the
transaction and can be compared afterwards. Temp tables created in a
transaction disappear with it if you use `ON COMMIT DROP`.

## Hint 2

The inserted row must sort *above* page 1 — `placed_at = now()` does that
with the descending order — so that everything shifts down by exactly one
position.

## Hint 3

The duplicate count is a join:
`SELECT count(*) FROM p1 JOIN p2 USING (id)`. Do the same for `p3` and the
contrast is the whole exercise.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it as a bug report you have received. "The same order appears twice
in the list, sometimes" is unreproducible when you look, because it depends
on a write landing between two reads. This experiment turns it into a
deterministic demonstration, which is what you need to get the fix
prioritised.

## Hint 2

Note the symmetric failure: a *deletion* above the current page shifts rows
up and a row is never shown at all. That one produces no bug report, because
nobody notices what they did not see — which makes it the more dangerous of
the two.

## Hint 3

Be careful to give the inserted row a primary key that does not collide.
`(SELECT max(id) + 1 FROM perf.orders)` inside the transaction is fine here;
in production a sequence handles it, and the difference matters if you
adapt this script.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b07_pagination_and_counting / ex8 — offset pagination shows a row twice
BEGIN;

CREATE TEMP TABLE p1 ON COMMIT DROP AS
SELECT id, placed_at FROM perf.orders
ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 5 OFFSET 0;

INSERT INTO perf.orders
  (id, customer_id, tenant_id, status, channel, placed_at, total_cents, ship_country)
SELECT max(id) + 1, 1, 1, 'pending', 'web', now(), 1000, 'US'
FROM perf.orders;

CREATE TEMP TABLE p2 ON COMMIT DROP AS
SELECT id, placed_at FROM perf.orders
ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 5 OFFSET 5;

CREATE TEMP TABLE p3 ON COMMIT DROP AS
SELECT o.id, o.placed_at
FROM perf.orders o,
     LATERAL (SELECT placed_at, id FROM p1
              ORDER BY placed_at ASC, id ASC LIMIT 1) AS cur
WHERE (o.placed_at, o.id) < (cur.placed_at, cur.id)
ORDER BY o.placed_at DESC, o.id DESC
LIMIT 5;

SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM p1 JOIN p2 USING (id))::int AS offset_duplicates,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM p1 JOIN p3 USING (id))::int AS keyset_duplicates,
       'offset is unstable'                             AS verdict,
       'A row inserted above the current position shifts every later row down '
       || 'by one, so the last row of page 1 becomes the first row of page 2; '
       || 'a cursor names a row instead of a position and cannot shift.'
                                                        AS mechanism;

ROLLBACK;

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — ship a paginator

Build the whole thing: a function that returns a page and the cursor for the
next one, correct under concurrent writes, constant cost per page.

Write `challenge/indexes.sql` with the index, and `challenge/solution.sql`
defining:

```sql
perf.page_orders(p_tenant int, p_after text DEFAULT NULL, p_limit int DEFAULT 20)
  RETURNS TABLE (id bigint, placed_at timestamptz, total_cents bigint,
                 next_cursor text, has_more boolean)
```

Requirements, all measurable:

- ordering is `placed_at DESC, id DESC` within one tenant;
- `p_after` is an opaque cursor string your function both produces and
  consumes — encode the `(placed_at, id)` pair, do not expose raw columns;
- a `NULL` cursor returns the first page;
- the function fetches `p_limit + 1` rows and never more;
- `has_more` is exact;
- `next_cursor` is the cursor for the last returned row, or `NULL` when
  there is no next page;
- the plan for the internal query is an index scan with no `Sort`.

Then add a demonstration: call the function three times in sequence, feeding
each `next_cursor` into the next call, and return the nine rows with a
`page_no` column.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b07_pagination_and_counting challenge`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Encode the cursor as base64 of a text pair so callers cannot construct one
by hand:
`encode(convert_to(extract(epoch from placed_at)::text || ':' || id::text,
'UTF8'), 'base64')`, and reverse it with `decode`/`convert_from` plus
`split_part`.

## Hint 2

Inside the function, branch on `p_after IS NULL`: without a cursor the
predicate is just `tenant_id = p_tenant`; with one it adds the row-value
comparison. Write it as a single query with
`(p_after IS NULL OR (placed_at, id) < (cur_ts, cur_id))` and let the
planner fold the constant.

## Hint 3

Fetch `p_limit + 1` into a CTE, compute `has_more` as
`count(*) OVER () > p_limit` inside that CTE, then return the first
`p_limit` rows with `next_cursor` computed per row — the caller only needs
the last one, and returning it on every row keeps the SQL simple.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Design the cursor's contract before the SQL. It must be opaque (so you can
change the sort key later without breaking clients), stable (so it means the
same thing tomorrow), and self-describing enough that a malformed one fails
loudly rather than returning page one. Those three properties are what make
this a shippable API rather than an exercise.

## Hint 2

Watch the `(p_after IS NULL OR ...)` pattern for a plan trap: with a
parameter the planner may build a generic plan that cannot use the index
condition. If `EXPLAIN (GENERIC_PLAN)` shows a filter instead of an index
condition, split the function into two queries chosen by an `IF`, which
costs six lines and guarantees the plan.

## Hint 3

Test the boundary explicitly: a page whose last row shares a `placed_at`
with the first row of the next page. If your cursor only carries the
timestamp, that row is dropped or repeated — which is why the `id` is in the
cursor, and why the test belongs in your demonstration.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b07_pagination_and_counting / challenge — a shippable keyset paginator
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION perf.page_orders(
  p_tenant int,
  p_after  text DEFAULT NULL,
  p_limit  int  DEFAULT 20)
RETURNS TABLE (id bigint, placed_at timestamptz, total_cents bigint,
               next_cursor text, has_more boolean)
LANGUAGE plpgsql STABLE AS $$
DECLARE
  cur_ts timestamptz;
  cur_id bigint;
  raw    text;
BEGIN
  IF p_after IS NOT NULL THEN
    raw := convert_from(decode(p_after, 'base64'), 'UTF8');
    cur_ts := to_timestamp(split_part(raw, ':', 1)::numeric);
    cur_id := split_part(raw, ':', 2)::bigint;
    IF cur_id IS NULL THEN
      RAISE EXCEPTION 'malformed cursor: %', p_after;
    END IF;
  END IF;

  RETURN QUERY
  WITH page AS (
    SELECT o.id, o.placed_at, o.total_cents,
           count(*) OVER () AS fetched
    FROM perf.orders o
    WHERE o.tenant_id = p_tenant
      AND (p_after IS NULL OR (o.placed_at, o.id) < (cur_ts, cur_id))
    ORDER BY o.placed_at DESC, o.id DESC
    LIMIT p_limit + 1
  ),
  trimmed AS (
    SELECT p.*, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY p.placed_at DESC, p.id DESC) AS rn
    FROM page p
  )
  SELECT t.id, t.placed_at, t.total_cents,
         encode(convert_to(extract(epoch from t.placed_at)::text
                           || ':' || t.id::text, 'UTF8'), 'base64'),
         (t.fetched > p_limit)
  FROM trimmed t
  WHERE t.rn <= p_limit
  ORDER BY t.placed_at DESC, t.id DESC;
END $$;

-- Demonstration: three pages, each fed by the previous cursor.
WITH RECURSIVE pages AS (
  SELECT 1 AS page_no,
         (SELECT max(next_cursor) FROM perf.page_orders(7, NULL, 3)) AS cursor
  UNION ALL
  SELECT p.page_no + 1,
         (SELECT max(next_cursor) FROM perf.page_orders(7, p.cursor, 3))
  FROM pages p
  WHERE p.page_no < 3
)
SELECT p.page_no, r.id, r.placed_at, r.total_cents, r.has_more
FROM pages p
CROSS JOIN LATERAL perf.page_orders(
        7,
        CASE WHEN p.page_no = 1 THEN NULL
             ELSE (SELECT cursor FROM pages q WHERE q.page_no = p.page_no - 1)
        END, 3) r
ORDER BY p.page_no, r.placed_at DESC, r.id DESC;

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 — audit six endpoints for cliffs

Six pieces of real application SQL. For each, say whether it falls off a
cliff as the table grows, name the mechanism, and give the fix.

```
E1  SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY placed_at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET :page*20;
E2  SELECT count(*) FROM events WHERE tenant_id = $1;      -- every page load
E3  SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = ANY($1);               -- $1 is 50k ids
E4  SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY random() LIMIT 1;
E5  SELECT id FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = $1
      ORDER BY placed_at DESC LIMIT 50;                    -- indexed
E6  SELECT * FROM events WHERE tenant_id = $1;             -- export, no limit
```

Edit `review1/solution.sql` to return **one row per endpoint**, ordered by
label, with columns `e`, `cliff` (boolean), `mechanism` (one clause),
`grows_with` (`'offset'`, `'table size'`, `'list length'`, `'result size'`,
or `'nothing'`), and `fix` (one clause).

Then add a second statement returning **one row, three columns**:
`already_fine` (the label that needs no change), `worst` (the label you
would fix first, given a table growing by 50 million rows a year), and
`why_worst` (one sentence).

**Measurable goal:** exactly one row has `cliff = false`, and every
`grows_with` value is used at least once.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b07_pagination_and_counting review1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

For each, ask "what does the database have to produce that it does not
return?". That quantity is what the cost grows with.

## Hint 2

E5 is the control case: an equality plus an ordered index plus a small
`LIMIT` is genuinely constant, and recognising a healthy query matters as
much as spotting a sick one.

## Hint 3

E6's problem is not the plan — it is that the client materialises the whole
result. The fix is a server-side cursor and `FETCH` in batches, or an
explicit keyset loop.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Rank by growth rate, not by current latency. E1 grows with the page number a
user chooses, so it is bounded by user behaviour; E2 grows with the whole
table on every page load, so it degrades for everyone at once. That
distinction is what makes E2 the one to fix first.

## Hint 2

E3 has two costs, and naming both is the complete answer: 50,000 literals
inflate planning time before execution begins, and the executor then does
50,000 index descents. `= ANY($1::bigint[])` fixes the first; joining
against `unnest($1)` lets the planner choose a hash join and fixes the
second.

## Hint 3

E4 is the one people defend as "it is only one row". `ORDER BY random()`
assigns a random value to every row and sorts them all; the cost is the
whole table, every call. The fixes are a `TABLESAMPLE`, a random offset over
a known count, or a precomputed random key column with a cursor.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b07_pagination_and_counting / review1 — six endpoints, five cliffs
SELECT *
FROM (VALUES
  ('E1', true,  'OFFSET makes the server produce and discard every skipped row',
   'offset',      'keyset cursor on (placed_at, id) with a matching index'),
  ('E2', true,  'an exact count under MVCC must visit every matching row',
   'table size',  'estimate from EXPLAIN, or a sharded maintained counter'),
  ('E3', true,  '50k literals cost planning time before a single row is read',
   'list length', 'pass one array parameter and join against unnest($1)'),
  ('E4', true,  'ORDER BY random() assigns and sorts a value for every row',
   'result size', 'TABLESAMPLE, or a precomputed random key plus a cursor'),
  ('E5', false, 'equality plus an ordered index plus a small LIMIT stops early',
   'nothing',     'no change; keep the (tenant_id, placed_at DESC) index'),
  ('E6', true,  'the client materialises the entire result set in memory',
   'result size', 'DECLARE a cursor and FETCH in batches, or loop by keyset')
) AS v(e, cliff, mechanism, grows_with, fix)
ORDER BY e;

SELECT 'E5' AS already_fine,
       'E2' AS worst,
       'E1 degrades only for users who page deeply, but E2 runs on every '
       || 'page load and its cost grows with the whole table, so at 50 '
       || 'million new rows a year it degrades for everyone simultaneously.'
            AS why_worst;

lessons.title: V3·B8 — Bloat, VACUUM and maintenance you can schedule
lessons.summary: Every UPDATE writes a new row version and leaves the old one behind, so a table that never grows in rows can double in bytes. This sector measures bloat honestly, explains what VACUUM does and does not reclaim, finds the long transaction or replication slot that is blocking it, works out the freeze arithmetic before wraparound becomes an emergency, and ends with a maintenance runbook that prioritises itself.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·B8 — Bloat, VACUUM and maintenance you can schedule

Every sector in this volume assumed a healthy table. This one is about what
happens when nobody maintains it, which is the state most production
databases are in until somebody reads this material.

PostgreSQL never updates a row in place. An `UPDATE` writes a new version of
the row and marks the old one as dead as of your transaction id; a `DELETE`
just marks. The old versions stay in the table because other transactions
may still need to see them, and they are removed later, by `VACUUM`. That
one design decision — MVCC without an undo log — buys you readers that never
block writers, and it charges you maintenance.

## What bloat is, concretely

A table with 2,000,000 live rows and 6,000,000 dead ones occupies four times
the pages it needs. Every sequential scan reads four times the bytes. Every
index over it points into a heap that is four times as sparse, so index
scans touch more pages. Cache holds a quarter as much useful data. Nothing
about your queries changed; everything about them got slower.

```sql
SELECT relname, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup,
       round(100.0 * n_dead_tup / nullif(n_live_tup + n_dead_tup, 0), 1) AS dead_pct,
       last_vacuum, last_autovacuum
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
WHERE schemaname = 'perf'
ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC;
```

`n_dead_tup` is an estimate maintained by the statistics collector; for the
truth, `pgstattuple` reads the table and reports exact live and dead bytes,
at the cost of a full scan. Use the cheap one for monitoring and the
expensive one when you are about to do something drastic.

## What VACUUM actually does

Four jobs, and knowing which is which prevents most confusion:

1. **Reclaims dead tuple space for reuse** inside the table. The file does
   not shrink; the space becomes available for future inserts. Only trailing
   empty pages are truncated back to the OS.
2. **Updates the visibility map**, which is what makes index-only scans real
   (V3·B2) and lets future vacuums skip pages.
3. **Freezes old rows**, rewriting their `xmin` as frozen so that the
   32-bit transaction counter can wrap around safely.
4. **Updates statistics** — only `VACUUM ANALYZE` does this; plain `VACUUM`
   updates `reltuples` and `relpages` but not the histograms.

`VACUUM FULL` is a different thing entirely: it rewrites the whole table
into a new file, returns the space to the operating system, and holds an
`ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock for the duration — no reads, no writes, on a table
you are rewriting because it is large. On anything busy, use `pg_repack` or
`pg_squeeze`, which do the same work with brief locks.

## Why vacuum sometimes cannot help

`VACUUM` may only remove a dead tuple if no existing snapshot can still see
it. Anything holding an old snapshot pins the horizon for the *whole
database*:

- a transaction left `idle in transaction` by an application that forgot to
  commit;
- a long-running analytical query or a held cursor;
- a replication slot with no consumer, or a standby with
  `hot_standby_feedback = on` running a long query;
- an orphaned prepared transaction (`pg_prepared_xacts`).

The symptom is bloat that grows while autovacuum runs constantly and
achieves nothing. The diagnosis is one query against `pg_stat_activity`,
`pg_replication_slots` and `pg_prepared_xacts`, comparing each holder's xmin
against the current one — ex5 builds it, and it belongs in your monitoring.

## HOT updates: the bloat you can avoid

If an update changes no indexed column *and* the new version fits on the
same page, PostgreSQL performs a **heap-only tuple** update: the new version
is chained to the old one on the same page, and no index entries are
written. That is dramatically cheaper, and the space is reclaimable by
ordinary page pruning without a full vacuum.

Two things break it. Indexing a column that updates frequently — a `status`
that changes five times per order, indexed for a queue — and a page with no
free space. The second is what `fillfactor` addresses:

```sql
ALTER TABLE perf.orders SET (fillfactor = 85);
```

Leave 15% of each page empty so updates have somewhere to go. It costs disk
on an insert-only table and pays for itself many times over on an
update-heavy one. `pg_stat_user_tables.n_tup_hot_upd` against `n_tup_upd`
tells you your current ratio.

## Freezing and the counter that wraps

Transaction ids are 32 bits. Rows older than `autovacuum_freeze_max_age`
(200 million by default) must be frozen or the database will refuse writes
to protect itself. Autovacuum escalates to an "aggressive" vacuum as the age
approaches, and if it never finishes — because it is being cancelled, or the
table is enormous, or a slot is holding the horizon — you eventually get a
shutdown-to-single-user-mode incident that will define your week.

```sql
SELECT relname, age(relfrozenxid) AS xid_age,
       round(100.0 * age(relfrozenxid)
             / current_setting('autovacuum_freeze_max_age')::numeric, 1) AS pct
FROM pg_class JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = relnamespace
WHERE relkind = 'r' AND nspname = 'perf'
ORDER BY age(relfrozenxid) DESC;
```

Anything above 50% deserves attention; above 80% deserves a calendar entry.

## Index bloat is its own problem

A B-tree does not reclaim a deleted entry's space until the whole page
empties, and a page that repeatedly fills and half-empties never merges with
its neighbours. On an update-heavy table the indexes can therefore outgrow
the heap:

```sql
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pgstattuple;
SELECT avg_leaf_density, leaf_fragmentation FROM pgstatindex('perf.orders_pkey');
```

A leaf density near 90 is healthy; near 40 means the index is mostly air.
The online fix is `REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, which builds a second copy
— so you need the disk headroom — and leaves an `INVALID` index behind if
it fails, which your maintenance script must check for and drop.

## Mission set

Ten missions: measure bloat two ways and reconcile them, prove what `VACUUM`
does and does not return to the operating system, raise your HOT update
ratio with `fillfactor` and one dropped index, compute autovacuum thresholds
and propose per-table settings, find the transaction blocking the horizon,
build a wraparound alert, reindex without blocking, and work out how fast
autovacuum is actually allowed to go.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b08_bloat_vacuum_maintenance`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - sql/v3b08_bloat_vacuum_maintenance

Maintenance is the part of performance work that is invisible until it is
urgent. All of it follows from one fact: old row versions stay in the table
until something proves nobody needs them.

## Notes

**Every row carries `xmin` and `xmax`.** `xmin` is the transaction that
created this version, `xmax` the one that deleted or superseded it.
Visibility is decided by comparing those against your snapshot, which is
why a `SELECT` never blocks and why the old versions must physically remain.
`SELECT xmin, xmax, ctid FROM t LIMIT 5` shows them; running an `UPDATE` and
looking again shows the mechanism directly.

**Dead tuples are removed only when they are invisible to everyone.**
"Everyone" means the oldest snapshot in the cluster, including replicas with
`hot_standby_feedback`, replication slots, and prepared transactions. One
forgotten `BEGIN` in a psql window can prevent vacuum from removing a single
row from any table in the database.

**`VACUUM` reuses space; it does not return it.** After vacuuming a table
where you deleted 90% of rows, the file is the same size and 90% of it is
free space recorded in the free space map, available to future inserts. The
file only shrinks if the free pages happen to be at the end, where `VACUUM`
can truncate them — which requires a brief `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock it will
skip rather than wait for.

**`VACUUM FULL` rewrites and locks.** It is correct and it is a maintenance
window: no reads, no writes, for as long as it takes to rewrite the table
and every index. `pg_repack` achieves the same result with a copy plus a
trigger-maintained change log and only brief locks, which is why it is
standard on anything that cannot go offline.

**Page pruning happens without vacuum.** Any access to a page can prune
dead tuples from HOT chains within it, which recovers most of the space from
HOT updates without waiting for autovacuum. This is why a well-tuned
`fillfactor` on an update-heavy table matters so much: it keeps updates HOT,
and HOT bloat is self-cleaning.

**Autovacuum's thresholds are per table and easy to compute.** It vacuums
when dead tuples exceed `autovacuum_vacuum_threshold` (50) plus
`autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor` (0.2) × `reltuples`, and analyses at the
0.1 scale factor. On a 100-million-row table that is 20 million dead rows
before the first vacuum, which is far too lax; per-table overrides
(`ALTER TABLE ... SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.02)`) are normal
practice on large tables.

**Autovacuum is deliberately throttled.** It accumulates cost — 1 per page
found in cache, 2 per page read, 20 per page dirtied (`vacuum_cost_page_hit`,
`_miss`, `_dirty`) — and sleeps for `autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay` (2 ms)
every time it reaches `autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit` (200). That works out
to a few tens of megabytes per second on default settings, which on a
terabyte table means vacuum cannot keep up regardless of how many workers
you give it. Raising the cost limit is the knob; ex8 does the arithmetic.

**`max_parallel_maintenance_workers` speeds up index vacuuming**, not the
heap pass, and only for manual `VACUUM` — autovacuum never parallelises.

**Freezing is not optional.** Transaction ids are 32 bits with a
2-billion-transaction visible window. Rows must be frozen before their age
reaches `autovacuum_freeze_max_age`, and PostgreSQL will start refusing
writes rather than allow the counter to wrap and make old data look like
the future. Monitoring `age(relfrozenxid)` is the cheapest insurance in the
system.

**Index bloat is a separate problem with a separate fix.** B-trees do not
reclaim space from deleted entries as effectively as heaps, and a table that
receives many updates can end up with indexes larger than the data.
`REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY` rebuilds without blocking writes, at the cost
of a second copy of the index on disk during the rebuild.

**`maintenance_work_mem` decides how many index passes a vacuum makes.**
Dead item pointers are collected into memory bounded by that setting; when
it fills, vacuum must stop and scan *every index* before it can continue the
heap. A 64 MB default against a table with tens of millions of dead tuples
means several full index scans per vacuum, which is the usual explanation
for a vacuum that takes hours on a table that should take minutes.

**Vacuum can be cancelled, repeatedly and silently.** An autovacuum holding
a lock that conflicts with a user statement yields — it is cancelled and
logged — so a table receiving frequent `ALTER`s or `TRUNCATE`s can go
weeks without a completed vacuum while `pg_stat_user_tables` shows
autovacuum starting constantly. The tell is `autovacuum_count` barely
moving while the process appears in `pg_stat_activity`.

**`pg_stat_progress_vacuum` is live and underused.** It reports the phase,
`heap_blks_scanned` against `heap_blks_total`, and the number of index
passes so far. During an incident it answers "is this making progress or
not" in one query, which is worth more than any estimate.

## Mission notes

**ex1–ex2** measure bloat and prove what `VACUUM` does to the file size.

**ex3** raises the HOT update ratio, which is the only fix that prevents
bloat rather than cleaning it up.

**ex4** turns the autovacuum formula into a per-table proposal.

**ex5** finds the snapshot holder, the single most valuable query in this
sector.

**ex6** builds the wraparound alert you want to have before you need it.

**ex7** reindexes without blocking; **ex8** computes autovacuum's actual
throughput ceiling from the cost settings.

## Further reading

- [Routine vacuuming](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/routine-vacuuming.html)
  — thresholds, freezing, wraparound, in the manual's own words.
- [`VACUUM`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-vacuum.html) and
  [cost-based delay](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html#RUNTIME-CONFIG-RESOURCE-VACUUM-COST).
- [`pgstattuple`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/pgstattuple.html)
  — exact bloat, at the cost of a scan.
- [HOT updates](https://github.com/postgres/postgres/blob/master/src/backend/access/heap/README.HOT)
  — the design document, short and readable.
- [pg_repack](https://reorg.github.io/pg_repack/) — online table rewrite.

you are rewriting because it is large. On anything busy, use `pg_repack` or
`pg_squeeze`, which do the same work with brief locks.

## Why vacuum sometimes cannot help

`VACUUM` may only remove a dead tuple if no existing snapshot can still see
it. Anything holding an old snapshot pins the horizon for the *whole
database*:

- a transaction left `idle in transaction` by an application that forgot to
  commit;
- a long-running analytical query or a held cursor;
- a replication slot with no consumer, or a standby with
  `hot_standby_feedback = on` running a long query;
- an orphaned prepared transaction (`pg_prepared_xacts`).

The symptom is bloat that grows while autovacuum runs constantly and
achieves nothing. The diagnosis is one query against `pg_stat_activity`,
`pg_replication_slots` and `pg_prepared_xacts`, comparing each holder's xmin
against the current one — ex5 builds it, and it belongs in your monitoring.

## HOT updates: the bloat you can avoid

If an update changes no indexed column *and* the new version fits on the
same page, PostgreSQL performs a **heap-only tuple** update: the new version
is chained to the old one on the same page, and no index entries are
written. That is dramatically cheaper, and the space is reclaimable by
ordinary page pruning without a full vacuum.

Two things break it. Indexing a column that updates frequently — a `status`
that changes five times per order, indexed for a queue — and a page with no
free space. The second is what `fillfactor` addresses:

```sql
ALTER TABLE perf.orders SET (fillfactor = 85);
```

Leave 15% of each page empty so updates have somewhere to go. It costs disk
on an insert-only table and pays for itself many times over on an
update-heavy one. `pg_stat_user_tables.n_tup_hot_upd` against `n_tup_upd`
tells you your current ratio.

## Freezing and the counter that wraps

Transaction ids are 32 bits. Rows older than `autovacuum_freeze_max_age`
(200 million by default) must be frozen or the database will refuse writes
to protect itself. Autovacuum escalates to an "aggressive" vacuum as the age
approaches, and if it never finishes — because it is being cancelled, or the
table is enormous, or a slot is holding the horizon — you eventually get a
shutdown-to-single-user-mode incident that will define your week.

```sql
SELECT relname, age(relfrozenxid) AS xid_age,
       round(100.0 * age(relfrozenxid)
             / current_setting('autovacuum_freeze_max_age')::numeric, 1) AS pct
FROM pg_class JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = relnamespace
WHERE relkind = 'r' AND nspname = 'perf'
ORDER BY age(relfrozenxid) DESC;
```

Anything above 50% deserves attention; above 80% deserves a calendar entry.

## Index bloat is its own problem

A B-tree does not reclaim a deleted entry's space until the whole page
empties, and a page that repeatedly fills and half-empties never merges with
its neighbours. On an update-heavy table the indexes can therefore outgrow
the heap:

```sql
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pgstattuple;
SELECT avg_leaf_density, leaf_fragmentation FROM pgstatindex('perf.orders_pkey');
```

A leaf density near 90 is healthy; near 40 means the index is mostly air.
The online fix is `REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, which builds a second copy
— so you need the disk headroom — and leaves an `INVALID` index behind if
it fails, which your maintenance script must check for and drop.

## Mission set

Ten missions: measure bloat two ways and reconcile them, prove what `VACUUM`
does and does not return to the operating system, raise your HOT update
ratio with `fillfactor` and one dropped index, compute autovacuum thresholds
and propose per-table settings, find the transaction blocking the horizon,
build a wraparound alert, reindex without blocking, and work out how fast
autovacuum is actually allowed to go.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b08_bloat_vacuum_maintenance`

## Worked example — bloat, two ways

```sql
-- cheap, from the stats collector, good enough for monitoring
SELECT n_live_tup, n_dead_tup,
       round(100.0 * n_dead_tup / nullif(n_live_tup + n_dead_tup, 0), 1) AS dead_pct
FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'orders';
--  2000000 | 5910233 | 74.7

-- exact, from a full scan
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pgstattuple;
SELECT table_len, tuple_percent, dead_tuple_percent, free_percent
FROM pgstattuple('perf.orders');
--  704 MB  |  23.1  |  71.8  |  4.6
```

The table holds 164 MB of live data in a 704 MB file. Vacuum will not shrink
that file; it will make the 71.8% reusable, after which the table stops
growing until the workload changes. If you need the 540 MB back — because
the bloat came from a one-off migration that will not recur —
that is a `pg_repack`, not a vacuum.

## Worked example — the transaction holding everything hostage

```sql
SELECT pid, state, xact_start, now() - xact_start AS age,
       backend_xmin, query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE backend_xmin IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY age(backend_xmin) DESC LIMIT 5;
```

```
 pid  | state               | age      | backend_xmin | query
 8123 | idle in transaction | 04:12:38 |    918273645 | SELECT 1
```

Four hours of `idle in transaction` on a connection whose last statement was
`SELECT 1`. Every dead tuple created in the last four hours, in every table
in the database, is unremovable. The fix is in the application — a
connection returned to the pool without commit or rollback — and the
stopgap is `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`, which every production
system should set.

## Common mistakes

- **Running `VACUUM FULL` on a busy table to "fix performance".** It takes
  an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock for the whole rewrite.
- **Assuming `VACUUM` shrinks the file.** It reclaims space for reuse.
- **Tuning autovacuum workers instead of the cost limit.** More workers
  each throttled to a few MB/s is still a few MB/s each.
- **Indexing a column that updates constantly** and wondering why HOT never
  fires.
- **Leaving `fillfactor` at 100 on an update-heavy table.**
- **Ignoring replication slots.** An unused slot is a permanent vacuum
  horizon and, eventually, a full disk.
- **Not setting `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`.**
- **Discovering `age(relfrozenxid)` for the first time during an incident.**

## Interview angle

*"Your biggest table is 800 GB, mostly bloat. What do you do?"*

Answer in order of risk. First, stop the bleeding: find what is holding the
vacuum horizon — idle transactions, replication slots, long queries — because
until that is fixed nothing else helps. Second, make autovacuum able to keep
up on this table specifically: lower the scale factor, raise the cost limit,
and confirm from `pg_stat_progress_vacuum` that it is now completing rather
than being cancelled by lock conflicts. Third, decide whether you need the
disk space back at all: if the workload will refill the free space, vacuum is
enough; if the bloat was a one-off migration, schedule `pg_repack`.

Then the part that separates senior answers: prevention. Raise the HOT
update ratio with `fillfactor` and by dropping indexes on frequently updated
columns, partition the table if the bloat is concentrated in old data that
could be dropped instead of vacuumed, and add monitoring for `n_dead_tup`,
`age(relfrozenxid)` and the oldest `backend_xmin` so the next occurrence is
a ticket rather than an incident.

## Check yourself

1. Why does an `UPDATE` leave a dead tuple behind?
2. Name four things `VACUUM` does.
3. Does `VACUUM` return disk space to the operating system? When?
4. What lock does `VACUUM FULL` take, and what is the online alternative?
5. List four things that can hold back the vacuum horizon.
6. What are the two conditions for a HOT update?
7. What does `fillfactor = 85` buy, and what does it cost?
8. Compute autovacuum's vacuum threshold for a 50-million-row table at
   default settings.
9. How fast is autovacuum allowed to go at default cost settings, roughly?
10. What happens as `age(relfrozenxid)` approaches
    `autovacuum_freeze_max_age`?
11. Why can indexes bloat worse than the table, and what is the online fix?
12. Which two settings would you always set on a production instance to
    protect the vacuum horizon?
13. `n_dead_tup` is high and autovacuum ran ten minutes ago. What do you
    check next?
lessons.fullReading:
# Reading - sql/v3b08_bloat_vacuum_maintenance

## The bargain PostgreSQL made

Most databases implement MVCC with an undo log: the current row lives in
place, and old versions are written to a separate structure that is
discarded when no transaction needs them. Oracle and MySQL's InnoDB work
this way. PostgreSQL instead keeps every version in the table itself,
tagged with the transaction ids that created and destroyed it, and cleans up
afterwards.

The upside is substantial and is why the design has survived: rollback is
free (nothing to undo — the new version simply never becomes visible), there
is no undo log to size or to run out of, readers never block writers, and
the code is simpler. The downside is exactly one thing: someone has to come
back and remove the dead versions, and if nobody does, the table grows
without the data growing.

That "someone" is `VACUUM`, and everything in this sector is about making
sure it runs, that it is allowed to do its job, and that it can keep up.

## What a vacuum pass actually does

A vacuum of one table proceeds in phases you can watch live in
`pg_stat_progress_vacuum`. It scans the heap, consulting the visibility map
to skip pages where every tuple is already known all-visible — which is why
the second vacuum of a mostly-static table is dramatically faster than the
first. On pages it does read, it collects the item pointers of dead tuples
into memory bounded by `maintenance_work_mem`. When that fills, it must stop
and do an index pass for each index, then resume the heap — so a
too-small `maintenance_work_mem` makes vacuum scan every index several times
over, which is the most common reason a vacuum that "should take minutes"
takes hours.

After the index passes it returns to the heap to mark the dead line pointers
reusable, updates the free space map and the visibility map, and finally
attempts to truncate trailing empty pages. That truncation needs an
`ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock, which vacuum will take only if it can get it
immediately and will release the moment anyone else waits — which is why a
busy table's file rarely shrinks even when the tail is empty.

Freezing happens in the same pass. Tuples older than `vacuum_freeze_min_age`
have their `xmin` marked frozen; pages where every tuple is frozen get the
all-frozen bit in the visibility map, which future vacuums skip entirely.
Once `age(relfrozenxid)` exceeds `autovacuum_freeze_max_age`, autovacuum
runs an *aggressive* vacuum that cannot skip pages — the one that takes a
long time on a huge table and that people cancel, which is how wraparound
emergencies are made.

## Why it falls behind

Autovacuum is throttled on purpose. It maintains a cost counter — 1 for a
page found in shared buffers, 2 for a page it must read, 20 for a page it
dirties (`vacuum_cost_page_dirty`) — and when the counter reaches
`autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit` it sleeps for
`autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay`. With the defaults of 200 and 2 ms, and
assuming a mix of hits and dirties, the sustained rate is roughly a few tens
of megabytes per second per worker. On a 2 TB table that is not a tuning
detail, it is the difference between finishing and never finishing.

The knobs that matter, in order: `autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit` (raise it —
1,000 to 3,000 on modern storage is unremarkable),
`autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor` per table (lower it on large tables so
vacuum starts sooner and does less each time),
`maintenance_work_mem` (raise it so the index passes happen once), and only
then `autovacuum_max_workers`, which without a higher cost limit merely
divides the same budget among more processes.

The other failure mode is the horizon. `VACUUM` may remove a dead tuple only
if it is invisible to every snapshot in the cluster, so a single idle
transaction, an abandoned replication slot, or a standby with
`hot_standby_feedback = on` running a four-hour report freezes the horizon
and makes vacuum a no-op that still costs I/O. Two settings prevent most of
this in practice: `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` and, on the
replication side, a monitored bound on slot lag with an alert well before
the disk fills.

## Prevention: HOT, fillfactor, and partitioning

The cheapest bloat is the bloat never created. A heap-only tuple update —
no indexed column changed, and room on the same page — writes no index
entries and can be cleaned by ordinary page pruning without a vacuum at all.
The two levers are physical and logical: `fillfactor` below 100 leaves room
on the page, and *not* indexing volatile columns keeps the update eligible.
A queue table indexed on the `status` column it updates five times per row
is the canonical example of getting this exactly backwards; a partial index
on the one interesting status (V3·B4) is both smaller and less HOT-hostile.

Partitioning changes the problem rather than solving it. Bloat concentrated
in recent data still needs vacuum, but *deletion* of old data becomes
`DROP TABLE` on a partition — instant, no dead tuples, no vacuum — instead of
a `DELETE` that creates millions of them. For time-series and log tables,
that single property is often the strongest argument for partitioning.

## What to schedule, and what to monitor

The maintenance you can actually put in a calendar is short. `ANALYZE` after
every bulk load and migration. A weekly job that reports the top tables by
`n_dead_tup`, by `age(relfrozenxid)` percentage, and by estimated index
bloat. `REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY` for indexes over a size threshold and a
bloat threshold, during whatever passes for a quiet hour. A quarterly review
of per-table autovacuum settings for anything that has grown by an order of
magnitude.

The monitoring is shorter still and matters more: oldest `backend_xmin`
across `pg_stat_activity`, `pg_replication_slots` and `pg_prepared_xacts`;
`age(relfrozenxid)` as a percentage of `autovacuum_freeze_max_age`; and
dead-tuple percentage per table. Three graphs, and you will never meet the
version of this problem that makes the news.

## When not to intervene

When the dead-tuple percentage is stable. A table that sits at 20% dead and
does not grow has reached equilibrium: vacuum is keeping up, the free space
is being reused, and rewriting it buys nothing except a maintenance window
and risk. Bloat is only a problem when it is *growing*, or when it is large
enough that the extra pages are pushing useful data out of cache.

And resist `VACUUM FULL` as a reflex. It is the right tool exactly once —
after a one-off event that will not recur, when you need the disk back, and
when you can take the lock. Every other time, the answer is to make
autovacuum able to keep up, which is the fix that also prevents the next
occurrence.

## The shape of a maintenance week

A workable rhythm, for a system of a few hundred gigabytes. Daily: an
automated report of the top ten tables by dead-tuple percentage and the
oldest snapshot holder, delivered somewhere a human reads it. Weekly: the
runbook query from this sector's challenge, and action on anything at
priority one or two. Monthly: a review of per-table autovacuum settings for
relations that have grown by an order of magnitude, and a look at index
bloat with `pgstatindex` on the largest indexes. Quarterly: a check that
the freeze ages are trending flat rather than up, which is the only signal
that says your vacuum settings are keeping pace with your write rate.

None of that is difficult, and all of it is the sort of work that never
appears on a roadmap. The argument that gets it scheduled is the one this
sector arms you with: a table at 75% dead tuples reads four times as many
bytes for every query, which means every latency number in the system is
paying for it, including the ones the product team cares about. Bloat is not
a database-administration concern that competes with feature work; it is a
multiplier on the cost of every feature already shipped.

The corollary is that these queries belong in the repository, not in
somebody's psql history. A `maintenance/` directory with the runbook, the
horizon query and the freeze-age alert, reviewed like any other code, is
what turns this sector from knowledge into practice.

## Further reading

- [Routine vacuuming](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/routine-vacuuming.html)
- [`VACUUM`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-vacuum.html),
  [`pg_stat_progress_vacuum`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/progress-reporting.html)
- [Vacuum cost delay settings](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html#RUNTIME-CONFIG-RESOURCE-VACUUM-COST)
- [README.HOT](https://github.com/postgres/postgres/blob/master/src/backend/access/heap/README.HOT)
- [pg_repack](https://reorg.github.io/pg_repack/) and
  [pgstattuple](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/pgstattuple.html)

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — measure the bloat, twice

Create some honestly:

```sql
UPDATE perf.orders SET total_cents = total_cents + 1;   -- rewrites every row
UPDATE perf.orders SET total_cents = total_cents - 1;   -- and again
```

Edit `ex1/solution.sql` to return **one row, seven columns** comparing the
cheap estimate with the exact measurement:

| column | source |
| --- | --- |
| `live_tup` | `pg_stat_user_tables.n_live_tup` |
| `dead_tup` | `pg_stat_user_tables.n_dead_tup` |
| `dead_pct_est` | from those two, one decimal |
| `table_mb` | `pg_relation_size`, one decimal |
| `live_mb` | `pgstattuple.tuple_len`, one decimal |
| `dead_pct_exact` | `pgstattuple.dead_tuple_percent`, one decimal |
| `wasted_mb` | `table_mb - live_mb`, one decimal |

**Measurable goal:** `dead_pct_est` and `dead_pct_exact` agree within 10
percentage points, and `wasted_mb` exceeds 100.

Add a comment stating which of the two measurements you would put in a
monitoring dashboard, and why.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3b08_bloat_vacuum_maintenance ex1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

```sql
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pgstattuple;
SELECT * FROM pgstattuple('perf.orders');
```

It returns `table_len`, `tuple_count`, `tuple_len`, `dead_tuple_count`,
`dead_tuple_len`, `free_space` and the derived percentages.

## Hint 2

`pgstattuple` reads the whole table, so it is a diagnostic, not a monitor.
`pg_stat_user_tables` is free and approximate. That contrast is the point of
the comment you have to write.

## Hint 3

Cross join the two sources in a CTE each; both return exactly one row for
one table, so no join key is needed.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Predict the file size before you measure. Two full-table updates create two
dead versions per row, so the file should be roughly three times the live
data — 164 MB of rows in a file near 500 MB. If yours is smaller,
autovacuum got there first, which is itself worth noticing.

## Hint 2

Note that `n_dead_tup` is maintained by the statistics collector and reset
by a stats reset or a crash, so it can disagree with reality in both
directions. `pgstattuple` cannot — it counts. When they disagree by a lot,
believe the expensive one and check when the stats were last reset.

## Hint 3

`pgstattuple_approx` exists and is the middle option: it uses the visibility
map to skip pages, so it is far cheaper than the exact version and much more
accurate than the collector's estimate. Mention it in your comment if you
want the complete answer.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3b08_bloat_vacuum_maintenance / ex1 — estimated bloat versus measured bloat
-- Dashboard: use pg_stat_user_tables (free, approximate, safe to poll).
-- Reach for pgstattuple only when deciding on a rewrite; it scans the table.
-- pgstattuple_approx is the middle ground: skips all-visible pages.
WITH s AS (
  SELECT n_live_tup::numeric AS live_tup, n_dead_tup::numeric AS dead_tup
  FROM pg_stat_user_tables
  WHERE schemaname = 'perf' AND relname = 'orders'
),
p AS (
  SELECT table_len::numeric, tuple_len::numeric, dead_tuple_percent::numeric
  FROM pgstattuple('perf.orders')
)
SELECT s.live_tup::bigint                                       AS live_tup,
       s.dead_tup::bigint                                       AS dead_tup,
       round(s.dead_tup / nullif(s.live_tup + s.dead_tup, 0) * 100, 1)
                                                                AS dead_pct_est,
       round(p.table_len / 1024 / 1024, 1)                      AS table_mb,
       round(p.tuple_len / 1024 / 1024, 1)                      AS live_mb,
       round(p.dead_tuple_percent, 1)                           AS dead_pct_exact,
       round((p.table_len - p.tuple_len) / 1024 / 1024, 1)      AS wasted_mb
FROM s CROSS JOIN p;
